In a multi-package project, each package has its own entry in packageDirectories with its own dependencies array. The order of entries determines dependency resolution. Correctly structured sfdx-project.json is required for 'sf package version create' to work.

topics.question: Unlocked packages as a migration path from org-based to package-based development
topics.answer: Unlocked packages are the recommended intermediate step from org-based to fully package-based development. They impose package structure (components must be explicitly included) but do not require a namespace or ISV licensing. Migration path: (1) Identify a bounded domain of metadata (e.g., all Account-related customizations). (2) Extract those components into a package directory. (3) Create the unlocked package and generate a version. (4) Install the package in target orgs instead of deploying raw metadata. Prerequisites: source control with SF DX project format, Dev Hub enabled, team trained on CLI package commands. Start with a small, low-risk domain to build confidence before migrating the full org.

objectives.title: Describe methods to ensure delivery of quality code

topics.question: Defining Salesforce Apex and LWC coding standards
topics.answer: Apex standards: use a trigger handler framework (one trigger per object, handler class with separate methods per event). Bulkify all DML and SOQL (no SOQL/DML in loops). Use 'with sharing' by default (explicit sharing model on every class). Naming conventions: TriggerHandler_Object, Service classes, Selector classes for SOQL. Document public methods with JSDoc-style comments. LWC standards: component per concern, no direct DOM manipulation outside @track properties, use wire for data, no hardcoded IDs. Enforce standards via: code review checklist, PR templates, static analysis rules in CI pipeline.

topics.question: Pull request review process for Salesforce development
topics.answer: A PR review ensures code quality before it reaches the integration branch. Reviewers should check: (1) No SOQL/DML in loops. (2) Proper bulkification. (3) Unit tests with meaningful assertions (not just coverage). (4) Sharing model declared on every class. (5) No hardcoded IDs or org-specific values. (6) Metadata dependencies included (e.g., custom labels, custom settings). (7) Destructive changes documented and intentional. Required approvals: at minimum 1 peer reviewer + tech lead for major changes. PRs gate CI execution: CI pipeline runs only when PR is opened or updated, ensuring validation before merge. Failed CI blocks merge.

topics.question: PMD and Salesforce Code Analyzer for Apex static analysis
topics.answer: PMD: open-source static analysis tool with Apex rule sets. Rules enforced: no SOQL in loops (ApexSOQLInjection, AvoidSoqlInLoops), no DML in loops (AvoidDmlStatementsInLoops), empty catch blocks, unused variables, overly complex methods. Fast to run, integrates with CI. Salesforce Code Analyzer (scanner): built on PMD but adds ESLint (LWC), RetireJS (JS dependencies), and Graph Engine for dataflow analysis (detects SOQL injection, XSS). More comprehensive but slower. Use PMD for fast CI gate on Apex; use Code Analyzer for scheduled deep analysis (weekly security scans). Configure severity thresholds: fail build on critical/high violations, report-only on medium/low.

topics.question: Integrating static analysis into the CI pipeline
topics.answer: Two governance modes: (1) Hard gate: build FAILS if static analysis finds violations above a threshold (e.g., any 'Critical' PMD violation blocks merge). This enforces zero tolerance for the worst patterns. (2) Reporting-only gate: violations are reported as warnings in the PR but do not block merge; used during team onboarding or for lower-severity rules. Best practice: start with reporting-only to establish a baseline, then progressively tighten the threshold as the team addresses violations. Avoid adding a hard gate on a codebase with hundreds of existing violations - it will block all work. Use a 'ratchet' approach: fail only on NEW violations introduced in the PR, not pre-existing ones.

objectives.title: Describe capabilities, limitations, and considerations of Metadata and Tooling APIs

topics.question: Metadata API capabilities for deployment
topics.answer: Metadata API supports deploying and retrieving most Salesforce metadata types (custom objects, fields, Apex classes, triggers, flows, layouts, reports, etc.). Deployment is asynchronous: submit a deploy request, poll for status. Supports deployment of up to 10,000 files per deploy. Can be used via SF CLI (which wraps the API), third-party tools, or direct API calls. Supports test execution options (RunLocalTests, RunSpecifiedTests, RunAllTests, NoTestRun) at deploy time. Key capability: can deploy to any connected Salesforce org, not just point-to-point like Change Sets.

topics.question: Metadata API limitations: unsupported metadata types
topics.answer: Not all Salesforce metadata is deployable via Metadata API. Examples of limited or unsupported types: (1) Some standard objects' settings (cannot deploy certain standard field configurations). (2) Reports and dashboards: can deploy report type metadata but not report data/results. (3) Territory management configurations. (4) Salesforce CPQ metadata (some types). (5) Experience Cloud (Community) site content. (6) Certain custom settings values (the type is deployable, but data requires separate approach). Manual deployment candidates: connected app OAuth secrets, named credentials with secrets, certain org-wide email settings, some platform encryption settings.

topics.question: Tooling API vs. Metadata API for deployment
topics.answer: Tooling API is designed for incremental, real-time development operations: compile individual Apex classes synchronously, retrieve code coverage for specific classes, query metadata for IDE tooling. Use Tooling API when: you need synchronous Apex compilation feedback, you are building a developer tooling integration, or you need to query metadata attributes not exposed via Metadata API. Use Metadata API when: you are deploying a set of components as part of a release (full or delta deployments), or running tests as part of a CI validation. SF CLI uses both under the hood: push/retrieve uses Metadata API; language server uses Tooling API.

topics.question: Deploying metadata with dependencies
topics.answer: Cross-component references must be respected in deployments. If Class A references Class B, both must be deployed together (or Class B must already exist in the target org). Common dependency failures: deploying a Flow that references a custom field before the custom field is deployed; deploying an Apex class that references a custom label not included in the package. Solutions: (1) Deploy all components in a single deployment package (safest). (2) Use a two-pass deployment: deploy foundational components first (objects, fields, classes), then deploy the components that depend on them. (3) Use tools like Copado that automatically resolve dependency order.

topics.question: Destructive changes in Salesforce deployments
topics.answer: To delete metadata components via Metadata API, include a destructiveChanges.xml file (post-deploy deletions) or destructiveChangesPre.xml (pre-deploy deletions) in the deployment package alongside a package.xml. destructiveChanges.xml lists components to delete after the additive changes are deployed. destructiveChangesPre.xml deletes components BEFORE additive changes are applied (use when you are replacing a component that conflicts with a new one). Limitation: cannot combine destructive changes and additive changes in a Change Set deployment (CLI does not have this limitation). Risk: once deleted, metadata is gone (no native rollback); always backup before destructive deployments.

topics.question: Deployment rollback strategies
topics.answer: Salesforce has no native one-click rollback for Metadata API deployments. Mitigation patterns: (1) Backup before deployment: retrieve current production metadata and store it as a 'rollback package' in source control. (2) Destructive rollback: if new code/config caused issues, deploy the previous version of the metadata. (3) Version control revert: revert the Git tag to the previous release and redeploy. (4) Feature flags: disable a feature via custom metadata or permission set without redeployment. (5) Quick deploy of previous validation: if you validated the previous version recently, quick deploy it back. Document rollback procedures in the deployment runbook and test them.

objectives.title: Describe approaches to handle pre and post-deployment steps

topics.question: Deployment runbook design
topics.answer: A deployment runbook is a step-by-step document that ensures consistent, error-free production deployments. Contents: (1) Pre-deployment checklist (steps to execute before the deployment starts). (2) Deployment steps (commands to run, order, expected outputs). (3) Validation steps (smoke tests to run immediately after deployment). (4) Rollback procedures (what to do if deployment fails or causes issues). (5) Communication plan (who to notify at each step). (6) Go/no-go decision criteria. Runbooks should be version-controlled alongside the deployment package they describe. The Release Manager owns the runbook; the deployment team follows it.

topics.question: Pre-deployment checklist
topics.answer: Before starting a production deployment: (1) Communicate maintenance window to users and stakeholders. (2) Disable automation that could interfere: deactivate Flows, Process Builders, or workflow rules that would trigger on test/deployment records. (3) Pause scheduled batch jobs that could run during deployment. (4) Back up current production metadata (retrieve to a 'pre-deploy' branch in source control). (5) Verify validation run passed (or run a fresh validation). (6) Confirm all approval gates are complete (CAB approved, UAT signed off). (7) Ensure rollback package is ready. (8) Notify the support team to be on standby.

topics.question: Managing user access before and during a deployment window
topics.answer: For high-risk deployments, consider: (1) Enabling a maintenance page or message (Salesforce does not have a native maintenance mode; use a custom login flow or outbound messaging). (2) Restricting access to specific profiles by temporarily adding an IP restriction or login hours restriction to force users out. (3) For truly zero-impact deployments: use feature flags (custom metadata or permission sets) to deploy code without exposing it to users, then activate after deployment. (4) After deployment: re-enable login access and notify users. User access management steps should be in the deployment runbook with the specific profiles/permission sets to modify.

topics.question: Post-deployment steps
topics.answer: Immediately after a successful deployment: (1) Re-enable deactivated automations (Flows, Process Builders, workflow rules). (2) Assign new permission sets to the appropriate users or public groups. (3) Activate new record types and update page layout assignments. (4) Run post-deployment data scripts (seed lookup data, update custom setting values, assign roles). (5) Execute smoke tests / validation scripts to confirm key business processes work. (6) Re-schedule batch jobs that were paused. (7) Notify stakeholders that deployment is complete and the system is available. Document all post-deployment steps in the runbook with expected completion time per step.

topics.question: Post-deployment data migrations
topics.answer: Data migrations are required when: (1) A new field is introduced that must be populated for existing records (backfill). (2) Records must be reassigned to new record types. (3) A new object is introduced and existing data must be migrated from another object. (4) Custom setting or custom metadata values must be set in production (cannot deploy via package if values are environment-specific). Tools: Data Loader (manual, GUI), SF CLI data commands (scriptable), Batch Apex (for complex transformations), or ETL tools (MuleSoft, Informatica). Always run data migrations in a staging sandbox first. Have a rollback script for data migrations.

topics.question: Reports, dashboards, connected apps, and custom settings: Metadata API limitations and manual candidates
topics.answer: Reports: Report Type metadata is deployable; actual report definitions are deployable via Metadata API but can be fragile if referenced fields/objects differ. Report subscriptions and scheduled reports are not deployable. Dashboards: similar to reports - dashboard XML is deployable but running user and schedule settings are manual. Connected Apps: the metadata is deployable but OAuth secrets (consumer key/secret) must be reconfigured manually in the target org. Custom Settings: the object type is deployable; the actual data/records within Custom Settings must be deployed separately (via Data Loader, CLI data commands, or included in package as Default values for Hierarchy type). These items should be explicitly listed in the deployment runbook as manual steps.

objectives.title: Describe approaches to manage and deploy technical reference data

topics.question: Distinguishing technical reference data from transactional data
topics.answer: Technical reference data: configuration stored as object records that drives application behavior. Examples: picklist value sets (if stored as custom metadata), integration endpoints in Custom Settings, feature flag records in Custom Metadata Types, tax rates in a custom object used by code logic. Transactional data: business records created by users/integrations (Accounts, Opportunities, Cases). Technical reference data must be deployed as part of the release process because code depends on it existing correctly. Transactional data is never deployed between environments (it is seeded for testing, masked for privacy). The boundary: if your code queries it, it is reference data and must be managed as a deployment artifact.

topics.question: Custom Metadata Types vs. Custom Settings for storing reference data
topics.answer: Custom Metadata Types (CMT): records are metadata - they can be included in packages, deployed via Metadata API, and version-controlled. Support SOQL queries in Apex. Deployable across environments as part of a deployment package. Best for configuration that must be consistent across orgs and environment-agnostic or environment-specific via named records. Custom Settings: object data, NOT metadata. Cannot be deployed via standard Metadata API (only the object structure is deployable; the records require Data Loader or a post-deploy script). Support Hierarchy type (override at org, profile, user level). Use CMT when deploying configuration values is part of the release. Use Custom Settings for data that may differ per user/profile.

topics.question: Managing environment-specific reference data using Custom Metadata with deployment-time overrides
topics.answer: For environment-specific configuration (e.g., different integration endpoints per environment): Create CMT records with an environment identifier field (e.g., Environment__c = 'Production', 'Staging', 'Dev'). Apex code queries the correct record at runtime based on a deterministic check. Alternatively, create separate CMT records per environment and deploy only the relevant record to each org. For Custom Settings: use a post-deployment script to set the correct values per environment (automate this in the CI/CD pipeline post-deploy step). Custom Settings with manual updates are error-prone; prefer CMT where possible.

topics.question: Deploying reference data using Salesforce CLI data commands, Data Loader, or package records
topics.answer: Salesforce CLI data commands ('sf data upsert bulk', 'sf data import tree'): scriptable, integrates with CI/CD pipeline, supports JSON/CSV, good for repeatable seeding of CMT records or Custom Setting values. Best for automating post-deploy data steps. Data Loader: GUI-based, batch upserts/inserts, uses CSV files. Good for one-time or infrequent data migrations. Managed/Unlocked package records: Custom Metadata records can be included directly in a package and installed with it - the cleanest approach for CMT configuration. Unlocked packages can ship CMT records as part of the package version. Trade-off: package records require package version creation for every config change; CLI scripts are faster for frequent config updates.

objectives.title: Describe and recommend an appropriate testing methodology

topics.question: Testing pyramid for Salesforce
topics.answer: Unit tests (base of pyramid, most numerous): Apex unit tests, individual class/trigger behavior, fast, isolated, developer-owned. Integration tests (middle): test interactions between Apex components, flows, and external systems; run in a sandbox; QA-owned. System tests: end-to-end business process testing in a production-like environment; test the full stack from UI to database; QA and BA-owned. UAT (top, fewest): business stakeholder validation of acceptance criteria; human-driven; business-owned. The pyramid shape means most tests should be at the unit level (cheap, fast) with progressively fewer as you go up (expensive, slow). Invert the pyramid and you get slow, brittle test suites.

topics.question: Shift-left testing strategy for Salesforce
topics.answer: Shift-left means moving testing earlier in the development lifecycle: developers write unit tests before or alongside code (TDD/BDD), static analysis runs on every commit (not just before release), integration tests run in CI on every PR (not just in UAT). Benefits: defects found earlier cost less to fix (the 'rule of 10x' - a bug found in dev costs 1x; in UAT costs 10x; in production costs 100x). Shift-left in Salesforce: run Apex tests in scratch org during development; use Apex test frameworks (SFDC Unit Test); integrate PMD/Code Analyzer in PR pipeline; require QA sandbox validation before UAT, not after feature code freeze.

topics.question: Recommending test methodology for an org with complex automation and integrations
topics.answer: For complex orgs: (1) Apex unit tests cover all trigger and service logic (bulkified, positive and negative paths). (2) Apex integration tests cover cross-object behavior and flow invocations from Apex. (3) Flow and process builder tests in sandbox (Salesforce does not currently have a robust automated flow test framework beyond Apex invocations). (4) End-to-end tests using Provar or Copado Robotic Testing for critical business processes (Order-to-Cash, Lead-to-Opportunity). (5) Manual exploratory testing for edge cases and new UI features. (6) Integration endpoint mocking for external system calls. Balance automation (reliable, repeatable) with strategic manual testing (adaptive, exploratory).

topics.question: Regression test strategy for a high-volume, frequently-released Salesforce org
topics.answer: Automate: high-value, stable, frequently-run tests (core business process flows, critical Apex logic, standard object interactions). These are the tests that, if they fail, mean a release is not ready. Test manually: new features with unstable UIs, edge cases that are rare but high-impact, exploratory testing of new functionality. Deprioritize: low-risk configuration changes (report layouts, email templates) that do not interact with code. Regression suite management: review and prune the suite quarterly - remove tests for deprecated features, add tests for new high-risk areas. Keep the automated suite under 30 minutes to maintain CI pipeline speed.

topics.question: Browser/UI automation testing for Salesforce Lightning
topics.answer: UI automation tools for Salesforce Lightning: Selenium (open-source, requires significant Salesforce-specific framework work, Lightning-specific selectors are complex), Provar (purpose-built for Salesforce, no-code/low-code test creation, built-in Lightning support), Copado Robotic Testing / Agentia Testing (Robot Framework-based, AI-assisted test creation, integrates with Copado pipelines). When to introduce: after the core Apex unit test layer is stable; when manual regression of critical UI flows takes more than 2-3 hours per release; when release frequency increases to weekly or more. Start with 5-10 high-value end-to-end scenarios rather than trying to automate everything immediately.

objectives.title: Describe the appropriate test execution methodology and coverage requirements

topics.question: Code coverage calculation in Salesforce
topics.answer: Org-wide coverage = (total executable lines covered by at least one test) / (total executable lines in the org). Calculated across ALL Apex in the org, not per-class. A coverage check is triggered: at every production deployment that includes Apex (if RunLocalTests or higher is specified), when you manually run tests. How to interpret: if org-wide is 74%, you cannot deploy any Apex to production. If it is 80%, you have a 5% buffer. Coverage per class: shown in Developer Console and SF CLI test output. Classes with 0% coverage are the biggest risk - one such class added to a high-coverage org can drag the overall percentage below 75%.

topics.question: Apex test execution options
topics.answer: Three main options: RunLocalTests: runs all tests in the org EXCEPT those from managed packages. Most common for production deployments. RunAllTests: runs ALL tests including managed package tests. Use when managed package tests contribute to coverage or when a full regression is required. RunSpecifiedTests: runs only the test classes you specify. Fastest option for CI on a specific feature. Coverage implications: RunSpecifiedTests only counts coverage for the classes touched by those specific tests - org-wide coverage may appear low. For production deployment with RunSpecifiedTests, Salesforce validates that the DEPLOYED components have at least 75% coverage from those specified tests, not org-wide.

topics.question: RunSpecifiedTests vs RunLocalTests vs RunAllTests
topics.answer: RunSpecifiedTests: fastest, runs only named test classes, coverage counted only for classes covered by those tests, used in CI for targeted validation of a feature branch. Coverage requirement: 75% for each deployed Apex class. RunLocalTests: runs all non-managed-package tests, comprehensive, used for production deployments, coverage requirement is 75% org-wide. RunAllTests: runs everything including managed packages, slowest, can time out in large orgs with slow managed package tests. Use RunAllTests only when managed package tests are required for coverage and in non-time-sensitive full regression scenarios.

topics.question: When Salesforce requires RunLocalTests or higher for production deployments
topics.answer: Salesforce requires test execution (at minimum RunLocalTests) for any production deployment that includes Apex classes or triggers. Deployments that do NOT include Apex (metadata-only: layouts, fields, custom objects, reports) can use NoTestRun, which skips test execution and is much faster. For CI validation deployments (not production): you can use NoTestRun or RunSpecifiedTests to keep pipeline duration short. For production: if you use RunSpecifiedTests, you must specify tests that cover all deployed Apex components at 75%. If you skip tests using NoTestRun on a production Apex deployment, the deployment is rejected.

topics.question: Managing test execution time in large orgs
topics.answer: Strategies to keep CI pipeline duration acceptable: (1) RunSpecifiedTests in CI (not RunLocalTests); map test classes to the components they cover in a manifest. (2) Parallel test execution: Salesforce runs tests in parallel by default; avoid test anti-patterns that break parallelism (shared static state, SeeAllData=true). (3) Test isolation: ensure @testSetup is used correctly so data is created efficiently. (4) Identify and fix slow test classes (Developer Console, Tooling API coverage reports). (5) For production, run RunLocalTests in a separate job while feature validation jobs use RunSpecifiedTests. Target: CI validation under 20 minutes; full regression under 60 minutes.

topics.question: Test coverage degradation risk in package-based development
topics.answer: In package-based development, each package has its own test classes. When a package is installed in an org, its tests contribute to org-wide coverage. Risk: if a dependent package is not tested (RunLocalTests excludes managed package tests from coverage calculation), and that package contains untested Apex, coverage may appear higher than it actually is. Ensure dependent package tests run and are counted: use RunAllTests when managed packages contribute significant Apex. In unlocked package development: each package must independently maintain 75% coverage for its own Apex components. Use 'sf apex run test' scoped to the package directory during CI to validate package-level coverage.

objectives.title: Describe and recommend a unified test data strategy

topics.question: Unified test data strategy design
topics.answer: A unified test data strategy provides consistent, representative, and secure test data across all environments. Components: (1) Data inventory: catalog what data types are needed per environment tier (unit tests need minimal data; UAT needs production-representative data). (2) Data generation: use test data factories for unit tests; use masked production data for QA/UAT sandboxes. (3) Data governance: never use real PII in non-production environments; enforce data masking policies. (4) Data lifecycle: align data refresh cycles with sandbox refresh cycles. (5) Data seeding automation: scripts that reseed environments post-refresh. Goal: any developer or tester can onboard to any environment and have the data they need without manual setup.

topics.question: Partial Copy sandbox and test data seeding
topics.answer: A Partial Copy sandbox includes production metadata plus a sample of production data (configured via sandbox template - up to 10,000 records per selected object). This makes it the ideal source of representative data for QA testing without the cost and refresh limitations of a Full Copy sandbox. Use it for: QA test execution where realistic data relationships are needed. For seeding lower environments (Developer sandboxes, scratch orgs): export data from the Partial Copy sandbox using CLI data export commands, apply masking to remove PII, then import into lower environments using CLI data import. This creates a consistent, representative dataset that developers and QA can rely on.

topics.question: Data masking and anonymization strategies for Salesforce test environments
topics.answer: Data masking transforms production PII into realistic but fake data before it is placed in non-production environments. Techniques: (1) Substitution: replace real names/emails with fake ones (e.g., John Smith > Test User 1). (2) Shuffling: shuffle values within a column so field types remain realistic but are no longer associated with real people. (3) Pseudonymization: replace identifiable values with tokens, keeping a mapping table in a secure location. Tools: Salesforce Data Mask (native AppExchange tool), Informatica, or custom Apex batch scripts. Masking should happen BEFORE a Full Copy or Partial Copy sandbox is given to non-privileged users. Document which fields require masking in a data classification policy.

topics.question: Test data lifecycle management
topics.answer: Test data becomes stale when: sandboxes are refreshed (data is overwritten or cleared), the production data model changes (new required fields, changed relationships), business processes change (old test scenarios no longer reflect real flows). Prevention: (1) Store test data seeding scripts in source control alongside code - they are updated when the schema changes. (2) Automate post-sandbox-refresh data seeding as part of the sandbox refresh pipeline. (3) Review test data quarterly against current business processes. (4) Tag test data records with a creation timestamp and scenario name for easy identification and cleanup. Stale test data leads to false-passing tests and QA frustration.

objectives.title: Analyze and explain use cases and considerations for managed, unmanaged, and unlocked packages

topics.question: Managed package use cases
topics.answer: Managed packages are used by ISVs (Independent Software Vendors) to distribute Salesforce applications on AppExchange. Key characteristics: namespace required, IP protected (code is obfuscated/locked), subscriber upgrade lifecycle managed by the publisher (1GP or 2GP), installed via AppExchange or install URL. Limitations post-release: cannot remove fields, objects, or classes from a released managed package version (they become deprecated); cannot change API names of existing components. Use managed packages when: you are building a product for external customer distribution, IP protection is required, and you need a formal subscriber upgrade model.

topics.question: Unlocked package use cases
topics.answer: Unlocked packages (2GP) are used for internal modular deployment within a customer's own orgs. No namespace required (unless desired). Source-driven: components are managed in source control, packages are built from that source. Components are not IP-protected. Ideal for: decomposing a large org into manageable modules (Account domain, Billing domain, etc.), enabling independent release of different org areas, standardizing shared components across multiple internal orgs. Unlike managed packages, you can evolve the package more freely (with caveats around destructive changes in subscriber orgs).

topics.question: Choosing between managed, unmanaged, and unlocked packages
topics.answer: Managed: choose when building an AppExchange product for external customers, IP protection needed, formal upgrade lifecycle required. Unmanaged: choose for one-time template distribution (e.g., a starter kit), development samples, or when you want the installer to own and modify the code freely with no upgrade path. Unlocked: choose for internal delivery, modular org architecture, source-driven development, when upgrade-ability with some flexibility is needed. Key question: will subscribers upgrade this package over time? If yes, choose managed (ISV) or unlocked (internal). If it is a one-time install with no future upgrades, unmanaged may suffice.

topics.question: Package versioning: major vs. minor versions and semantics
topics.answer: Package versions follow semantic versioning (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH.BUILD). MAJOR: significant release with potentially breaking changes (new dependencies, removed components). Subscribers must manually opt in. MINOR: new features added backward-compatibly; subscribers can upgrade with lower risk. PATCH: bug fixes; lowest risk upgrade. BUILD: internal build number (auto-incremented). In Salesforce 2GP: 'sf package version create' generates a new version; 'Released' flag marks a version as production-ready and immutable. Beta versions can be used for testing before releasing. Key: once a package version is released, it cannot be changed - create a new version for any changes.

topics.question: Package dependencies: defining and managing dependencies between unlocked packages
topics.answer: In a multi-package project, packages can depend on other packages. Dependencies are declared in sfdx-project.json under the 'dependencies' array for each package directory. Dependencies specify: package ID and version number. At install time, dependent packages must be installed first. Circular dependencies are not allowed - maintain a clean dependency hierarchy (foundational packages at the bottom, application packages at the top). Use a package dependency graph to visualize and manage complexity. CI pipeline should build and validate packages in dependency order. Changes to a foundational package require re-testing all packages that depend on it.

topics.question: Namespace considerations for managed vs. unlocked packages
topics.answer: Managed packages: a namespace is REQUIRED. The namespace prefix is added to all component API names (e.g., MyNamespace__MyField__c). This prevents conflicts with subscriber org components but makes component names verbose and harder to change. Unlocked packages: a namespace is OPTIONAL. Without a namespace, component API names remain the same as in source control. With a namespace, same rules as managed packages apply. Implications: namespaced packages are harder to migrate to a different namespace later. Choose namespace for: multi-subscriber distribution (managed) or when you want component isolation across orgs. Namespace decisions are essentially permanent - plan carefully.

topics.question: Deprecated components and subscriber impact during package upgrades
topics.answer: In managed packages, you cannot delete a component from a released version - you must deprecate it. Deprecation marks the component as 'do not use' but it remains installed in subscriber orgs. Subscribers see deprecation warnings in setup. Impact: deprecated Apex classes still count toward governor limits; deprecated fields still occupy the subscriber's field limit. Subscribers should migrate away from deprecated components before the publisher removes support. For unlocked packages: you can remove components in newer versions, but removal will fail in subscriber orgs that have customizations or data dependencies on the removed component. Always communicate deprecation/removal with a migration guide.

objectives.title: Apply sandbox strategy to a specific release plan

topics.question: Mapping a sandbox environment strategy to a release plan with multiple parallel streams
topics.answer: For three parallel streams (e.g., Feature A, Feature B, Hotfix): each stream gets its own Developer or Developer Pro sandbox for isolated development. All streams merge into a shared Integration sandbox for combined testing. Integration builds deploy to a QA sandbox (Partial Copy) for QA sign-off. After QA, changes promote to UAT sandbox (Partial Copy) for business validation. After UAT, all approved streams are bundled and deployed to Staging (Full Copy) for pre-production validation. Finally, production deployment. The key is that streams are isolated in development but converge progressively as they move up the pipeline.

topics.question: Staging sandbox role in the release plan
topics.answer: The Staging sandbox (Full Copy) serves as the final pre-production gate. Its role: (1) Validate the complete deployment package in a production-equivalent environment (same metadata, same data volume, same integrations). (2) Execute performance and load testing to identify governor limit issues at scale. (3) Provide a final UAT opportunity for stakeholders who need to sign off on production-equivalent behavior. (4) Validate rollback procedures in a safe environment before production. Staging must be refreshed from production after every production release to maintain parity. It should never be used for development - treat it as read-only except for authorized release deployments.

topics.question: Hotfix stream integration into an ongoing release plan
topics.answer: When a critical production bug occurs mid-release cycle: (1) Branch the hotfix from the production Git tag (not from the in-progress release branch). (2) Fix and test in the dedicated hotfix sandbox. (3) Fast-track through Staging if time permits (or skip to production with documented risk acceptance if truly critical). (4) Deploy to production. (5) Immediately merge the hotfix changes back to the main/develop branch and all in-flight feature branches. (6) Redeploy to Integration/QA/UAT sandboxes to ensure the hotfix is included in the next regular release. Conflict resolution: if the hotfix conflicts with in-flight feature work, resolve the conflict in the feature branch, not in the hotfix branch.

topics.question: Integrating a training environment into the release plan
topics.answer: The training sandbox (typically Developer Pro or Partial Copy) is used for end-user training on new features before they go to production. When to refresh: refresh it after a UAT sign-off so that training users can practice on the exact features about to go live, but not so close to the production deployment that training is disrupted by last-minute changes. Isolation: training sandbox must NEVER receive in-progress development changes - it should only receive officially released (UAT-approved) feature sets. Data ownership: the training team owns the data in the training sandbox; use representative but fake records. The Release Manager should coordinate the training sandbox refresh as part of the release calendar.

objectives.title: Describe and recommend an appropriate release management strategy

topics.question: Release management process: change freeze, go/no-go, release notes, post-release monitoring
topics.answer: Change freeze: a period (typically 1-2 weeks before a major release) during which no new features can be introduced to the release pipeline; only bug fixes and critical changes allowed. Go/no-go criteria: defined checklist that must be fully satisfied before production deployment is authorized (e.g., all UAT test cases passed, no open P1 defects, CAB approved, rollback plan documented). Release notes: a document for stakeholders describing what is changing, any user-facing behavior changes, and what was fixed. Post-release monitoring: monitor key metrics for 24-48 hours post-deployment (error logs, support ticket volume, key business process completion rates, Apex exception emails).

topics.question: Release cadence selection
topics.answer: Continuous delivery (CD): deploy to production whenever a feature is ready (after automated gates pass); requires high test automation maturity and feature flag capability. Best for product teams with low change risk and high confidence in automation. Sprint-based: deploy at the end of each sprint (every 2 weeks); predictable, manageable, good for teams transitioning from waterfall. Most common in Salesforce implementations. Scheduled major release: quarterly or bi-annual large bundled releases; lowest risk appetite, highest governance overhead; common in regulated industries. Match cadence to business risk tolerance, support team capacity, and change management capability.

topics.question: Coordinating a release across multiple Salesforce orgs
topics.answer: Multi-org releases require: (1) Shared release calendar with deployment windows for each org. (2) Dependency sequencing - if Org A provides an API consumed by Org B, deploy Org A first. (3) Shared reference data synchronization - if both orgs share reference data (e.g., product catalog), synchronize this data before deploying the code that uses it. (4) Coordinated rollback - define whether rolling back one org requires rolling back all orgs (usually yes, to maintain integration compatibility). (5) Cross-org regression testing - validate integrations between orgs post-deployment. A Release Manager or Release Train Engineer must own cross-org coordination.

topics.question: Feature flagging and dark launching in Salesforce
topics.answer: Feature flagging: deploy code to production but keep it inactive until a flag is switched on. In Salesforce: use Custom Metadata Type records (e.g., Feature_Flag__mdt with an IsActive__c checkbox) queried by Apex at runtime. Use Permission Sets to control which users see new UI elements (Lightning components check for permissions). Dark launching: code is deployed and running (for load testing, logging, side effects) but its results are not exposed to users. Benefits: decouple deployment from release (deploy on Tuesday, activate feature on Friday without redeployment), instant rollback by flipping a flag, gradual rollout to specific user groups. Avoid using Custom Settings for feature flags - prefer CMT for deployability.

topics.question: Blue-green and canary release patterns applied to Salesforce
topics.answer: Blue-green: maintain two identical production environments (blue = current live, green = new version deployed and validated). Switch traffic from blue to green when ready; rollback is instant by switching back. In Salesforce, true blue-green is not natively supported (there is only one production org). Approximate it with: feature flags + permission set-controlled activation (green is deployed but only accessible to a test group; blue behavior remains for all others). Canary release: gradually roll out a feature to a small percentage of users, monitor, then expand. Implement in Salesforce with: permission set assignments (assign the 'new feature' permission set to 5% of users first), custom metadata flags with user/profile conditions, or Experience Cloud audience targeting.

objectives.title: Explain the implications of incorporating requests directly in a production environment

topics.question: Implications of making configuration changes directly in production
topics.answer: Direct production changes: (1) Break the source of truth - source control no longer reflects what is in production. (2) Cause configuration drift - future deployments from source control may overwrite or conflict with the direct change. (3) Bypass quality gates - no peer review, no CI validation, no automated tests. (4) Create audit gaps - depending on tool, the change may not be traceable to a business requirement or approver. (5) Risk downstream sandboxes becoming out-of-sync - lower environments do not know about the change until it is back-propagated. In regulated environments, direct production changes may violate SOX, HIPAA, or other compliance controls.

topics.question: Urgent production change request under pressure
topics.answer: When stakeholders demand an immediate production change, evaluate: (1) What is the actual risk of NOT making the change right now? (quantify business impact: revenue at risk, users blocked, compliance violation). (2) What is the risk of making the change directly? (configuration drift, missed dependencies, no rollback path). (3) Is the change truly so urgent it cannot go through even a fast-track process (1-2 hours)? (4) If proceeding directly: document the reason, get verbal/email approval from a designated authority, make the minimal change needed, and commit to retrieving and back-propagating the change within 24 hours. Never let urgency become the default path to production.

topics.question: Emergency change process design
topics.answer: A sanctioned emergency change process allows fast production changes while preserving governance. Key elements: (1) Pre-defined trigger criteria (what qualifies as an emergency). (2) Pre-authorized approvers (a list of individuals who can authorize emergency changes without a full CAB meeting). (3) Streamlined process: developer makes change in hotfix sandbox > gets approval from pre-authorized approver > deploys to production > documents the change in the change management system within 4 hours. (4) Mandatory post-change steps: retrieve from production, commit to source control, back-propagate to lower environments, complete formal change record. (5) Post-incident review: analyze root cause and how to prevent recurrence.

objectives.title: Explain implications of direct production changes and steps to integrate into ALM

topics.question: Steps to integrate a direct production change back into the ALM pipeline
topics.answer: Process: (1) Retrieve the changed metadata from production using 'sf project retrieve start' targeting the specific components that were changed. (2) Create a branch in Git (e.g., 'hotfix/direct-prod-change-YYYYMMDD'). (3) Commit the retrieved metadata to the branch with a message explaining what was changed, why, and who authorized it. (4) Create a PR for peer review - even though the change is already in production, code review documents the change for future reference. (5) Merge to main branch after review. (6) Deploy from source control to all lower sandboxes (Integration, QA, UAT, Staging) so they are in sync with production. (7) Update the change management ticket.

topics.question: Detecting and reconciling configuration drift
topics.answer: Drift detection approaches: (1) Tools: Gearset, Copado Org Differences, Salesforce DevOps Center change tracking, or custom scripts comparing Metadata API retrieval outputs from production vs. source control. (2) Manual: periodic 'org compare' runs that diff production against the main branch in source control. (3) Proactive: enable source-tracking sandboxes or scratch orgs to detect uncommitted changes in development. Reconciliation process: identify the delta (what is in production but not in source control, and vice versa), evaluate each delta item (intentional change or drift?), retrieve intentional changes and commit them, deploy missing source-controlled changes to production through the normal pipeline.

topics.question: Governance controls to prevent unauthorized direct production changes
topics.answer: Controls: (1) Production org lockdown: restrict 'Modify All Data' and 'Customize Application' permissions to a service account used only by the CI/CD pipeline. Remove these permissions from admin profiles. (2) Change approval workflows: require all changes to be submitted via a change management system (ServiceNow, Jira) before any deployment is authorized. (3) Audit trail monitoring: configure Salesforce Event Monitoring to alert on direct logins to production and configuration changes not made by the CI/CD service account. (4) Segregation of duties: the person who develops a change cannot be the person who deploys it to production. (5) Regular access reviews: quarterly review of who has production admin access.

objectives.title: Compare and contrast approaches for managing common release artifacts in a multi-org scenario

topics.question: Strategies for managing shared metadata components across multiple Salesforce orgs
topics.answer: Three approaches: (1) Packages: shared components are built into an unlocked (or managed) package, versioned, and installed in all target orgs. Gold standard - changes are versioned and tracked. (2) Template repos: a shared Git repository contains the canonical version of shared metadata; each org's pipeline pulls from this repo. Less automated but more flexible. (3) Manual synchronization: admins manually replicate changes across orgs. Highest risk of divergence, not scalable. Packages are the recommended approach for mature orgs. Template repos work for teams not yet ready for full package-based development. Manual sync should be eliminated as soon as possible.

topics.question: Using unlocked packages to share and version common components across multiple orgs
topics.answer: In the package subscriber model: a 'common' or 'foundation' unlocked package contains shared components (utility Apex classes, common custom objects, shared layouts). Each consuming org installs this package as a dependency. When a shared component is updated: create a new package version, test it in a scratch org, release it, then update the dependency version in each consuming org's sfdx-project.json and trigger that org's CI pipeline to install the updated version. Update propagation: consuming orgs must explicitly upgrade to the new version (unlike automatic managed package updates, unlocked package subscribers control their own upgrade timing).

topics.question: Release artifact governance in a multi-org landscape
topics.answer: Governance requirements: (1) Ownership: define which team/org owns each shared component and is responsible for its quality and backward compatibility. (2) Approval: changes to shared components require higher-level approval (cross-org impact means more stakeholders). (3) Promotion: shared component changes must be tested in ALL consuming orgs before being released, not just the originating org. (4) Versioning: strict semantic versioning for shared packages to prevent breaking changes from silently propagating. (5) Communication: a changelog or release notes for each shared package update, distributed to all consuming org teams. Without clear governance, shared components become a source of cross-org breakage.

topics.question: Cross-org change management coordination
topics.answer: When changes affect multiple connected orgs: (1) Dependency tracking: map which orgs consume which shared components; maintain a dependency registry. (2) Aligned release windows: schedule deployment windows across all affected orgs in the correct dependency order (foundational orgs first, consuming orgs second). (3) Regression testing: after deploying to a consuming org, run integration tests that exercise the cross-org interface (APIs, events, data shares). (4) Cross-org rollback plan: if a shared component update breaks a consuming org, the rollback must be coordinated - rolling back the shared package in one org while others have upgraded can cause API version mismatches. (5) Communication: a shared release calendar visible to all org teams.

topics.question: Event logs and deployment history for post-release monitoring and diagnosis
topics.answer: Post-release monitoring tools: (1) Salesforce Event Monitoring (add-on): provides detailed event logs (API calls, logins, Apex exceptions, report exports) queryable via EventLogFile object. Use to detect unexpected behavior or errors after a deployment. (2) Apex Exception Email notifications: configure in Setup to email developers when unhandled Apex exceptions occur in production - the first alert of a deployment issue. (3) Deployment history: in Setup > Deployment Status, view past deployments and their results. (4) Debug logs: targeted logging for specific users immediately after deployment to diagnose issues. (5) Health Check and Salesforce Optimizer: periodic org health assessments. Establish a post-release monitoring checklist with specific log queries to run 24 hours after every production deployment.

objectives.title: Frame the AgentOps mindset shift from deterministic to probabilistic change management

topics.question: Why traditional ALM assumptions break for LLM-driven agents
topics.answer: Deterministic metadata changes produce predictable outcomes; LLM-driven agents interpret natural language, dynamically chain tools, and produce responses that vary based on context, memory, and semantic interpretation. The same utterance can produce two different, equally valid responses at different times — that is by design, but it means a "deploy and verify once" mindset fails. Your quality gates, your assertions, and your rollback strategies must all evolve to account for this fundamental runtime difference.

topics.question: Probabilistic vs. deterministic quality gates
topics.answer: Traditional gates rely on exact-match assertions: Apex code coverage thresholds, PMD static analysis, and field-value checks. Agentforce gates replace exact-match output assertions with LLM-as-a-Judge scoring across dimensions like coherence, completeness, and instruction adherence. A response is evaluated by another LLM model (Salesforce's SFR-Judge) on a pass/fail or HIGH/LOW/UNCERTAIN scale, meaning your pipeline must be designed to accept and act on probability scores rather than binary green/red results.

topics.question: Behavioral baseline as the new "regression test"
topics.answer: A stored JSON evaluation output captured from a known-good agent state becomes the primary comparison point for detecting future drift. This replaces the traditional idea of a single pass/fail regression suite. On every release branch, run `sf agent test run --json` and store the output as a pipeline artifact. When a production incident is reported later, you compare the current evaluation JSON to the most recent clean baseline to determine whether a deployment caused the change or whether it came from an LLM platform update — two very different remediation paths.

topics.question: Rollback nuance: metadata rollback vs. behavioral rollback
topics.answer: Reactivating a prior BotVersion via `sf agent activate --version {prior}` restores agent behavior in seconds without redeploying any metadata, because the prior version's compiled runtime graph is already present in the org. Redeploying prior metadata from source control restores structure but requires a full publish cycle. Clients need to understand these are not always the same fix. A behavioral regression may be solved entirely by BotVersion reactivation, while a broken action implementation requires a code-level rollback. Knowing which situation you are in before you start is the difference between a 2-minute recovery and a 30-minute one.

topics.question: Configuration drift vs. behavioral drift
topics.answer: Configuration drift is the org's metadata state diverging from what is in source control — the familiar ALM problem. Behavioral drift is the agent acting differently even when no metadata change has been made, typically caused by a background LLM platform update from Salesforce. These two failure modes require completely different responses: configuration drift is fixed by redeploying from source control; behavioral drift requires an authoring update to re-align instructions with the model's new interpretation patterns. Monitoring must distinguish between them, which is why behavioral baselines are captured independently of deployment events.

topics.question: Expanded security surface: prompt injection vs. code/SOQL injection
topics.answer: Traditional Salesforce security testing focuses on SOQL injection, code injection, and sharing-model bypasses. Agentforce adds a new attack vector: adversarial text embedded in data the agent retrieves or processes. The ForcedLeak vulnerability (CVSS 9.4) demonstrated this concretely — malicious instructions in a Web-to-Lead form were later retrieved during a summarization task, causing the agent to treat the payload as system instructions and exfiltrate data. Every agent that ingests externally sourced data must be red-team tested for this class of attack, in addition to all existing security practices.

topics.question: Mapping traditional ALM roles to AgentOps roles
topics.answer: The familiar Release Manager, Architect, and QA roles all persist in AgentOps, but each expands. The Release Manager now tracks evaluation pass rates as a readiness metric alongside open defects. The Architect is responsible for ensuring behavioral baselines are captured before changes reach integration, not just that code compiles. The QA Engineer owns the `AiEvaluationDefinition` test suite, writing utterances and configuring LLM-as-a-Judge scoring criteria — a skill that has no direct equivalent in traditional Apex testing. A new Security Reviewer role takes on adversarial red-team testing and Einstein Trust Layer validation, which must be signed off before any agent processes real customer data.

topics.question: Educating clients on why "it passed UAT" isn't "done"
topics.answer: UAT with a fixed set of utterances only proves behavior at a single point in time, using the current underlying LLM model. Because Salesforce periodically updates the LLM platform behind Agentforce, agent behavior can shift without any metadata change being deployed. This means ongoing production monitoring is not an optional nice-to-have — it is a required operating discipline. Clients who have been trained on traditional UAT-as-final-gate thinking need a concrete explanation of why periodic evaluation runs and STDM telemetry review remain necessary after go-live.

topics.question: Setting client expectations for ongoing monitoring cost/effort
topics.answer: Budget conversations should explicitly include three recurring cost categories that have no traditional ALM equivalent: periodic evaluation suite runs against production (monthly at minimum, more frequently after deployments), STDM dashboarding setup and maintenance in Data Cloud, and scheduled behavioral health checks to detect model-level drift independent of deployments. These are operating costs, not one-time project costs, and should appear in the client's ongoing support agreement rather than the implementation SOW.

topics.question: Positioning AgentOps as a layer on top of, not a replacement for, existing ALM
topics.answer: Consultants should frame AgentOps to clients as additive rigor, not a replacement for what the team already does well. Apex unit tests, source control discipline, CI/CD pipelines, and CAB governance all still apply and still catch the same classes of failure they always have. Probabilistic evaluation, behavioral baselining, and adversarial security testing are layered on top of that foundation to address the new failure modes that LLM-driven agents introduce. Clients who are already mature in Salesforce ALM have a strong foundation to build on — the delta is real but bounded.

objectives.title: Establish governance roles, responsibilities, and change approval paths

topics.question: Release Manager responsibilities and runbook ownership
topics.answer: The Release Manager coordinates all activities required to move an agent change from development to production. They maintain the release calendar, chair Change Advisory Board (CAB) reviews for high-risk AI changes, and own the deployment runbook end to end. Release readiness tracking now includes evaluation pass rates and open security findings alongside the traditional open-defect count. The Release Manager does not write Agent Script, but must understand the risk profile of each change well enough to make go/no-go recommendations to the CAB.

topics.question: Agent Developer / Architect responsibilities
topics.answer: The Agent Developer or Architect owns the Agent Script, subagent design, and underlying action implementations. A key AgentOps-specific responsibility is ensuring every change is retrievable into source control immediately — not after UAT, not after testing, but as the first act after any work in Agentforce Builder. They are also responsible for ensuring behavioral baselines are captured before changes reach the integration sandbox, giving the QA team a clean comparison point for regression detection.

topics.question: QA / Evaluation Engineer responsibilities
topics.answer: The QA or Evaluation Engineer owns the `AiEvaluationDefinition` test suite in its entirety. This includes writing representative utterances, defining expected subagent routing per test case, configuring LLM-as-a-Judge scoring criteria, and establishing JSONPath-based custom evaluations for business rule enforcement. They are the last technical sign-off before a change enters UAT, and their evaluation pass-rate threshold is the primary integration gate. This role requires understanding both the agent's intended behavior and the probabilistic nature of how it will be scored.

topics.question: Security Reviewer responsibilities
topics.answer: The Security Reviewer is responsible for adversarial red-team testing — submitting prompt injection payloads, indirect payload attacks, and exfiltration attempts to verify the agent refuses them. They also verify the Einstein Trust Layer configuration: data masking patterns, toxicity detection thresholds, PII scope, and the zero-retention policy. No agent that processes real customer data should enter a production environment without a signed-off security review from this role.

topics.question: Business Owner / UAT Approver responsibilities
topics.answer: The Business Owner validates agent behavior against the original business requirements in the UAT environment, using the Agentforce Builder live preview to interact with realistic scenarios. They provide the final go/no-go before the change moves to staging, and their sign-off must be documented for the compliance record. This role should be briefed on what a realistic failure mode looks like — not just happy-path demos — so their sign-off reflects genuine confidence rather than a successful scripted walkthrough.

topics.question: Risk classification model for change types
topics.answer: Not every Agentforce change requires the same approval overhead. Iterating on prompt instructions within an existing subagent is low risk and needs only a PR peer review plus an evaluation suite pass. Adding or removing a subagent is medium risk and requires QA sign-off in addition to PR review. Modifying `ruleExpression` security guards, releasing a net-new agent to production, or changing a shared Prompt Template used across multiple agents are all high risk and require a full CAB review plus the relevant specialist sign-offs. Applying the right level of governance to the right change type is how teams stay both secure and fast.

topics.question: CAB review triggers (ruleExpression changes, net-new agents, shared templates)
topics.answer: Three change categories reliably require full CAB review. First, any relaxation of a `ruleExpression` security guard — these are the declarative controls that prevent the agent from accessing high-risk actions before preconditions are met, and loosening them has a direct security impact. Second, any first-time production deployment of a net-new agent, since the full blast radius of the new agent is unknown until it has been through the complete governance cycle. Third, any modification to a shared Prompt Template that is referenced by more than one agent, since a seemingly small wording change can affect routing and response quality across all dependent agents simultaneously.

topics.question: Emergency/hotfix approval path
topics.answer: When a production defect requires immediate resolution, a pre-authorized emergency approver can bypass the standard CAB queue and greenlight a hotfix deployment. The key constraint is that this pre-authorization must exist before the incident occurs — you cannot improvise who the emergency approver is during an outage. A post-incident review is mandatory after every emergency approval, covering root cause, what governance step failed to catch the issue, and what process change prevents recurrence. Emergency approval is a safety valve, not a routine shortcut.

topics.question: Preventing unauthorized production changes via profile/permission restriction
topics.answer: The `Customize Application` permission in production should be restricted to the CI/CD service account only, with standing edit access removed from admin profiles. This is the primary technical control that prevents developers or administrators from making direct changes in Agentforce Builder that bypass source control, CI validation, and evaluation gates. Any change to agent behavior must originate as a commit. If a direct production change is ever necessary in an emergency, it must be retrieved to source control and back-propagated to all lower environments within 24 hours, with the justification and approver documented.

topics.question: Event Monitoring alerts on Bot/GenAiPlannerBundle/AiAuthoringBundle changes
topics.answer: Configure Salesforce Event Monitoring to generate alerts whenever a `Bot`, `GenAiPlannerBundle`, or `AiAuthoringBundle` record is modified in production by any account other than the CI/CD service account. This detective control catches direct UI edits that the permission restriction failed to prevent, or changes made by administrators who retained access due to a provisioning oversight. Alert routing should go to the Release Manager and Security Reviewer simultaneously so the unauthorized change can be investigated and remediated before it affects users.

objectives.title: Design a multi-sandbox environment strategy tailored to Agentforce

topics.question: Recommended environment hierarchy (Dev → Integration → QA → UAT → Staging → Prod)
topics.answer: The recommended six-tier hierarchy flows from Developer Sandbox through Integration, QA, UAT, Staging, and Production. Each tier has a distinct gate before promotion: syntax validation and Apex unit tests in Developer, automated evaluation suites in Integration, full evaluation plus security red-teaming in QA, business owner sign-off in UAT, production-equivalent dry run in Staging, and deliberate scheduled activation in Production. Skipping a tier to accelerate delivery typically results in discovering the skipped tier's failure class in a later, more expensive environment.

topics.question: Purpose and gate criteria of each environment tier
topics.answer: Developer sandboxes exist for individual feature work and early syntax validation; no shared testing happens here. Integration validates the combined state of all in-progress work after feature branch merges; no direct changes are permitted. QA is purpose-built for structured evaluation with masked representative data; adversarial prompt injection tests and multi-turn conversation scenarios run here. UAT is the business-facing validation tier where business owners interact with realistic scenarios and provide documented sign-off. Staging is a Full Copy environment where the complete production deployment runbook executes as a dry run. Production activation is a deliberate, scheduled step.

topics.question: Feature flag/licensing verification per environment
topics.answer: Einstein Setup, Agentforce Agents feature enablement, and Prompt Template licensing must be explicitly verified in every target org before each pipeline run. A sandbox refresh does not guarantee that feature flags from production are carried over. Missing feature flags produce misleading errors like "Feature is not currently enabled" that have nothing to do with the metadata being deployed and can cause significant debugging time loss if not caught in a pre-flight check. Add this verification as the first step of every CI pipeline run.

topics.question: Agent User provisioning per environment
topics.answer: The `default_agent_user` field in a `Bot` record references an org-specific user record by ID. That user must exist in every target org with an Einstein Agent license and the correct permission sets assigned. This is not a configuration that transfers via metadata deployment. Create an agent user substitution step in your deployment runbook for every environment crossing, and include a validation check in the pre-flight step that confirms the user exists and has the required license before the pipeline proceeds.

topics.question: Data Cloud/STDM/CRM Connector setup per environment
topics.answer: If the agent uses knowledge grounding via the Agentforce Data Library, or if STDM telemetry will be queried for observability in that environment, the Data Cloud CRM Connector must be active and the appropriate Data Cloud permissions must be provisioned separately in each org. Metadata deployment does not activate the CRM Connector, and it does not provision Data Cloud permissions. This is a common source of post-deployment confusion where the agent appears to deploy correctly but knowledge retrieval fails silently because the grounding infrastructure was never set up in the target environment.

topics.question: Sandbox refresh impact on active BotVersion
topics.answer: When a sandbox is refreshed from production, the active BotVersion resets to whatever version was active in the production snapshot at the time of the refresh. Any in-flight testing is immediately disrupted because the agent's behavior reverts to the production baseline state, not the state under test. If the refreshed sandbox is mid-test-cycle, the evaluation suite must be rerun from scratch. Plan sandbox refreshes explicitly around the release calendar, and communicate refresh windows to the QA and Evaluation Engineering teams well in advance.

topics.question: Post-refresh evaluation suite re-baselining
topics.answer: Immediately after any sandbox refresh, run the full evaluation suite before allowing the environment to be used for any new testing. This establishes a clean baseline for the refreshed state and confirms that the evaluation infrastructure itself is functioning correctly in the newly refreshed org. Any evaluation failures at this point are either pre-existing issues carried from production or environment setup problems, both of which must be resolved before new feature work begins in the environment.

topics.question: Dedicated hotfix sandbox parity requirements
topics.answer: Maintain a dedicated hotfix sandbox that is kept at or close to production parity at all times. This sandbox is reserved exclusively for emergency production fixes and is never used for ongoing feature development. If feature development work lands in the hotfix sandbox, its production parity guarantee is broken and it can no longer serve its purpose when an emergency actually occurs. Treat production parity as a strict invariant for this environment, including agent user provisioning, permission sets, and Data Cloud connectivity.

topics.question: Aligning refresh cadence with release calendar
topics.answer: Sandbox refresh timing should be coordinated with the release calendar before each planning cycle, not determined ad hoc. A refresh that lands in the middle of a QA evaluation cycle can discard days of carefully assembled test state. A refresh that lands right before a UAT cycle starts creates re-provisioning overhead at the worst possible time. Publishing a refresh schedule alongside the release calendar gives all teams the visibility they need to plan around it.

topics.question: Advising clients on right-sizing sandbox types (Developer vs. Partial vs. Full Copy) for agent workloads
topics.answer: Recommend Developer sandboxes for individual feature work, where the primary need is syntax validation and interactive debugging via `sf agent preview`. Recommend Partial Copy sandboxes for QA and UAT, where representative but masked production data is required for evaluation suite accuracy and business-owner testing realism. Reserve Full Copy sandboxes for Staging only, where production-equivalent data volume and disaster recovery procedure validation require a true production mirror. Full Copy sandboxes are expensive to refresh and maintain — using one for QA is unnecessary and wasteful.

objectives.title: Advise clients on hotfix and emergency environment handling

topics.question: Hotfix branch sourcing from production tag vs. main
topics.answer: Emergency hotfix branches must originate from the production release tag in Git, not from `main`. The `main` branch at the time of the incident may contain unreleased features from in-flight work that should not ship as part of an emergency fix. Branching from the production tag guarantees the hotfix contains only the code and configuration currently live in production, plus the targeted fix. This is a discipline that must be established in the team's Git workflow before an incident occurs — not discovered during one.

topics.question: Accelerated deployment path for emergencies
topics.answer: Emergency fixes can skip the standard integration and QA sandbox promotion queue, but they cannot skip `sf agent validate authoring-bundle` syntax checking or a critical-path evaluation suite covering the affected functionality. These two gates take minutes to execute and exist to prevent an emergency fix from introducing a new defect into production. Every other gate can be bypassed with appropriate emergency approval; these two cannot.

topics.question: Emergency approver pre-authorization
topics.answer: The identity of the emergency approver — and the conditions under which they can approve — must be documented and communicated to the entire team before any incident occurs. During an active production outage, you cannot afford to spend time identifying who has the authority to approve an emergency deployment. Define the emergency approver in the governance documentation, ensure they have the technical access required to approve, and confirm the runbook contains their contact information.

topics.question: 24-hour back-propagation rule
topics.answer: Any direct or emergency production change must be retrieved to source control and deployed back to all lower environments within 24 hours of the production fix going live. This prevents the hotfix from being silently overwritten by the next regular release that promotes from an environment that never received the fix. The 24-hour window is not aspirational — treat it as a hard SLA with a named owner responsible for completion.

topics.question: Post-incident review requirement
topics.answer: Every hotfix, regardless of severity, triggers a mandatory post-incident review. The review documents the root cause, identifies which governance gate failed to catch the issue before production, and defines the process or testing change that prevents recurrence. This review is not optional cleanup after the emergency is resolved — it is part of the emergency change process. Schedule it within 48 hours of the hotfix going live while memory is fresh.

topics.question: Balancing speed vs. governance in emergencies
topics.answer: The tension between governance and speed during an incident is best resolved before the incident happens. Work with clients to pre-define the criteria that qualify a change as a genuine emergency: typically revenue impact at a defined threshold, a user-blocking defect affecting a critical workflow, an active security vulnerability, or a compliance violation. When an incident occurs, classification against pre-defined criteria takes seconds. Without pre-defined criteria, every stakeholder will have a different opinion about what constitutes an emergency, and the governance discussion itself becomes the bottleneck.

topics.question: Communicating hotfix risk tradeoffs to business stakeholders
topics.answer: Business stakeholders approving an emergency bypass should understand the specific risk being accepted. Skipping the integration and QA sandbox promotion means the fix has not been evaluated against the full test suite or exercised with representative data at scale. Back-propagation within 24 hours is what converts that temporary risk acceptance into a permanent safe state. Frame the approval as "accept reduced testing confidence now, restore full confidence within 24 hours via back-propagation," not as "skip all testing forever."

topics.question: Hotfix sandbox usage boundaries (no feature dev)
topics.answer: The hotfix sandbox's value comes entirely from its production parity. The moment a developer uses it for in-progress feature work, its state diverges from production and it can no longer serve as a reliable validation environment for emergency fixes. Enforce this boundary technically by restricting deployment access to the hotfix sandbox to a dedicated service account that is not used for feature branch work, and by monitoring for unauthorized deployments via Event Monitoring.

topics.question: Reconciling hotfix with in-flight release branches
topics.answer: Immediately after a hotfix deploys to production, merge the hotfix branch into `main` and into every active feature branch. Feature branches that do not receive the hotfix will regress over the fix on their next promotion. This merge should be treated as blocking — no feature branch deploys to integration until the hotfix merge is confirmed. The Release Manager is responsible for coordinating this merge across all active branches, since individual feature developers may not be aware of all other in-flight branches.

topics.question: Documenting emergency change justification for audit
topics.answer: Compliance and audit functions require a paper trail for every production change, especially emergency changes that bypassed standard governance. The change record must capture: the specific business justification for emergency classification, the name of the pre-authorized approver who granted emergency approval, the exact timestamp of approval and deployment, and the planned back-propagation completion date. This documentation is created during the incident, not reconstructed afterward. Include a documentation step in the emergency runbook to ensure it happens under pressure.

agentops.title: Source Control, Metadata Architecture & Deployment Engineering

objectives.title: Establish branching and bundle versioning strategy

topics.question: Branch structure: main / release / feature / hotfix
topics.answer: The `main` branch mirrors production at all times — if production runs Agent Script version X, `main` contains Agent Script version X. Release branches stabilize committed bundles with `<target>` fields pinned, acting as the integration point for everything going into a specific release. Feature branches hold draft bundles that support iterative publishing during development. Hotfix branches originate exclusively from production release tags, never from `main`, ensuring emergency fixes contain only production-verified code plus the targeted change.

topics.question: Draft vs. committed AiAuthoringBundle states
topics.answer: Draft bundles have no `<target>` field in `bundle-meta.xml` and support iterative publishing to development sandboxes — each publish overwrites the previous runtime state. Committed bundles have a `<target>` field that pins them to a specific `{Bot}.{BotVersion}` pair, making them immutable versioned snapshots. Publishing a committed bundle to a development sandbox fails because the versioned identity is already claimed. Mixing draft and committed bundle states across environments is the most common source of confusing deployment failures on Agentforce projects.

topics.question: `<target>` field semantics
topics.answer: The `<target>` field in `bundle-meta.xml` is the mechanism that converts an iteratively-publishable draft into a locked, versioned artifact. When set to `{Bot}.{BotVersion}` (for example, `My_Agent.v2`), the bundle can only be published to create that specific BotVersion — it becomes an immutable snapshot. This field must be absent during active development and added only during the UAT promotion step when the bundle is transitioning to a release candidate. Getting this transition wrong in either direction (too early or too late) causes deployment failures or unintended overwrites.

topics.question: When to pin a bundle to a BotVersion
topics.answer: Pin the bundle during UAT promotion by adding the `<target>` field to `bundle-meta.xml` and assigning a `versionTag` for release traceability. This is the formal transition from development artifact to release candidate. Before this point, the bundle should remain in draft state to support rapid iteration during feature development and integration testing. After this point, the bundle is immutable and any required change must be made in a new draft bundle that will eventually be pinned to the next BotVersion.

topics.question: Repository structure for aiAuthoringBundles, genAiPlannerBundles, bots
topics.answer: The repository contains `aiAuthoringBundles/` (Agent Script source and bundle-meta.xml, one folder per draft and per committed version), `genAiPlannerBundles/` (the intelligence layer including the machine-generated `agentGraph/graph.json`, the `agentScript/` copy, and `localActions/`), and `bots/` (the Bot identity metadata and explicitly named BotVersion files). Understanding this layout is required for meaningful PR review — a reviewer who doesn't know the structure can't distinguish a safe Agent Script iteration from a dangerous security guard relaxation.

topics.question: graph.json as a machine-generated artifact — never hand-edit
topics.answer: The `agentGraph/graph.json` file is compiled from the Agent Script source when you publish to a sandbox. It is the runtime graph that the Agentforce reasoning engine actually executes.
