Editing it directly breaks the correspondence between the authored `.agent` file and the compiled runtime, causing behavior that cannot be diagnosed by reading the Agent Script. If you modify the `.agent` file directly in source control, you must publish to a sandbox and re-retrieve to regenerate `graph.json` before committing. Deploying an updated Agent Script without its corresponding updated `graph.json` is a serious deployment risk that produces hard-to-diagnose runtime drift.

topics.question: Local vs. global (Asset Library) subagents/actions structure
topics.answer: Local subagents and actions (the default in API v65+) are embedded directly in the `GenAiPlannerBundle`, minimizing shared-component risk. Global `GenAiPlugin` and `GenAiFunction` records from the Agent Asset Library are shared across multiple agents, meaning a change to a global component has a blast radius that spans every agent referencing it. Cross-agent impact analysis is mandatory before modifying any global Asset Library component. For new projects, prefer local subagents and actions unless there is a genuine reuse requirement that justifies the added governance complexity.

topics.question: Retrieval pitfalls: Agent pseudo-type exclusions
topics.answer: Using `Agent:My_Agent` as the retrieval target in a CLI command or `package.xml` silently excludes the `AiAuthoringBundle`. You will retrieve the `Bot`, `BotVersion`, `GenAiPlannerBundle`, `GenAiPlugin`, and `GenAiFunction` records but the Agent Script source file — the primary artifact developers work with — will be missing. Always retrieve `AiAuthoringBundle` explicitly as a separate metadata type. This silent exclusion has caused teams to work from stale Agent Script for entire sprint cycles, only discovering the discrepancy when a change they authored appeared absent from source control.

topics.question: BotVersion explicit-naming requirement (no wildcard)
topics.answer: `BotVersion` does not support wildcard retrieval (`<members>*</members>`). Every BotVersion that needs to be in source control must be named explicitly in `package.xml` using the `{Bot}.{version}` format (for example, `My_Agent.v1`). Wildcard retrieval against BotVersion either fails silently or returns nothing, depending on the CLI version. When releasing a new version, update the retrieval manifest to add the new BotVersion name before running the post-deployment retrieval that captures the released state.

topics.question: Two-pass retrieval verification technique for completeness
topics.answer: Salesforce can report a successful retrieval even when the output is incomplete. Run two retrieval passes: first a wildcard retrieval, then a named retrieval for the same bundle. Compare the output directory structures for gaps — specifically the presence of `schema.json` files in each `localActions/` subdirectory, the `agentGraph/graph.json` file, and consistent bundle folder depth. Structural inconsistencies between the two passes indicate a partial retrieval that should not be committed to source control. Common triggers for partial retrieval include platform upgrade periods and orgs with corrupted `GenAiPlannerBundle` state.

objectives.title: Master the four-layer Agentforce metadata model

topics.question: Bot (identity layer)
topics.answer: The `Bot` metadata type defines who the agent is: its display name, `botType` (either `InternalCopilot` for employee-facing agents or `ExternalCopilot` for customer-facing agents), channel configuration, privacy and logging settings, and session timeout behavior. This is the outermost layer — changing the `botType` has implications for which permission sets are required, which channels are available, and how the agent surfaces in Setup. Changes to the Bot identity layer should be treated as high-risk changes requiring CAB review because they affect the agent's fundamental access model.

topics.question: BotVersion (scaffold layer)
topics.answer: The `BotVersion` houses the dialog logic, conversation variables, the LLM planner reference (`genAiPlannerName`), tone, language configuration, and error dialog mappings. Only one BotVersion can be active at a time. Deploying a new BotVersion to an org does not automatically make it active — activation is a separate, deliberate CLI step (`sf agent activate`). This separation is intentional and provides the deployment window between "structure is present" and "users are exposed to the new behavior," during which smoke tests can be run in production before activation.

topics.question: GenAiPlannerBundle (intelligence layer)
topics.answer: The `GenAiPlannerBundle` is the agent's intelligence layer and the most complex metadata type in the stack. It contains local subagent definitions (`localTopics` in v65+), local action definitions (`localActions`), the compiled runtime graph (`agentGraph/graph.json`), `attributeMappings` for secure PII propagation between actions, and `ruleExpressions` that gate subagents and actions behind boolean conditions. Changes to this layer have the highest risk of behavioral regression because they directly alter what the agent can do and under what conditions. Every Agent Script iteration requires a corresponding updated `GenAiPlannerBundle` carrying the regenerated `graph.json`.

topics.question: AiAuthoringBundle (authoring layer)
topics.answer: The `AiAuthoringBundle` contains the `.agent` Agent Script source file and the `bundle-meta.xml` version-pinning metadata. This is the primary artifact that developers write and that peer review should focus on. It is the only layer where human-authored intent is directly expressed in readable form — all other layers are either compiled outputs or platform-managed metadata. The authoring bundle is also the only layer that exists in both draft and committed states, making the `<target>` field transition a key lifecycle event.

topics.question: AiEvaluationDefinition / AiTestingDefinition as quality-gate metadata
topics.answer: `AiEvaluationDefinition` and `AiTestingDefinition` records encapsulate evaluation utterances, expected subagent routing, conversation history for multi-turn tests, and LLM-as-a-Judge scoring criteria. Because these are deployed as standard Salesforce metadata, they can be source-controlled, reviewed, and versioned alongside the agent they test. This makes the evaluation suite a CI/CD-native quality gate rather than a manual testing artifact. The agent must be published before test definitions can reference it — attempting to run evaluations against an unpublished agent produces an error stating the agent does not exist.

topics.question: GenAiPromptTemplate and its grounding sources
topics.answer: `GenAiPromptTemplate` records are Prompt Builder templates deployed as metadata. They can be grounded by Einstein Search Retrievers (which carry org-specific IDs that require substitution between environments), Data Cloud retrievers, or Flow-backed grounding. Each grounding source type has its own portability challenge when promoting across environments. Templates grounded by Template-Triggered Prompt Flows that call Invocable Apex have an additional deployment constraint: the Flow and Apex must be deployed in a separate transaction from the template itself to avoid a compilation failure.

topics.question: attributeMappings for secure data propagation
topics.answer: `attributeMappings` in the `GenAiPlannerBundle` allow sensitive outputs from one action — such as a verified identity flag or a user's email address — to be passed directly to another action without routing the value through the LLM's context window. This is the primary technical control against prompt-injection-based data exfiltration. Any PII or security-sensitive value that needs to travel between actions should use an `attributeMapping` rather than being read from the LLM's output text. Review of `attributeMapping` coverage should be part of every security sign-off.

topics.question: ruleExpressions as declarative security/business gates
topics.answer: `ruleExpressions` are boolean conditions defined in the `GenAiPlannerBundle` that lock specific subagents or actions behind verified preconditions. For example, a financial transaction action can be gated behind an `isIdentityVerified = true` flag that is set only by a trusted authentication action. Unlike an instruction in Agent Script telling the model "only do this after verification," a `ruleExpression` is evaluated by the platform before the LLM is involved at all, making it impossible for a malicious prompt to bypass. Any relaxation of a `ruleExpression` is a high-risk change requiring CAB review.

topics.question: API version compatibility rules across seasonal releases
topics.answer: The format and API version of agent metadata must be matched explicitly during Salesforce seasonal release preview windows, when sandboxes and production may be on different API versions. A v65-format bundle deployed to a v65 org using the v65 API works. A v65-format bundle deployed to a v64 org, or a v65-format bundle deployed using a v64 API call, both fail. Set the `--api-version` flag explicitly in every CLI command during any preview window or cross-version environment transition. Relying on the CLI's default API version during a release window is a common source of hard-to-diagnose deployment failures.

topics.question: Explaining the metadata model to clients using an architecture diagram
topics.answer: The four-layer model (Identity/Scaffold/Intelligence/Authoring) provides a clean visual vocabulary for explaining what is being changed and why to non-technical business stakeholders. Presenting a CAB change as "we are modifying the intelligence layer to add a new order cancellation capability, gated by an existing identity verification rule" is far more meaningful to a business approver than "we are updating the GenAiPlannerBundle." Maintaining a simple architecture diagram in the project documentation and referencing it during governance conversations significantly reduces the time spent on risk explanation.

objectives.title: Sequence multi-phase deployments correctly

topics.question: Phase 1 — base platform dependencies (Apex/Flow/objects)
topics.answer: Apex classes, triggers, custom objects, custom fields, and autolaunched flows must be fully deployed and compiled before any Agentforce metadata that references them. Agent actions reference these structures directly by API name, and if the target does not exist in the org at deployment time, the result is an unresolved reference error that halts the entire deployment. For net-new agents, this means the full action implementation stack must be ready before a single Agentforce metadata type is deployed. Phase 1 maps to the standard Salesforce deployment practices your team already knows.

topics.question: Phase 2 — GenAiPromptTemplate deployment timing
topics.answer: `GenAiPromptTemplate` metadata must be deployed after its underlying Apex classes and Flows are compiled (Phase 1) but before any agent actions that invoke the template (Phases 4 and 5). Deploying the template before its grounding Flows exist results in a compilation failure. Deploying agent actions that invoke the template before the template exists results in an unresolved reference. If the template is grounded by a Template-Triggered Prompt Flow that calls Invocable Apex, do not include the Flow/Apex and the template in the same deployment transaction — use the bifurcated strategy.

topics.question: Phase 3 — global Asset Library components
topics.answer: Global `GenAiFunction` and `GenAiPlugin` records from the Agent Asset Library must be deployed after the underlying Apex and Flows they reference (Phase 1) but before the `GenAiPlannerBundle` that references them (Phase 4). For agents that use only local subagents and actions embedded in the bundle (the default in API v65+), this phase can be skipped entirely. Include it only when the agent explicitly references shared Asset Library components, and note that any change to a shared component requires the cross-agent impact analysis described in the governance section.

topics.question: Phase 4 — GenAiPlannerBundle and AiPlannerVoiceDef
topics.answer: The `GenAiPlannerBundle` carries the agent's reasoning and orchestration layer: subagent definitions, action definitions, the compiled graph, attribute mappings, and security rule expressions. It must be present in the target org before the `AiAuthoringBundle` can be published, because the publish step links the Bundle to the Planner via `BotVersion.PlannerId`. For voice-channel agents, the `AiPlannerVoiceDef` voice configuration deploys immediately after the planner bundle in the same phase, since it depends on the planner existing in the org.

topics.question: Phase 5 — AiAuthoringBundle deploy + publish + activate
topics.answer: Deploying the `AiAuthoringBundle` moves the Agent Script source to the target org but does not make the agent live. Publishing (`sf agent publish authoring-bundle`) is the step that compiles the Agent Script, creates or updates the runtime `Bot`, `BotVersion`, and `GenAiPlannerBundle`, and links them together. After publishing, run the behavioral evaluation gate (`sf agent test run`) to confirm the compiled runtime behaves as authored. Only after the evaluation gate passes should you activate the new BotVersion (`sf agent activate`), which is the step that exposes users to the new behavior.

topics.question: Net-new vs. existing-agent deployment scope differences
topics.answer: Deploying a net-new agent to a target org for the first time requires all five phases, with no shortcuts. The `GenAiPlannerBundle` is mandatory because `BotVersion.PlannerId` is a required field — omitting it produces an immediate deployment failure. Deploying an update to an existing agent requires only the phases containing changed metadata types, plus a verification that the `PlannerId` linkage in BotVersion is intact. Agent Script iteration only (no subagent or action changes) requires deploying the updated `AiAuthoringBundle` and the updated `GenAiPlannerBundle` carrying the regenerated `graph.json` — never one without the other.

topics.question: Bifurcated transaction strategy for Prompt Flow + Apex conflicts
topics.answer: When a `GenAiPromptTemplate` is grounded by a Template-Triggered Prompt Flow that calls Invocable Apex, deploying the template and the Flow/Apex in the same metadata transaction triggers a compilation failure. The Apex `@InvocableMethod` schema cannot be resolved at the same time as generative AI entity validation within a single transaction. The fix is two sequential deployments: Transaction 1 deploys the Flow and Apex only; Transaction 2, after Transaction 1 completes successfully, deploys the `GenAiPromptTemplate` and any `AiAuthoringBundle`. This pattern cannot be resolved through code changes — it requires the bifurcated transaction approach unconditionally.

topics.question: Einstein Search Retriever ID substitution across orgs
topics.answer: `GenAiPromptTemplate` components that reference Einstein Search Retrievers embed an org-specific Retriever ID. When the template is promoted to a target org, that source-org ID does not exist in the target org, causing a misleading template corruption error. The fix: deploy the Retriever component to the target org first, query the target org for the new Retriever ID using SOQL, then rewrite the Retriever ID in the `GenAiPromptTemplate` XML before deployment. Automate this substitution as a pipeline step so it does not require manual intervention on every environment promotion.

topics.question: Avoiding "no-op" deployments of unchanged committed bundles
topics.answer: Deploying a committed (versioned) `AiAuthoringBundle` that has not been modified since it was last deployed reports a successful deployment but changes nothing in the target org. Salesforce treats it as a no-op because the bundle is already at that version. This is a silent failure mode — the deployment pipeline turns green, but the intended behavioral change did not propagate. Always verify that behavioral changes actually reached the target org through `sf agent test run` output comparison, not through deployment status alone.

topics.question: Building a CI pipeline that encodes phase ordering automatically
topics.answer: Design your CI pipeline stages to mirror the five-phase dependency chain, with each phase as a named pipeline stage that must complete before the next begins. Developers should not need to remember the ordering — it should be enforced by the pipeline definition itself. This architecture ensures that no developer can accidentally deploy an `AiAuthoringBundle` before the `GenAiPlannerBundle` it depends on, regardless of what they include in a feature branch commit.

objectives.title: Execute the end-to-end deployment workflow and manual runbook steps

topics.question: Pre-flight verification checklist
topics.answer: Before any deployment to any target environment, verify: Einstein Setup is enabled, Agentforce Agents feature is enabled, Prompt Template licenses are active, the `default_agent_user` exists with an Einstein Agent license and correct permission sets, and the Data Cloud CRM Connector is active for knowledge-grounded agents. Missing any of these prerequisites produces errors that appear to be deployment failures but are actually environment configuration gaps, which can waste significant diagnostic time if the pre-flight step is skipped.

topics.question: sf agent validate / publish / test run / activate command flow
topics.answer: The CLI command sequence is: `sf agent validate authoring-bundle` (syntax gate), `sf project deploy start` (move metadata phases 1-5), `sf agent publish authoring-bundle` (compile the runtime and create the BotVersion), `sf agent test run` (behavioral evaluation gate), then `sf agent activate` (promote the new BotVersion to active). Each of these is a distinct sequential step, and each must complete successfully before the next begins. The most common sequencing error is treating `deploy` and `publish` as the same step — they are not. Deploy moves metadata; publish compiles the runtime.

topics.question: Peer review checklist for .agent file changes
topics.answer: Agent Script PRs should be reviewed against a specific checklist: logic correctness of `before_reasoning`, `reasoning`, and `after_reasoning` blocks; subagent `description` field changes (which directly affect how the LLM routes incoming utterances); new or modified conversation variables and their downstream consumers; any relaxation of `ruleExpression` security guards (which requires CAB-level approval, not just peer review sign-off); nested `if` blocks (which the compiler rejects and must be flattened before the PR merges); and changes to action `target:` references (which must be verified to exist in every environment the change will reach).

topics.question: Promotion mechanics through each environment tier
topics.answer: The core deployment sequence — validate, deploy phases 1-5, publish, test run, activate — repeats at each environment tier. What changes as you move toward production is the depth of required sign-offs and the scope of the evaluation suite. Integration requires an automated evaluation pass. QA requires the full suite including adversarial tests. UAT requires business-owner interaction. Staging requires a complete dry-run of the production runbook. Do not abbreviate the evaluation at any tier under schedule pressure — that is precisely when behavioral regressions go undetected until production.

topics.question: UAT bundle transition (draft → committed, versionTag)
topics.answer: When promoting to the UAT sandbox, transition the `bundle-meta.xml` by adding the `<target>` field pinned to the target BotVersion (for example, `<target>My_Agent.v2</target>`) and assigning a `versionTag` for release traceability. This formal transition marks the bundle as a release candidate. Business owners should not begin UAT testing until this transition is confirmed, because any further Agent Script changes made after the transition require a new draft bundle, not edits to the now-committed one. Document the transition timestamp in the release record.

topics.question: Staging dry-run purpose and scope
topics.answer: Execute the complete production deployment runbook against the Staging (Full Copy) environment before the production deployment window opens. This is the final verification that the sequencing works end to end, that all manual runbook steps complete without issues, and that the rollback procedure (reactivating the prior BotVersion) can be executed within the required Recovery Time Objective. If anything fails in Staging, there is time to investigate and correct before the production window. If anything fails in the production window without a Staging dry run having been completed, there is no safety net.

topics.question: Manual-only configuration steps (channel assignment, Data Cloud activation, permission sets)
topics.answer: Several Agentforce configuration steps cannot be automated via the Metadata API and must appear as explicit human steps in the deployment runbook. These include: enabling the Agentforce feature in Setup, activating the new BotVersion (automatable via `sf agent activate` but still a deliberate step), Data Cloud ingestion connection setup, Data Cloud stream activation, channel assignments (Slack, WhatsApp, and other messaging channels), standard Salesforce-provided subagent assignments via Agentforce Builder, and search index re-crawling for knowledge-grounded agents. Missing any of these in the runbook results in a technically successful deployment that is functionally incomplete.

topics.question: Common deployment error patterns and their root causes
topics.answer: Three error patterns appear repeatedly across Agentforce projects. `Required fields are missing: [PlannerId]` means the `GenAiPlannerBundle` was not deployed before the `AiAuthoringBundle` publish step for a net-new agent. `UNKNOWN_EXCEPTION` on bundle retrieval or validation after a seasonal upgrade typically means the platform auto-converted the org to a new format and left orphaned XML references in the `GenAiPlannerBundle`. Template corruption errors on `GenAiPromptTemplate` deployments that have not changed usually mean an Einstein the source org is hardcoded in the template XML and does not exist in the target org.

topics.question: Distinguishing metadata deployment success from behavioral change confirmation
topics.answer: A green deployment pipeline confirms that metadata structure moved from one org to another without error. It does not confirm that the agent's behavior changed in the way you intended. A committed bundle that was already deployed at that version produces a successful no-op. An Agent Script change that introduced a logic error will deploy successfully and fail behaviorally. Always run `sf agent test run` and compare the JSON output to the prior baseline as the actual confirmation that intended behavior is present — not the deployment exit code.

topics.question: Building a client-ready deployment runbook template
topics.answer: A complete deployment runbook packages the pre-flight checklist, the five-phase deployment command sequence with exact CLI syntax, all manual steps that require human action (with the named responsible role for each), the post-deployment smoke test procedure, and the rollback trigger criteria and commands. Clients who can operate the runbook themselves are significantly less dependent on the implementation partner for routine releases, which reduces operational risk and support cost over time. Template the runbook during the project and validate it end-to-end during the Staging dry run.

objectives.title: Build a layered testing strategy across the Agentforce testing pyramid

topics.question: Apex unit tests for action implementations
topics.answer: Every Apex class powering an agent action must have standard Apex unit test coverage using `@IsTest(SeeAllData=false)` and test data factories. Tests must assert on the specific `outputParam` values returned under varied inputs, not just achieve line coverage. Bulk behavior must be covered because the LLM may invoke an action repeatedly across a conversation. Error conditions — record not found, callout timeout, null required fields — must return explicit error outputs, not unhandled exceptions. Use `System.runAs()` to validate that the agent user's permission set is sufficient for all SOQL queries and DML operations the action performs.

topics.question: Deterministic logic tests for Agent Script conditionals
topics.answer: Agent Script's `available when` guards, `ruleExpression` conditions, and conversation variable state transitions execute deterministically and can be tested like a state machine. Verify that a guarded action cannot be invoked when its precondition is `false`. Verify that the correct variable is set when a specific action completes. Verify that a subagent locked by a boolean condition cannot be accessed before that condition is satisfied. Use `sf agent preview start` / `sf agent preview send` / `sf agent preview end` to drive specific Agent Script paths interactively during development and capture the expected state transitions.

topics.question: LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation fundamentals
topics.answer: The Agentforce Testing Center uses Salesforce's SFR-Judge models to evaluate agent responses probabilistically. Instead of asserting that a specific output string appears, the evaluation asks whether the response is coherent, complete, concise, and adherent to the subagent's authored instructions. Scores are expressed as pass/fail for binary metrics, HIGH/LOW/UNCERTAIN for instruction adherence, and exact-match for routing and action sequencing. Understanding what each metric actually validates allows the QA engineer to write test cases that exercise the right behavioral properties rather than gaming pass rates with easy utterances.

topics.question: Multi-turn conversation testing for memory retention
topics.answer: Real users provide context incrementally across multiple turns, pivot topics, and reference information from earlier in the conversation. Single-shot test utterances do not cover these patterns. Inject a `conversationHistory` array into the test input metadata to simulate prior turns and verify that the agent correctly retains working memory — for example, that an account ID established in turn 1 is correctly passed to an action in turn 4. Multi-turn tests also catch topic-pivot failures where the agent loses established context when the user shifts subject, and stateful flag failures where a boolean set by a prior action does not persist.

topics.question: Security red-teaming as a distinct test layer
topics.answer: Adversarial prompt injection testing is not a one-time pre-launch checkbox. It is a continuous test layer that must run as part of the QA evaluation suite on every promotion. Red-team test cases should include attempts to override system instructions via user input, attempts to extract PII or internal system information through conversational manipulation, ForcedLeak-style indirect injection tests for agents that retrieve externally-submitted data, and attempts to invoke high-risk actions (financial transactions, data writes) before identity verification gates are satisfied. A passing red-team suite should be a Gate 3 requirement.

topics.question: End-to-end/UI testing across the full digital supply chain
topics.answer: The Agentforce Testing Center evaluates the agent's reasoning and conversational output. It does not verify that downstream systems actually changed state as a result of an agent action. End-to-end tests fill this gap by verifying that the Flow actually updated the record, the external API call actually executed with the correct payload, and the CPQ or ERP system reflects the change the agent claimed to make. These tests require a full integration environment with realistic downstream system connectivity, which is why they are positioned at the top of the testing pyramid.

topics.question: Mapping each pyramid layer to the failure class it catches
topics.answer: Apex unit tests catch implementation bugs in action logic. Deterministic logic tests catch errors in `available when` guards, `ruleExpression` conditions, and variable state transitions. LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation catches routing failures, response quality regressions, and instruction adherence drift. Multi-turn conversation tests catch stateful memory failures and context retention bugs across turns. Security red-teaming catches adversarial exploits and injection vulnerabilities. End-to-end tests catch integration failures and downstream system state discrepancies. Each layer is designed to catch a specific class of failure that the other layers cannot detect.

topics.question: Why no single layer is sufficient on its own
topics.answer: Teams that deploy Agentforce with only Apex unit tests and no probabilistic evaluation will discover routing failures and response quality regressions in production. Teams that run LLM evaluation but skip security red-teaming will deploy agents vulnerable to prompt injection attacks they were never designed to resist. Teams that skip multi-turn conversation tests will find memory retention bugs only when real users encounter them in complex, multi-step conversations. The pyramid exists because each layer has genuine coverage gaps that can only be filled by the layers above and below it.

topics.question: Converting production failures into permanent regression cases
topics.answer: Every production session where the agent misrouted an utterance, returned an inadequate response, or failed to complete a user's task should be treated as a test case that was missing from the evaluation suite. Extract the utterance and conversation context from the STDM Step table, define the expected routing and response quality, and add it to the `AiEvaluationDefinition` suite. This converts the cost of a production failure into a permanent improvement to the regression coverage, reducing the likelihood of the same failure recurring after the next deployment.

topics.question: Advising clients on maturity-appropriate testing investment
topics.answer: Early-stage clients who are deploying their first Agentforce agent should focus on getting Apex unit tests, basic evaluation suite coverage, and the security red-team minimum (at least ForcedLeak-style tests for any agent ingesting external data) in place before go-live. Mature clients with established agents in production should invest in continuous multi-turn regression, automated adversarial testing pipelines, and monthly behavioral health checks. Prescribe the testing investment level based on where the client actually is in their AgentOps maturity journey, not where you would ideally like them to be.

objectives.title: Configure and operate the Agentforce Testing Center

topics.question: Standard evaluation metrics (Topic Classification, Action Sequencing, Coherence, Conciseness, Completeness, Instruction Adherence)
topics.answer: Topic (Subagent) Classification validates that the reasoning engine routed the utterance to the correct subagent, scored as an exact match against expected metadata. Action Sequencing validates that the agent invoked the correct actions in the correct order, scored as a sequence array match. Coherence verifies the response is logically sound and grammatically correct (LLM Judge pass/fail). Conciseness verifies the response is appropriately brief without omitting key information (LLM Judge pass/fail). Completeness verifies all requested information is present (LLM Judge pass/fail). Instruction Adherence scores whether the agent followed its authored subagent instructions (HIGH/LOW/UNCERTAIN).

topics.question: Creating AiEvaluationDefinition test suites via CLI
topics.answer: Use `sf agent generate test-spec --json --agent-api-name My_Agent --output-file specs/My_Agent_testSpec.yaml --target-org DevSandbox` to scaffold a YAML spec from the agent's schema. The generated spec provides the structural skeleton; you must customize it by adding representative utterances covering the full range of intended user intents, defining the expected subagent route for each utterance, and adding conversation history for multi-turn test cases. Deploy the completed spec to the org using `sf agent test create`, then execute it using `sf agent test run`.

topics.question: Generating starter YAML specs from agent schema
topics.answer: The agent must be published to a sandbox before `sf agent generate test-spec` can reference it, because the command queries the org's agent schema to build the spec structure. Attempting to run this against an unpublished agent produces `Error: Agent does not exist`. This means the typical workflow is: develop Agent Script, publish to dev sandbox, generate starter spec, customize spec, deploy spec, run evaluation. The spec generation step is early in the testing lifecycle, not late — write your evaluation cases before promotion, not after.

topics.question: Execution capacity limits and rate-limit avoidance
topics.answer: The Agentforce Testing Center enforces a maximum of 500 test cases per evaluation job and a maximum of 10 concurrent jobs per hour. Each test case consumes approximately 5 seconds of execution time and draws from the org's Einstein Requests allowance. Exceeding these limits produces Agent Rate Limit Errors that throttle org-wide AI requests, affecting production users if the evaluation runs against a production-adjacent org. Respect these limits by designing evaluation suites with awareness of the cap, and by timing evaluation runs outside of peak usage hours when running in shared environments.

topics.question: Batching strategy for large regression suites
topics.answer: Large regression suites — more than 50 test cases — should be segmented into batches of 20 to 30 cases to avoid rate-limit collisions during CI runs. Organize batches by functional area (order management, billing, identity verification) so that a rate-limit failure in one batch does not block unrelated functional areas from being evaluated. Each batch should be a separate `AiEvaluationDefinition` that can be run independently or in sequence, with individual batch pass rates reported separately for easier regression isolation.

topics.question: Continuous vs. monolithic evaluation scheduling
topics.answer: Evaluation suites should run continuously throughout the development lifecycle — at feature branch integration, at each environment promotion, after each sandbox refresh, and on a scheduled cadence against production. A monolithic evaluation gate that runs only immediately before deployment to production creates a false sense of security during development and makes failures expensive to diagnose because multiple changes have accumulated since the last evaluation run. Shift the evaluation left: catching a routing regression in the Integration sandbox costs a fraction of what it costs to catch it in UAT.

topics.question: Behavioral regression baselining and artifact storage
topics.answer: On every `release/*` branch, run `sf agent test run --json` against the target environment and store the complete JSON output as a named artifact in the CI artifact repository, alongside the deployed bundle version identifier and the deployment timestamp. This creates a durable behavioral record for every release. Store artifacts with retention policies that cover at least the last three releases so that root-cause analysis can compare behavior across multiple releases when an incident occurs.

topics.question: Comparing current runs to baseline to isolate deployment vs. model drift
topics.answer: When a production incident is reported, the first diagnostic question is: did a deployment cause this, or did an LLM platform update shift behavior without any metadata change? Compare the current evaluation JSON output to the most recent clean baseline artifact. If the scores dropped on a specific subagent after a deployment, the deployment is the likely cause. If the scores dropped gradually across a period with no deployments, the cause is model-level drift requiring an authoring update. These are completely different remediation paths, and the baseline artifact is what makes the distinction possible.

topics.question: Custom JSONPath evaluation criteria for compliance rules
topics.answer: Business rules that cannot be validated by standard LLM-as-a-Judge metrics can be enforced using JSONPath expressions against the execution payload. Target the deterministic action input payload — for example, `$.generatedData.invokedActions[*][?(@.function.name == 'DraftReplyEmail')].function.input.recipient` — rather than the non-deterministic final conversational response text. The LLM's phrasing of its response varies; the inputs it passed to a backend action do not. JSONPath evaluation on action inputs is the correct tool for compliance-sensitive assertions like "the agent passed the correct account ID to the transaction action."

topics.question: Choosing string_comparison vs. numeric_comparison operators
topics.answer: The Testing Center provides two evaluation operator types for custom JSONPath criteria. Use `string_comparison` with operators `equals`, `contains`, `startswith`, and `endswith` for text field assertions — for example, verifying that an email recipient address contains the correct domain. Use `numeric_comparison` with operators `equals`, `greater_than`, `less_than`, and range operators for quantitative assertions — for example, verifying that a discount percentage falls within an authorized range. Choosing the wrong operator type for the field being evaluated produces false negatives that silently pass incorrect behavior.

objectives.title: Validate Prompt Templates and pro-code debugging workflows

topics.question: Grounding accuracy validation for RAG-based templates
topics.answer: For Prompt Templates that use retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), verify that the retrieval pipeline returns the correct knowledge chunks for a representative set of merge field values. Test this in the QA sandbox using realistic CRM records that reflect actual customer data patterns, not synthetic placeholders. An incorrectly grounded prompt can produce responses that are confident-sounding but factually wrong, because the LLM is generating from incorrect context. Grounding accuracy validation is a distinct testing concern from agent routing validation, and it requires its own test cases targeting the template directly.

topics.question: Data masking compliance testing with representative PII
topics.answer: Confirm that PII in Prompt Template merge fields is correctly masked by the Einstein Trust Layer before the prompt leaves the Salesforce trust boundary. Test with records containing realistic PII patterns — names, email addresses, phone numbers, financial account numbers — not sanitized test data. Review the outbound prompt payload in the Trust Layer audit logs and verify that the actual PII values have been replaced with anonymized placeholders. Testing with sanitized records that contain no real PII will not reveal masking gaps in custom object fields or complex data relationships.

topics.question: Retriever ID portability across environments
topics.answer: Automate a CI pipeline check that queries the target org for the expected Einstein Search Retriever by `DeveloperName` and confirms it exists before any `GenAiPromptTemplate` deployment that references it. This check prevents the misleading "template corruption" error that occurs when a source-org Retriever ID is embedded in the template XML and does not exist in the target org. Run this check at the start of the Prompt Template deployment phase (Phase 2) so the pipeline fails fast with a clear error rather than a confusing compilation failure later.

topics.question: API version compatibility validation for templates
topics.answer: Deploy Prompt Templates using the same API version as the target org. During seasonal release preview windows, developer sandboxes may be on the new API version while production is still on the prior version, or vice versa. A format-version mismatch between the template metadata and the target org API produces deployment failures that are difficult to attribute to the version mismatch without explicit awareness of the difference. Add an API version comparison check to the pre-flight verification step for all Prompt Template deployments.

topics.question: sf agent preview start/send/end for interactive debugging
topics.answer: The `sf agent preview` command set provides a terminal-based interactive session against a live sandbox agent, enabling line-by-line testing of specific Agent Script paths during development. Use `sf agent preview start` to open a session, `sf agent preview send` to submit individual utterances, and `sf agent preview end` to close the session and generate the trace file. This is faster than running a full evaluation suite when you need to diagnose a specific routing decision or verify that a new action is being invoked correctly before writing formal test cases.

topics.question: Reading LLMStep, FunctionStep, ReasoningStep trace entries
topics.answer: Preview sessions generate step-by-step execution trace files in `.sfdx/agents/`. `LLMStep` entries show what instruction text reached the LLM and what the model decided to do — this is where you see whether your authored instructions are being interpreted as intended. `FunctionStep` entries show which action was invoked, what input parameters were passed, and what output was returned — this is where you diagnose action-level failures and input/output type mismatches. `ReasoningStep` entries show the model's planning chain for the turn — the sequence of reasoning decisions that led to the observed outcome.

topics.question: Apex Replay Debugger integration for action-level defects
topics.answer: When an agent action invokes backend Apex, the VS Code Agentforce extension can attach the Apex Replay Debugger to the execution thread, enabling step-through debugging of the traditional Apex code triggered by the probabilistic agent action. This bridges the gap between AI-layer debugging (reading LLMStep and FunctionStep trace entries) and code-layer debugging (stepping through Apex logic with breakpoints). It is the fastest path to diagnosing action-level failures where the agent correctly identified the action to invoke but the action itself is returning unexpected results.

topics.question: Importing preview sessions as permanent regression test cases
topics.answer: Successful `sf agent preview` sessions that confirm a correct conversational flow can be converted directly into `AiEvaluationDefinition` test cases by extracting the utterance, the expected subagent route, and the conversation history from the session trace. This converts exploratory testing work into durable regression coverage, ensuring that a verified behavior remains in the evaluation suite even as the agent evolves. Build this conversion step into the development workflow so that every manually verified behavior has a corresponding automated test case by the time the feature branch is ready for PR review.

topics.question: Distinguishing template-level testing needs from agent-level evaluation
topics.answer: Prompt Template validation — grounding accuracy, PII masking, Retriever ID portability, API version compatibility — is a separate discipline from agent evaluation. Agent evaluation tests the reasoning engine's routing, action sequencing, and conversational quality. Template validation tests the retrieval and grounding pipeline beneath the agent's instructions. Both must pass independently before a change reaches production. A passing agent evaluation suite does not imply that the underlying template is correctly grounded or that PII masking is functioning as expected.

topics.question: Explaining evaluation evidence to a client's compliance/audit function
topics.answer: Compliance and audit teams need an evidence trail that demonstrates behavioral quality was verified before production deployment. Package the following as the standard evidence set: the baseline JSON artifact from the most recent clean evaluation run, the custom JSONPath evaluation results showing that specific business rules were enforced, the Trust Layer audit logs confirming PII masking was in effect for the deployment window, and the red-team test results confirming the agent refused adversarial inputs. Presenting these as a structured evidence package makes CAB reviews and external audits significantly more efficient.

objectives.title: Apply Einstein Trust Layer controls and prompt-injection defenses

topics.question: Why AI expands the traditional security surface
topics.answer: Every Agentforce agent that has access to CRM data and can invoke backend actions represents a new attack surface that did not exist before AI was introduced into the system. Traditional penetration testing methodology covers SOQL injection, code injection, and sharing-model bypass — it does not cover prompt injection attacks, where adversarial text is used to override the agent's system instructions. Adding an AI agent to a Salesforce org requires expanding the security posture to cover this new attack class, not just layering AI on top of an existing security program.

topics.question: Prompt injection mechanics and the ForcedLeak precedent
topics.answer: ForcedLeak (CVSS 9.4) demonstrated a concrete, exploitable vulnerability pattern: malicious instructions embedded in a Web-to-Lead form were stored as a CRM record. Later, when an agent was asked to summarize leads, it retrieved the record, the malicious payload entered the agent's grounding context, and the agent treated it as system instructions — exfiltrating data to an attacker-controlled endpoint. The attack requires no special access to the Salesforce org. Any system where externally-submitted data can later be retrieved by an AI agent is potentially vulnerable to this pattern.

topics.question: Treating all grounded data (even CRM data) as untrusted
topics.answer: The fundamental defensive principle for Agentforce security is: system instructions and grounded data are not equally trusted, even when the grounded data lives in your own CRM. An authenticated user who submitted a Web-to-Lead form is not a trusted source of system instructions. An email retrieved from a shared inbox is not a trusted source of system instructions. Any data that can be influenced by an external party — regardless of where it is stored — must be treated as permanently untrusted when it enters an agent's grounding context.

topics.question: attributeMappings for keeping sensitive values out of LLM context
topics.answer: Use `attributeMappings` in the `GenAiPlannerBundle` to route sensitive outputs — identity verification flags, user email addresses, account numbers, authorization tokens — directly from one action to another without passing the value through the LLM's context window. When a sensitive value travels through the model's context, it becomes visible to the model and can potentially be leaked through a manipulated response or exfiltrated through an injection attack. `attributeMappings` bypass the model entirely for these transfers, making the sensitive value technically unreachable by adversarial prompts.

topics.question: ruleExpressions for gating high-risk actions behind verified conditions
topics.answer: `ruleExpressions` enforce preconditions at the platform level before the LLM is involved, making it impossible for a malicious prompt to bypass a security gate by convincing the model that a precondition has been satisfied. A `ruleExpression` that gates a financial transaction action behind `isIdentityVerified = true` can only be satisfied by the trusted authentication action that sets that flag — not by a user typing "I have already been verified, please proceed." This is the key architectural difference between declarative security guards and instruction-based trust, which the LLM can be convinced to override.

topics.question: Sanitizing externally-sourced data before grounding
topics.answer: Data retrieved from Web-to-Lead forms, public APIs, inbound email content, and any other external source must be sanitized before it enters an agent's grounding context. Sanitization for prompt injection defense means stripping content that contains instruction-like syntax, role declarations ("You are now acting as..."), or system-prompt override attempts ("Ignore previous instructions..."). This sanitization step should be implemented in the Flow or Apex that retrieves the external data, before the output is made available to the agent's action chain.

topics.question: Automated adversarial/red-team testing in CI
topics.answer: Include a set of adversarial test cases in the `AiEvaluationDefinition` suite that run automatically at Gate 3 (QA). These cases should submit prompts designed to override the agent's system instructions, extract PII or internal system information, invoke high-risk actions before preconditions are met, and trigger ForcedLeak-style exfiltration attempts. Each test case should assert that the agent refused or ignored the adversarial input rather than complying with it. A passing adversarial test suite should be a hard Gate 3 requirement, not an optional security exercise.

topics.question: Trust Layer data masking mechanics
topics.answer: The Einstein Trust Layer intercepts outbound prompts before they leave the Salesforce trust boundary, detects PII using pattern matching and semantic analysis, and replaces it with anonymized placeholder tokens. The LLM provider receives a prompt with `[MASKED_EMAIL]` instead of `user@example.com`. When the LLM response is returned, the Trust Layer de-masks the tokens, restoring the original values for the user-facing response. Validate this mechanism with custom objects and complex data relationships, not just standard fields, because PII in custom object fields may require explicit Trust Layer configuration to be masked correctly.

topics.question: Trust Layer toxicity detection and threshold tuning
topics.answer: Both outbound prompts (the grounded context sent to the LLM) and inbound responses (the LLM's raw output) are scored for toxic, biased, or inappropriate content. Outputs that exceed the configured toxicity threshold are blocked and logged in the audit trail. The default threshold is appropriate for general business use but may need tuning for specific deployment channels — a customer service agent for sensitive healthcare conversations may require a lower threshold than an internal productivity assistant. Validate the threshold configuration by testing with content representative of the most sensitive scenarios the agent will encounter.

topics.question: Zero data retention policy validation
topics.answer: Confirm that the org-level zero data retention setting is active, which instructs the LLM provider not to persist any prompt data outside the Salesforce trust boundary. Verify this in Setup under the Einstein settings and confirm it appears in the Trust Layer audit logs as an active policy. Test by reviewing the audit logs after a test conversation to confirm the zero-retention confirmation is present in each log entry. An org where this setting was accidentally disabled during a Setup change is a compliance violation that must be caught before go-live.

topics.question: Security review gate checklist before go-live
topics.answer: The security sign-off before production must cover: all `ruleExpression` guards on high-risk actions reviewed and confirmed correct; `attributeMappings` verified for all PII propagation paths; automated adversarial prompt injection test suite executed and passed; Einstein Trust Layer data masking validated with representative PII patterns including custom object fields; toxicity detection threshold reviewed and appropriate for the deployment channel; a ForcedLeak-style indirect injection test executed against any agent that retrieves externally-submitted data; and the Trust Layer zero data retention policy confirmed active. All items require sign-off from the Security Reviewer before the release proceeds.

objectives.title: Run structured release gates from dev through go-live

topics.question: Gate 1 criteria (developer sandbox)
topics.answer: Before a feature branch can open a pull request for merge, four criteria must be met: `sf agent validate authoring-bundle` must pass with zero errors; Apex unit tests on all action implementations must pass with adequate coverage; peer review of the `.agent` file must be completed with documented sign-off; and any `ruleExpression` relaxation must have prior CAB approval documented in the PR. A PR that includes a security guard relaxation without a CAB reference should be blocked from merge automatically by the pipeline. These criteria are fast to verify and catching violations here is orders of magnitude cheaper than catching them in UAT.

topics.question: Gate 2 criteria (integration sandbox)
topics.answer: After the feature branch merges to integration, the CI pipeline must execute the full deployment sequence without errors, the evaluation suite pass rate must meet the team-defined threshold (90% is the recommended starting baseline), action sequencing must be verified for all primary user journeys, and the current evaluation JSON must show no regression against the prior baseline artifact. A pass rate below threshold or a regression against the baseline blocks promotion to QA. The integration gate is the primary automated quality gate — it should be fast enough to run on every merge and sensitive enough to catch meaningful behavioral changes.

topics.question: Gate 3 criteria (QA sandbox)
topics.answer: Gate 3 requires evaluation suite pass rate maintained from integration, multi-turn conversation tests passing across all stateful scenarios, custom JSONPath evaluation criteria passing for all business rules, the full security red-team test suite executed and passed, and Einstein Trust Layer data masking validated with representative PII patterns. This is the most comprehensive technical gate in the process. A failed security red-team result at Gate 3 is a blocker — the change does not move to UAT until the security finding is resolved and the red-team suite is re-executed.

topics.question: Gate 4 criteria (UAT sandbox)
topics.answer: Gate 4 requires the business owner to interact directly with the agent in the UAT environment using the Agentforce Builder live preview, covering all primary user journeys and key edge cases. The business owner's sign-off must be documented — a verbal approval does not satisfy the compliance record. The `bundle-meta.xml` must have been transitioned from draft to committed state with the `<target>` field pinned to the target BotVersion. The versionTag must be assigned for release traceability. Gate 4 is the final business authorization before the change enters the production deployment pipeline.

topics.question: Gate 5 criteria (staging)
topics.answer: Gate 5 requires the full production deployment runbook to execute successfully against the Staging (Full Copy) environment, including all manual steps. The regression baseline from Staging must be compared to the QA baseline with no unexpected behavioral drift. The rollback procedure must be verified — specifically, confirm that reactivating the prior BotVersion actually works within the team's target Recovery Time Objective. CAB review must be completed for any high-risk changes (ruleExpression modifications, net-new agents, shared Prompt Template changes). Staging is the last opportunity to discover environmental issues before production.

topics.question: Gate 6 criteria (production go-live)
topics.answer: The production deployment must be executed during a pre-approved maintenance window, with the activation step (`sf agent activate`) performed as a separate deliberate action rather than automatically. Immediately after activation, run the smoke-test evaluation suite against production. Confirm STDM telemetry is flowing in Data Cloud by querying the `ssot__AiAgentSession__dlm` table. Verify that monitoring dashboards are active and baseline alert thresholds are configured. The on-call team must be briefed with the rollback procedure in hand and confirmation of who has authorization to execute it.

topics.question: Activation window planning and low-traffic scheduling
topics.answer: Deploying a new BotVersion to production does not automatically make it the active version for users. This intentional decoupling gives the team a window to confirm deployment success before exposing users to the new behavior. Plan the activation step during low-traffic periods — overnight for customer-facing agents in a single timezone, during business hours for internal tools where IT support is available. Have the rollback procedure ready to execute within minutes of activation. Monitor STDM telemetry and Trust Layer audit logs for the first 30-60 minutes after activation as the highest-risk window.

topics.question: Avoiding Friday/pre-holiday activations without on-call
topics.answer: Never schedule production activation on a Friday or immediately before a public holiday unless explicit on-call staffing is arranged and confirmed. Behavioral regressions in AI agents often require investigation of STDM telemetry and evaluation output, which takes time and expertise. If a regression is discovered on Friday evening, the team needs to be able to respond — not just execute the BotVersion rollback, but also investigate root cause and communicate status to business stakeholders. Treat pre-holiday activations as high-risk change windows requiring a separate risk approval.

topics.question: Seasonal release impact on agent behavior
topics.answer: Salesforce's three annual releases can affect agent behavior in ways that bypass standard metadata change management. API version shifts can change how `GenAiPlannerBundle` is structured or retrieved, producing format mismatches on the next deployment. LLM model updates behind the Agentforce platform can alter baseline response quality even when no metadata changes have been made, causing evaluation scores to drift. Critical Updates that affect Apex, Flows, or platform behavior can break action implementations. Opt in to Critical Updates in a non-production sandbox as soon as they become available and run the evaluation suite before auto-activation.

topics.question: Aligning UAT cycles ahead of seasonal upgrade windows
topics.answer: Run UAT cycles before the production upgrade window, not after. Salesforce seasonal releases auto-activate in production on a scheduled date — if UAT is running concurrently or after the upgrade, any behavioral change caused by the platform upgrade will appear to be caused by the feature under test, making root cause analysis extremely difficult. Schedule UAT to complete and business owner sign-off to be documented at least 4-6 weeks before the seasonal production upgrade window, so the two events are clearly separated in the change timeline.

objectives.title: Design rollback and hotfix recovery strategies

topics.question: Option 1 — reactivating a prior BotVersion
topics.answer: Reactivating a prior BotVersion using `sf agent activate --version {prior}` is the fastest rollback path, completing in seconds. It switches users to the prior agent version without redeploying any metadata, because the prior BotVersion's compiled runtime graph is already present in the org. This is the preferred path for behavioral or routing regressions where the underlying action implementations have not changed. The only precondition is that the prior BotVersion has not been deleted — which is why retaining at least the two most recent BotVersions in production is a hard requirement.

topics.question: Option 2 — redeploying prior AiAuthoringBundle from source control
topics.answer: If the prior BotVersion has been deleted from the org, or if the regression is in the underlying action implementations (Apex class, Flow) rather than the agent's reasoning layer, a full redeploy of the prior version from source control is required. This involves the complete five-phase deployment sequence followed by publish and activation, which takes significantly longer than a BotVersion reactivation. Reserve this path for cases where BotVersion reactivation alone cannot restore the correct behavior, and ensure the prior source control tag is clearly documented in the release record.

topics.question: Option 3 — targeted Apex/Flow-only rollback
topics.answer: When the behavioral issue is isolated to one action implementation — the action is returning incorrect outputs, failing with unhandled exceptions, or consuming excess governor limits — a targeted rollback of only the affected Apex class or Flow from source control is the most surgical option. This avoids the risk of reactivating an older BotVersion that may be missing other bug fixes from recent releases. Verify via STDM telemetry that the action failure rate (`FunctionStep` error counts in the Step table) drops to baseline levels after the targeted rollback is deployed.

topics.question: Preconditions for guaranteeing fast rollback availability
topics.answer: Fast rollback depends on decisions and preparations made before the production deployment, not during a live incident. The prior BotVersion must not have been deleted. The rollback command (`sf agent activate --version {prior}`) must be documented in the deployment runbook with the exact version number. The rollback procedure must have been tested during the Staging dry run to confirm it actually works within the target Recovery Time Objective. The on-call team must have read the runbook and must have the permissions required to execute the rollback without waiting for the original deployer to become available.

topics.question: Retaining minimum BotVersion history
topics.answer: Always retain at least the two most recent BotVersions in the production org. Deleting a BotVersion eliminates the fast-rollback safety net for that version. If a regression is discovered and the prior BotVersion has been deleted, the only recovery path is a full source-control redeploy, which takes significantly longer and carries more risk during an active incident. Define BotVersion retention as an organizational policy and enforce it as part of the post-deployment runbook — the prior version is confirmed present before the new version is activated.

topics.question: Rollback runbook testing during staging dry runs
topics.answer: The Staging dry run must include a verification that the rollback procedure works within the required Recovery Time Objective. Execute `sf agent activate --version {prior}` against the Staging environment and measure the time from command execution to confirmed behavioral restoration (verified by a smoke-test evaluation run). If the RTO target is not met, investigate whether the bottleneck is the activation step itself, the evaluation run, or the team's response coordination process, and address it before the production window.

topics.question: On-call readiness to execute rollback independently
topics.answer: The rollback command, the prior BotVersion identifier, and the verification steps must all be documented in the deployment runbook in sufficient detail that any on-call engineer can execute them without calling the original deployer. During an incident, the original deployer may be unavailable or may be actively diagnosing the root cause in parallel. The rollback must be executable by the first available qualified engineer. Test this by having a team member who was not involved in the deployment execute the rollback procedure during the Staging dry run.

topics.question: Severity classification for emergency hotfix qualification
topics.answer: Pre-define the criteria that classify an incident as a genuine emergency warranting hotfix process rather than the standard release cycle. Typical criteria include: measurable revenue impact above a defined threshold per hour, a user-blocking defect affecting a critical workflow with no workaround available, an active security vulnerability with confirmed exploitation evidence or high CVSS score, and a confirmed compliance violation with regulatory notification obligations. Classification against pre-defined criteria takes seconds. Without pre-defined criteria, severity classification becomes a stakeholder negotiation that delays both the decision and the fix.

topics.question: Post-incident review and root-cause documentation
topics.answer: Every rollback or hotfix deployment must be followed within 48 hours by a post-incident review that documents the root cause, identifies which specific governance gate failed to catch the issue, defines the process or testing change that prevents recurrence, and assigns an owner and deadline for each preventive action. The review output is added to the project governance record and referenced in the next CAB meeting. This review is not a blame exercise — it is a structured learning process that continuously improves the team's governance effectiveness.

topics.question: Advising clients on RTO targets for agent incidents
topics.answer: Help clients set Recovery Time Objectives for agent incidents by mapping each failure mode to its recovery path. Behavioral/routing regressions can be recovered via BotVersion reactivation in minutes — an RTO of 15 minutes is achievable. Action implementation failures requiring a targeted Apex rollback add deployment time — an RTO of 30-45 minutes is realistic. Full source-control redeployments for worst-case scenarios may take 60-90 minutes including evaluation verification. RTO targets must be set with the specific recovery path in mind, not as a single number that implies all agent incidents are equal in severity and recovery complexity.

objectives.title: Operate production observability across Trust Layer, STDM, and debug logs

topics.question: The three-system observability stack overview
topics.answer: Effective Agentforce production monitoring requires connecting three distinct telemetry systems simultaneously. The Einstein Trust Layer audit logs capture the security and compliance dimension: what data left the trust boundary, whether it was masked, and whether toxic content was blocked. The Session Telemetry Data Model (STDM) in Data Cloud captures the behavioral dimension: every routing decision, action invocation, variable state change, and error condition across every conversation. Standard Salesforce debug logs capture the implementation dimension: SOQL queries, governor limit consumption, and Apex execution details within action calls.

topics.question: Einstein Trust Layer audit log contents
topics.answer: Each Trust Layer audit log entry contains the original prompt (pre-masking), the masked prompt sent to the LLM provider, toxicity scores for both outbound and inbound content, grounding sources used in the prompt, the raw LLM response before de-masking, and a zero-retention confirmation. Review these logs after every deployment to verify that masking patterns are behaving as expected for the new or changed agent configuration. Anomalies — unexpected grounding sources, missing masking of known PII fields, toxicity scores near the threshold — should trigger immediate investigation before user traffic scales up.

topics.question: STDM's five core tables and their purposes
topics.answer: The STDM architecture spans five Data Cloud tables. `ssot__AiAgentSession__dlm` stores aggregate session-level metadata and initialization parameters. `ssot__AiAgentSessionParticipant__dlm` identifies users and agents involved in each session. `ssot__AiAgentInteraction__dlm` groups individual conversation turns within a session. `ssot__AiAgentInteractionMessage__dlm` stores the exact user utterances and raw agent responses per turn. `ssot__AiAgentInteractionStep__dlm` stores every micro-action by the reasoning engine — this is the most critical diagnostic table, revealing the exact execution path of every turn including subagent selection, action invocations, and variable mutations.

topics.question: Querying the Step table to reconstruct a failed session
topics.answer: When a user reports that the agent failed to complete a task, query the STDM Step table using the session ID to reconstruct the exact execution sequence. Join `ssot__AiAgentInteractionStep__dlm` to `ssot__AiAgentInteraction__dlm` and `ssot__AiAgentSession__dlm` using standard ANSI SQL in the Data Cloud Query Editor, ordering by turn number and step sequence. The query reveals which subagent was selected, which action was invoked, what input parameters were passed, what output was returned, and at which step an error or unexpected transition occurred. This is the definitive diagnostic tool for complex agent behavioral failures.

topics.question: Standard debug logs for Apex-level diagnostics within actions
topics.answer: When the STDM Step table shows an action invocation with an error output or unexpected result, the corresponding Apex debug log provides the implementation-level detail: the exact SOQL queries executed, DML statements, governor limit consumption, exception messages, and variable values at each point in the execution. Correlate the STDM FunctionStep timestamp with the Apex debug log timestamp to find the right log entry. Use the same debug log analysis techniques you would apply to any other Salesforce Apex diagnostic — agent actions are standard Invocable Apex classes from the platform's perspective.

topics.question: Establishing a production behavioral baseline within 24 hours of go-live
topics.answer: Within 24 hours of the first production activation of an agent (or a new BotVersion), run the regression evaluation suite against the production org and store the JSON output as the production baseline artifact. This baseline captures the agent's behavioral state in the actual production environment, which may differ slightly from UAT due to data differences, permission set assignments, or feature flag states. Future evaluation runs are compared against this production baseline, not the UAT baseline, to detect behavioral drift with production-representative context.

topics.question: Key health indicators: routing accuracy, action success rate, escalation rate
topics.answer: Monitor three primary health indicators on a continuous basis. Subagent routing accuracy — the percentage of sessions routed to the correct subagent for the user's expressed intent — indicates whether the reasoning engine is correctly interpreting user utterances. Action invocation success rate — the percentage of FunctionStep records that complete without error — indicates whether the underlying Apex and Flow implementations are functioning correctly in production. Escalation rate — the percentage of sessions where the user was transferred to a human agent — indicates whether the agent is capable of resolving the use cases it was designed for; an unexpected spike often signals a routing or quality regression.

topics.question: Session abandonment rate as a UX signal
topics.answer: Users who end a conversation before completing their intended task represent a failure mode that evaluation metrics alone may not surface. An agent that routes correctly and produces coherent responses can still frustrate users if its responses are too verbose, too slow, or require too many clarification turns. Track session abandonment rate as a leading indicator of user experience quality, segmented by the subagent where the user abandoned. A subagent with a significantly higher abandonment rate than others is a signal for an authoring review of that subagent's instruction set and response patterns.

topics.question: Einstein Requests consumption anomalies as a looping-behavior signal
topics.answer: The average Einstein Requests (ER) consumed per session should be relatively stable across a population of similar conversations. An unexpected spike in average ER per session — with no corresponding increase in conversation length or user traffic — is typically an early indicator of a looping agent (the reasoning engine repeatedly invoking an action without satisfying a termination condition) or an inefficient action chain (multiple sequential LLM calls where one would suffice). Configure Proactive Monitoring alerts for ER consumption anomalies before go-live, so the operations team is notified before the issue escalates to rate limiting.

topics.question: Agent Rate Limit Error monitoring and alerting
topics.answer: When Einstein Requests are exhausted or throttled at the org level, Salesforce generates Agent Rate Limit Error events. These events affect all AI activity in the org, not just the agent that triggered the rate limit. Configure Proactive Monitoring alerts in Setup to notify the operations team when ER consumption approaches the throttling threshold — not after the throttle is triggered, but before it. An unexpected spike in ER consumption is often a leading indicator of a looping agent, an inadvertent action chain, or an external traffic spike, all of which require investigation before the rate limit causes user-facing service degradation.

objectives.title: Build a continuous improvement loop from monitoring data

topics.question: Feeding STDM data back to the development team, not just ops
topics.answer: STDM telemetry is most valuable when it flows to the developers who authored the agent's instructions, not just the operations team watching dashboards. Developers who can see the exact subagent routing decisions, action invocation sequences, and variable state transitions from real user sessions will write better evaluation cases, identify ambiguous instructions before they cause incidents, and design more resilient action chains. Create a shared dashboard or a daily digest that gives developers visibility into real session patterns without requiring them to write STDM queries themselves.

topics.question: Converting production failures into new evaluation test cases
topics.answer: Every session captured in STDM where the agent misrouted an utterance, returned an inadequate response, or failed mid-action should become a new `AiEvaluationDefinition` test case within 48 hours of discovery. Extract the utterance from `ssot__AiAgentInteractionMessage__dlm`, the expected routing from the session context, and any multi-turn history required to reproduce the failure. Adding the case to the evaluation suite ensures that the specific behavioral gap that surfaced in production is covered in every future regression run — converting the cost of a production failure into a permanent improvement in coverage depth.

topics.question: Tracking Instruction Adherence trend lines over time
topics.answer: Plot the Instruction Adherence scores for each subagent over time as a trend line rather than point-in-time measurements. A score that holds steady at HIGH for 60 days and then begins declining is a signal worth investigating — especially if no metadata changes have been deployed during that period. Declining instruction adherence without a corresponding deployment event is the clearest indicator of LLM model-level drift, where the platform's underlying model has shifted its interpretation of the authored instructions. The trend data is what makes this distinction visible before users start reporting failures.

topics.question: Distinguishing authoring fixes from deployment on trend cause
topics.answer: When Instruction Adherence scores drop, the remediation path depends entirely on the cause. If scores dropped immediately after a deployment, the deployment changed the authored instructions in a way the model interprets differently — the fix is an authoring revision in a new feature branch, followed by the standard release cycle. If scores dropped gradually with no deployment event, the fix is also an authoring revision, but the cause is model-level drift — and rolling back a deployment will not help because nothing was deployed. Rolling back a BotVersion to address model-level drift actively makes the situation worse by also reverting any intentional improvements.

topics.question: Escalation pattern analysis by subagent
topics.answer: Segment escalation events by the subagent from which the escalation occurred, and track each subagent's escalation rate independently over time. A subagent with a consistently higher escalation rate than its peers signals one of three conditions: the subagent's instructions do not match the range of user intents it is being routed to handle, the subagent's available actions do not provide the resolution capabilities users need, or users in this domain have expectations the agent cannot meet as currently designed. Each root cause requires a different authoring response — instruction revision, new action implementation, or an explicit scope limitation communicated to users upfront.

topics.question: Monthly behavioral health checks independent of deployments
topics.answer: Schedule a recurring evaluation suite run against the production org on a fixed monthly cadence, independent of the deployment calendar. This run uses the same suite and the same comparison baseline as post-deployment evaluations, but its purpose is specifically to detect model-level drift that occurs between deployments. When nothing has shipped and scores drop, the investigation focuses on LLM platform updates and seasonal API changes, not deployment artifacts. Document the results of each monthly health check in the project governance record alongside deployment-triggered evaluation results.

topics.question: Toxicity block-rate monitoring as an injection-campaign indicator
topics.answer: The Trust Layer toxicity block rate — the percentage of responses blocked before reaching users — should be stable day over day under normal conditions. An unexpected spike in the block rate, particularly if it is concentrated in a specific channel or subagent, can indicate an active adversarial campaign targeting the agent with prompts designed to elicit toxic responses or trigger repeated LLM calls. Route toxicity block-rate alerts to the Security Reviewer in addition to the operations team, since an injection campaign requires a security response rather than just an operational one.

topics.question: Anomalous grounding source detection in audit logs
topics.answer: After every deployment, review the Trust Layer audit logs for grounding sources that are appearing in prompts but should not be — retrievers that were not configured, knowledge articles from an unexpected domain, or external data sources that were not intended to be part of the agent's context. Unexpected grounding sources are a signal of misconfiguration or, in more serious cases, a successful injection attack that has altered the agent's retrieval behavior. Review the grounding sources section of each audit log entry for at least the first 24 hours after a production deployment, when configuration errors are most likely to surface.

topics.question: Common deployment error catalog as a training tool for client teams
topics.answer: Maintaining a living catalog of documented deployment failure patterns — with root cause explanations and step-by-step remediation procedures — is one of the highest-leverage investments for reducing client support dependency.
