When a client administrator encounters `Required fields are missing: [PlannerId]`, they should be able to look it up in the catalog and resolve it without escalating to the implementation partner. Include at minimum: the PlannerId error (missing `GenAiPlannerBundle`), the `UNKNOWN_EXCEPTION` after seasonal format conversion (orphaned XML), the Retriever ID mismatch pattern, and the no-op committed bundle deployment scenario. Train client administrators on the catalog during handoff, not after their first incident.

topics.question: Building a client-facing AgentOps maturity scorecard
topics.answer: Summarize the client's current AgentOps maturity across five dimensions into a single scorecard: governance (roles defined, CAB process in place, unauthorized-change controls active), environment strategy (full six-tier hierarchy established, refresh cadence aligned to release calendar), testing depth (all pyramid layers in place, red-team suite active, multi-turn coverage present), security posture (attributeMapping coverage complete, Trust Layer validated, adversarial testing continuous), and monitoring coverage (STDM dashboards active, behavioral baseline established, monthly health checks scheduled). Use this scorecard at the start of each engagement phase to prioritize the highest-impact improvements and measure progress over time.

agentops.title: Ideation, Agent Script Authoring & Agent Interoperability

objectives.title: Design agent specifications before writing Agent Script

topics.question: Shifting from programmatic thinking to a Jobs-To-Be-Done framework
topics.answer: The ideation phase is led by an Agent Design Architect who maps business logic into agentic behavior. This requires a mindset shift away from traditional programmatic thinking — where you decompose a problem into functions and control flow — toward a "Jobs-To-Be-Done" framework, where you decompose a problem into the discrete jobs a user is trying to accomplish and the conversational path to get there. Architects who skip this reframing tend to produce subagents that mirror code modules rather than user intents, which degrades routing accuracy later.

topics.question: Building the Agent Specification Document before any Agent Script is written
topics.answer: Before writing a single line of Agent Script, architects must thoroughly complete the Agent Specification Document, capturing every potential interaction path. This document precedes and informs the technical build — it is the artifact that turns a business requirement into something an Agent Developer can actually implement. Skipping it produces subagents built on assumption rather than a mapped-out interaction model, leading to rework when the agent reaches evaluation and fails on scenarios that were never considered.

topics.question: Writing Intent Table rows at the correct level of granularity
topics.answer: The Intent Table maps exactly what the user wants, what the agent should do, and how it should respond. Granularity matters: "manage orders" is too vague to route or test against, while "look up order status by order number" is the right level — specific enough to become a subagent description, an evaluation utterance, and a defined action target in one motion. Vague intent rows are a leading cause of poor routing accuracy once the agent reaches evaluation, because the LLM router has no precise boundary to classify against.

topics.question: Defining Out of Scope topics and designating a fallback sub-agent
topics.answer: The specification must explicitly list topics the agent must refuse or redirect — for example, HR policy questions reaching a sales agent. Beyond listing them, the spec should designate a fallback or off-topic sub-agent to catch unhandled queries cleanly, rather than letting the primary reasoning engine improvise a response to a query it was never designed to handle. An agent without a defined fallback path tends to produce inconsistent, ungoverned responses to out-of-scope requests in production.

topics.question: Mapping Branching & Edge Cases as explicit specification rows
topics.answer: Add a row to the specification for every "what if" scenario: What if the user lacks permissions for the record they're asking about? What if the backend API times out? These branching and edge-case rows become the source material for both the before_reasoning/after_reasoning deterministic logic and the deterministic logic test suite later in the lifecycle. An edge case not captured in the spec is an edge case that won't be tested until a user finds it in production.

topics.question: Classifying Variables & Persistence needs (linked vs. mutable strings)
topics.answer: Identify which data must persist across conversation turns — for example, User Email or Order Number — and classify each as a linked or mutable string. This classification determines how the variable is declared and referenced in Agent Script and feeds directly into the conversation-variable design that before_reasoning and reasoning blocks depend on. Getting this classification wrong at the spec stage is a common source of working-memory bugs that surface later as multi-turn conversation test failures.

topics.question: When a single multi-topic agent should become multiple agents
topics.answer: A single agent is already multi-purpose and can serve multiple jobs-to-be-done via topics (subagents) — this is the default starting point, and most business problems do not require more than one agent. Architects should resist the instinct to split into multiple agents prematurely; unnecessary agent proliferation multiplies the governance, deployment, and monitoring overhead without a corresponding architectural benefit. Split only when one of four triggers applies: different lifecycle/release cadences, independent invocability via API or A2A, reusability across multiple agents, or fundamentally different brand/persona tone requirements.

topics.question: The four triggers for splitting into separate agents
topics.answer: Trigger 1 — Lifecycle: different teams require different release cadences and deployment boundaries, forcing them onto the same schedule if bundled. Trigger 2 — Independent Invocation: the capability needs to be called independently via a direct API call or over an Agent-to-Agent (A2A) platform. Trigger 3 — Reusability: the capability is needed by multiple other agents or surfaces, justifying extraction into its own independently versioned agent. Trigger 4 — Brand/Persona: the agent requires a fundamentally different tone (e.g., calm support vs. aggressive sales), which is configured at the agent level and cannot be cleanly served from one agent.

objectives.title: Author subagents using Agent Script's hybrid reasoning model

topics.question: Enabling Einstein Setup and the Agentforce Agents builder as prerequisites
topics.answer: Before any agent-specific work begins, navigate to Setup > Generative AI > Einstein Setup and turn Einstein on, then navigate to Agentforce Agents and toggle the builder on. This is the org-level enablement step that every later pre-flight checklist assumes is already done — without it, subsequent deployment or publish steps fail with feature-not-enabled errors that have nothing to do with the metadata itself.

topics.question: Installing packages and extracting invocable actions as agent tools
topics.answer: Install any unmanaged packages or flow templates the agent will depend on, then extract the invocable actions — Flow or Apex — that the agent will use as tools. Every action a subagent references in Agent Script must already exist as a deployed, invocable target in the org. This extraction step is the practical bridge between "the business logic exists somewhere in the org" and "the agent can actually call it."

topics.question: Subagent anatomy: description and actions as the two load-bearing keys
topics.answer: Every subagent (topic) is a modular conversation unit built around two load-bearing keys. The description field tells the Agent Router exactly when to select this subagent — it is effectively the routing signal the LLM planner matches incoming utterances against, making its wording as consequential as any routing configuration in the platform. The actions key holds full tool definitions, including inputs, outputs, and a target (for example, target: "flow://amenities_search" or target: "apex://GetCustomerInfo") that points at the invocable action extracted during setup.

topics.question: before_reasoning: deterministic logic that runs ahead of the LLM
topics.answer: The before_reasoning block executes deterministic logic before the LLM takes over — formatting data, verifying required fields are present, or triggering secondary actions such as computing a missing field. This block exists precisely because not every step in a conversation turn should be left to probabilistic interpretation; anything that must happen reliably and identically every time belongs here rather than in a natural-language instruction the model might interpret inconsistently.

topics.question: reasoning: the core natural-language instruction block
topics.answer: The reasoning block is the core block containing natural language instructions and the tools the model is allowed to use for this subagent. This is where the authored intent lives in the most human-readable form, and it is the block peer reviewers should scrutinize most closely, since a small wording change here can shift how the model interprets its available tools and its authority to use them.

topics.question: after_reasoning: deterministic logic that runs once the LLM yields
topics.answer: The after_reasoning block runs deterministic logic once the LLM yields control back — commonly used to transition to a thank-you state or to execute a silent follow-up trigger that shouldn't be described conversationally to the user. Like before_reasoning, this block guarantees an outcome happens regardless of how the model phrased its response, which is why deterministic logic tests target these blocks directly rather than relying on LLM-as-a-Judge scoring to confirm they ran.

topics.question: Reading the arrow (->) and pipe (|) syntax markers in Agent Script
topics.answer: Agent Script enforces a hard boundary between code and prompts using two syntax markers. The arrow (->) means "run this code deterministically" — it precedes instructions like run @actions.lookup_order with email=@variables.customer_email or a set statement assigning an output to a variable. The pipe character (|) means "AI Prompt / Generate response" — text following a pipe is natural language the model generates or is guided by, not code the platform executes literally. Misreading which marker governs a given line is a common source of confusion when reviewing unfamiliar .agent files.

topics.question: Worked example: conditional lookup with deterministic and generative branches
topics.answer: A representative reasoning block runs a deterministic lookup, stores the result in a variable, then branches: run @actions.lookup_order with email=@variables.customer_email, followed by set @variables.order=@outputs.order_data. The subsequent if @variables.order is None: branch uses a pipe-marked line to generate a clarifying response, while the else: branch uses a pipe-marked line referencing the variable directly in the generated text. This pattern — deterministic retrieval, then a pipe-marked branch for the conversational response — is the standard shape of a well-formed subagent reasoning block.

objectives.title: Configure model selection and debug with the Trace Panel

topics.question: Three-level model configuration hierarchy: Org Default, Agent Config, Sub-agent Config
topics.answer: Model selection follows a three-level override hierarchy. The Org Default level applies globally and serves as the standard baseline for all generative tasks in the org unless overridden. The Agent Config level overrides the Org default and is placed at the top of the agent script — use this when an entire agent requires a heavier model for complex workflows. The Sub-agent Config level overrides both Org and Agent settings and is the most granular level — ideal for mixed-workload agents where one subagent needs a fast classifier while another needs a heavy reasoning model.

topics.question: When to override model selection at the Agent vs. Sub-agent level
topics.answer: Override at the Agent Config level when an entire agent's workload requires a heavier model across all of its subagents — for example, an agent whose every topic involves multi-step reasoning over ambiguous natural language. Override at the Sub-agent Config level when the workload is mixed — for example, using a fast, low-cost classifier model for simple routing decisions in one subagent, while using a heavy reasoning model for data generation in another subagent within the same agent. Most subagents should be left at the Org default; overriding should be a deliberate choice justified by a specific cost, speed, or reasoning requirement.

topics.question: Live Test Mode as the fastest in-builder feedback loop
topics.answer: The Agentforce Builder contains a Live Test Mode where you can chat with the agent directly inside the build environment. This is the fastest available feedback loop during active development — faster than a full evaluation suite run or a CLI-based preview session — and it is where an Agent Developer should be validating each new subagent or action before committing it to source control.

topics.question: Trace Panel event: recognizeIntentFromUtterance
topics.answer: The Trace Panel's recognizeIntentFromUtterance event shows exactly how the router interpreted the user's message. When a subagent selection looks wrong, this is the first trace event to inspect — it reveals whether the router extracted the intent you expected from the utterance before any topic classification happened.

topics.question: Trace Panel events: classifyTopic and evaluateTopicFilter
topics.answer: The classifyTopic event shows which subagent the router selected based on the recognized intent, and evaluateTopicFilter shows whether any filter condition gated that subagent's availability. Together these two events are where a misrouting problem is actually diagnosed — a wrong description field will surface here as an incorrect classification, while an overly restrictive filter will surface as a subagent being skipped even when it was the right match.

topics.question: Trace Panel event: updateConversationVariables
topics.answer: The updateConversationVariables event fires when entities like orderNumber are extracted from the conversation and written into conversation variable state. This is the trace event to inspect when diagnosing a working-memory issue — if a variable that should have been populated from an earlier turn is missing here, the extraction step itself is the point of failure, not a later action or response step.

topics.question: Trace Panel event: generateAgentResponse
topics.answer: The generateAgentResponse event marks the final response-generation step, after all reasoning, action invocation, and variable updates have completed. Comparing what reached this step against what the user actually saw is a quick way to confirm whether a display or formatting issue occurred after generation, versus a reasoning issue that occurred before it.

topics.question: CLI-based batch validation with sf agent test run
topics.answer: For robust CI/CD validation beyond the interactive builder, use sf agent test run with the target-org flag and validate against pre-built batch tests to confirm regression bugs haven't been introduced. The Live Preview Trace Panel is for interactive, single-conversation debugging during development, while batch testing is for repeatable, automated batch validation in a pipeline.

objectives.title: Extend agents with A2A protocol and post-deployment governance

topics.question: Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol: Discovery via Agent Cards
topics.answer: Agents publish Agent Cards — JSON documents advertising their capabilities, required inputs, and authentication schemes. An Agent Card is how an external client agent (in-org or third-party) discovers what a given agent can do and what it needs to be given before it can be invoked, without requiring out-of-band documentation or a manual integration conversation.

topics.question: A2A Task & Execution: the Client-Server request model
topics.answer: A Client agent sends a Task request over HTTP using JSON-RPC 2.0, containing a message and its parts, and the Server agent executes that task. This Client/Server framing allows agents to orchestrate or be orchestrated by third-party systems rather than only ever operating inside their own conversation flow — the same agent can be a Server responding to another system's Task requests and, in a different interaction, act as a Client issuing its own.

topics.question: A2A Communication: negotiating UX and supporting sync, async, and push delivery
topics.answer: Agents exchange messages and negotiate user experience details — such as UI capabilities and content formats — as part of the A2A exchange. The protocol supports synchronous request/response, asynchronous delivery via server-sent events (SSE)/streaming, and push notifications, giving architects flexibility in how a long-running or multi-step A2A task reports progress back to the calling agent.

topics.question: A2A Security: enforcing authentication declared on Agent Cards
topics.answer: All A2A interactions enforce the authentication requirements declared on the Agent Cards. An architect enabling A2A interoperability for an agent must treat the Agent Card's declared authentication scheme as a hard contract — a Server agent will not accept a Task request that doesn't satisfy the scheme it advertised, which is the mechanism that keeps A2A interoperability from becoming an ungoverned open integration surface.

topics.question: Auditable Analytics: every decision, tool call, and inference logged in Data Cloud
topics.answer: Every single agent decision, A2A tool call, and LLM inference is logged in Data Cloud, providing a full audit trail for compliance and allowing teams to reconstruct exactly why an agent took a specific action. This is the high-level governance framing behind the STDM table structure — the STDM tables are the concrete implementation of this auditability principle.

topics.question: Data Governance & Permissions: agents inherit the acting user's access model
topics.answer: Agentforce acts on behalf of the user, strictly obeying Salesforce sharing rules, field-level security, and organizational hierarchies — data never leaks beyond what the human user is authorized to see. This is a foundational security property: an agent does not get its own independent, broader view of the org's data than the user driving the conversation already has, which materially bounds the blast radius of a misconfigured action or a successful prompt injection attempt.

objectives.title: Determine business strategies, goals, initiatives, and challenges to define the scope of a Salesforce project or business initiative.

topics.question: Distinguishing between a business goal, a business initiative, and a project scope when a sponsor presents a vague problem statement
topics.answer: A business goal is the high-level desired outcome (e.g., 'increase revenue by 15%'). A business initiative is the planned effort or program to achieve that goal (e.g., 'implement a CRM to improve sales tracking'). Project scope is the specific boundary of what will and will not be delivered in a given engagement (e.g., 'deploy Sales Cloud for the North America team with Opportunity management and reporting'). When a sponsor is vague, a BA's job is to ask clarifying questions to peel back the layers: first understand the goal (why), then the initiative (what broadly), then define scope (what specifically within this project).

topics.question: How a BA identifies and documents the business goals and strategic drivers at the start of a Salesforce engagement to define project scope
topics.answer: At project kickoff, the BA conducts discovery interviews and workshops with executive sponsors and key stakeholders. They ask questions like 'What does success look like in 12 months?' and 'What business problem are we solving?' The BA then documents findings in a project charter or business case, capturing: stated goals, measurable success criteria (KPIs), strategic drivers (e.g., competitive pressure, regulatory change), and how Salesforce will support each driver. This document becomes the anchor for all subsequent scope decisions.

topics.question: Techniques for uncovering unstated business challenges during initial discovery conversations with executives
topics.answer: Executives often describe symptoms, not root causes. BAs use open-ended questions ('What keeps you up at night about this process?'), active listening, and the '5 Whys' technique to drill deeper. Other tactics include reviewing existing reports or dashboards before the meeting to identify performance gaps, asking about past failed initiatives, and probing for pain points in handoffs between teams. The goal is to surface hidden challenges before they become late-stage surprises.

topics.question: How a BA documents a business case or project charter to capture objectives, success criteria, assumptions, and constraints for sponsor approval
topics.answer: A project charter typically includes: (1) Problem/Opportunity statement, (2) Business objectives with measurable KPIs, (3) Proposed solution overview, (4) In-scope and out-of-scope items, (5) Assumptions (what we believe to be true), (6) Constraints (fixed limitations like budget, timeline, or technology), (7) Stakeholders and roles, and (8) High-level milestones. The BA drafts this and walks sponsors through it for formal sign-off, establishing a shared baseline before work begins.

topics.question: Identifying and documenting project assumptions and constraints during discovery and why they must be validated with stakeholders
topics.answer: Assumptions are conditions believed to be true but not confirmed (e.g., 'all users have Salesforce licenses'). Constraints are fixed limitations that cannot be changed (e.g., 'go-live must be before Q4 close'). Both must be explicitly documented because unvalidated assumptions become risks—if the assumption turns out to be false, it can derail the project. Stakeholder validation ensures everyone agrees on the boundaries before design begins, preventing costly rework later.

topics.question: How a BA uses SWOT analysis or similar frameworks to align Salesforce project scope with business strategy
topics.answer: A SWOT analysis (Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, Threats) helps a BA evaluate whether a proposed Salesforce solution fits the business context. Strengths and opportunities inform what the solution should leverage; weaknesses and threats highlight risks and constraints that should shape scope. For example, if a weakness is poor data quality, the BA would include a data cleansing workstream in scope. SWOT ensures the Salesforce project addresses real strategic priorities rather than just solving a surface-level symptom.

topics.question: Recognizing when a stated project objective is misaligned with the underlying business strategy and how a BA should respond
topics.answer: Misalignment occurs when a tactical objective does not actually advance the company's strategic goals (e.g., automating a process the business plans to eliminate). The BA should flag the misalignment by revisiting the business strategy with the sponsor, presenting evidence of the disconnect, and facilitating a discussion to either realign the objective or formally document that the project is intentionally tactical. The BA should not silently proceed with a misaligned scope.

objectives.title: Discover how a customer is leveraging existing products to establish the current state.

topics.question: Why establishing current state is a prerequisite before defining future state requirements in a Salesforce engagement
topics.answer: Without understanding the current state, requirements may duplicate existing functionality, ignore technical debt, or miss critical dependencies. The current state baseline reveals what is working (keep), what is broken (fix), and what is missing (add). It also prevents over-engineering—if a feature already exists in Salesforce, it does not need to be rebuilt. Skipping current state analysis is a common cause of scope creep, as undocumented existing processes surface during UAT as 'new requirements.'

topics.question: Approaches a BA uses to document the current state of a customer's Salesforce implementation before recommending changes
topics.answer: Key approaches include: (1) Org walk-through with an admin to review existing configuration, (2) Process observation (shadowing users in their daily workflows), (3) Reviewing existing reports, dashboards, and data models, (4) Interviewing end users and power users about their actual usage vs. intended usage, and (5) Reviewing the org's setup audit trail or change history. The BA documents findings in process maps, data dictionaries, and system inventory lists.

topics.question: How a BA documents existing integrations, data flows, and customizations as part of current-state discovery
topics.answer: The BA creates an integration inventory that maps each connected system, the direction of data flow (inbound/outbound), frequency, and the business purpose. Customizations (Apex triggers, Flows, validation rules, custom objects) are cataloged with their business rationale. Data flows are diagrammed to show how records move between systems. This documentation is critical for assessing the impact of proposed changes and preventing integration failures during deployment.

topics.question: Identifying gaps between the customer's current Salesforce usage and best practices during discovery
topics.answer: The BA compares the customer's actual configuration and usage patterns against Salesforce's recommended best practices (e.g., using Process Builder when Flow is preferred, storing sensitive data in non-encrypted fields, or maintaining excessive custom code where declarative tools would suffice). Gaps are documented and presented as opportunities, not criticisms. This informs recommendations for the future state and helps prioritize technical debt reduction alongside new functionality.

objectives.title: Understand and explain Business Analyst roles and responsibilities in different phases of the implementation lifecycle.

topics.question: Distinguishing the BA's role from the project manager's and developer's roles during a Salesforce implementation
topics.answer: The BA focuses on the 'what' and 'why': eliciting, documenting, and validating business requirements. The Project Manager focuses on 'when' and 'how much': scheduling, budgeting, risk management, and delivery coordination. The Developer focuses on 'how': building the technical solution in Salesforce. In practice, the BA is the bridge—translating business needs into requirements the developer can build, and translating technical decisions back into business language for the stakeholders.

topics.question: The primary responsibilities of a BA during the requirements-gathering phase versus the build phase of a Salesforce project
topics.answer: During requirements gathering: eliciting requirements through interviews and workshops, documenting them in requirement specs or user stories, facilitating stakeholder review sessions, and achieving sign-off. During the build phase: answering developer questions about ambiguous requirements, reviewing work-in-progress demos, tracking defects vs. change requests, and managing any scope change requests through a formal process. The BA shifts from a discovery mode to a support and governance mode during build.

topics.question: How the BA role shifts from discovery to design to testing across implementation lifecycle phases
topics.answer: In discovery, the BA leads: facilitating sessions, documenting current state, and capturing requirements. In design, the BA supports: validating proposed solutions against requirements, reviewing wireframes/prototypes, and ensuring nothing is missed. In testing (UAT), the BA leads again: writing test scenarios, coordinating testers, facilitating sessions, and making go/no-go recommendations. The BA is always the guardian of requirements fidelity—ensuring the built solution matches what was agreed.

topics.question: The BA's role within an Agile/Scrum team: backlog grooming, sprint ceremonies, and iterative requirements refinement
topics.answer: In an Agile/Scrum context, the BA often collaborates closely with or acts as the Product Owner. Key responsibilities include: maintaining and prioritizing the product backlog, writing and refining user stories before sprint planning (grooming), participating in sprint planning to clarify story details, being available during the sprint to answer developer questions, reviewing demos at sprint review against acceptance criteria, and incorporating feedback into future stories during retrospectives.

topics.question: Identifying which BA activities are most critical during the deployment and post-go-live phases
topics.answer: During deployment: validating that all configurations are complete and match approved requirements, supporting UAT sign-off, contributing to training materials, and confirming data migration accuracy. Post-go-live: monitoring adoption metrics, capturing user feedback for the next iteration, documenting lessons learned, and supporting hypercare (the period immediately after go-live when users need extra support). These activities ensure the solution delivers the expected business value.

objectives.title: Apply the implementation lifecycle for planning business analysis activities.

topics.question: Sequencing BA activities (discovery, requirements, user stories, UAT) within a standard Salesforce implementation lifecycle
topics.answer: The standard sequence is: (1) Discovery — understand business goals and current state, (2) Requirements — elicit, document, validate, and baseline requirements, (3) User Stories — decompose requirements into sprint-ready stories with acceptance criteria, (4) Build — support developers, review demos, manage change requests, (5) UAT — coordinate testing with business users, track defects, obtain sign-off, (6) Deployment — validate and support go-live, (7) Post-go-live — monitor adoption and capture feedback. Each phase has BA deliverables that feed the next.

topics.question: How a BA plans their own work deliverables, timelines, and stakeholder engagement schedule at the start of an engagement
topics.answer: The BA creates a Business Analysis Plan that lists all BA deliverables (process maps, requirements doc, user stories, UAT scripts), maps each to a project milestone, and identifies which stakeholders are needed for each activity. The plan includes a stakeholder engagement schedule showing who needs to be available, when, and for how long. This is reviewed with the PM to ensure BA activities align with the overall project timeline and resource availability.

topics.question: How a BA creates a business analysis plan that aligns BA deliverables to project milestones
topics.answer: A Business Analysis Plan documents: the scope of BA work, the methods to be used (workshops, interviews, etc.), the deliverables and their owners, the timeline mapped to project milestones, and how changes will be managed. For example, requirements sign-off is mapped to the milestone before build begins. This plan is reviewed and agreed with the PM and key stakeholders to set expectations about BA capacity and sequencing.

topics.question: Identifying which phase of the implementation lifecycle is the correct point to baseline requirements and freeze scope
topics.answer: Requirements should be baselined (formally approved and version-controlled) at the end of the requirements phase, immediately before the build phase begins. At this point, all stakeholders have reviewed and signed off on the documented requirements. After baselining, any new or changed requirements must go through a formal change control process. Freezing scope too early (before adequate discovery) risks missing requirements; freezing too late means rework costs accumulate during build.

topics.question: Adjusting BA activities when a project switches from a waterfall to an agile delivery approach mid-engagement
topics.answer: When switching to agile mid-project, the BA shifts from producing comprehensive upfront documentation to writing iterative, sprint-sized user stories. Existing requirements are decomposed into a prioritized product backlog. The BA moves from milestone-driven sign-off cycles to continuous stakeholder engagement through sprint ceremonies. Formal change control is replaced by backlog reprioritization. The BA must help stakeholders understand that agile trades upfront certainty for flexibility and faster delivery of working software.

objectives.title: Analyze the customer's Salesforce environment(s) to identify opportunities and constraints.

topics.question: How a BA identifies technical constraints in a customer's environment that limit solution options
topics.answer: The BA works with the admin or architect to review: Salesforce edition (which features are available), governor limits (API call limits, storage, record limits), existing customizations that may conflict with proposed changes, active integrations that cannot be disrupted, and org-wide settings (sharing model, multi-currency, etc.). These constraints become inputs to solution design—they define the guardrails within which the future state must be built. The BA documents them and surfaces them during requirements discussions.

topics.question: Techniques for analyzing org limits, technical debt, and configuration constraints as inputs to scoping decisions
topics.answer: Techniques include: reviewing Salesforce Setup > System Overview for storage and API usage; auditing custom objects, fields, and relationships for complexity; reviewing open issues in the org's change/bug log; running a Salesforce Health Check or using tools like Salesforce Optimizer. Technical debt findings (e.g., obsolete workflows, redundant custom fields) inform the BA when proposing scope—some items may need remediation before new features can be added cleanly.

topics.question: Balancing business opportunity identification with realistic constraints when presenting analysis findings to stakeholders
topics.answer: The BA presents a balanced view: here is what the business could gain (opportunities), and here is what limits us (constraints). Framing matters—constraints should not be presented as blockers but as inputs to prioritization. For example, 'We cannot implement Feature X in Phase 1 due to integration dependencies, but it is a strong candidate for Phase 2.' This helps stakeholders make informed scope decisions without feeling like the project is being held hostage by technical issues.

objectives.title: Demonstrate knowledge of Salesforce capabilities, align them with business needs, and recommend potential solutions.

topics.question: Understanding the Salesforce standard data model (standard objects, record relationships, fields) at a level sufficient to assess solution feasibility during discovery
topics.answer: A BA needs to know that Salesforce organizes data into objects (like Accounts, Contacts, Opportunities, Cases) with standard fields and configurable relationships. Understanding that Accounts are parent to Contacts (lookup) and Opportunities (master-detail) helps the BA assess if a business requirement fits the standard model or needs customization. This knowledge lets the BA have credible conversations with admins and architects about feasibility without needing to know how to configure Salesforce directly.

topics.question: Mapping a stated business need to an appropriate Salesforce capability category without over-prescribing a specific configuration
topics.answer: When a stakeholder says 'We need to track follow-up tasks,' the BA maps this to the Activities/Tasks capability in Salesforce rather than immediately recommending a specific Flow or custom solution. The BA operates at the capability level (Sales Cloud, Service Cloud, Marketing Cloud, automation tools, analytics) rather than the configuration level. Over-prescribing a specific technical approach is the architect/developer's job. The BA's role is to confirm that Salesforce has a capability that can meet the need.

topics.question: How a BA evaluates whether a business requirement should be met with out-of-the-box Salesforce functionality versus custom development
topics.answer: The BA applies a 'declarative first' principle: can the requirement be met using standard Salesforce features (fields, page layouts, flows, validation rules, reports)? If yes, custom development adds unnecessary cost and maintenance risk. The BA evaluates by asking: Does standard functionality meet 80%+ of the need? Is the gap truly a business requirement or a preference for a specific UI? Is the workaround reasonable? Only when declarative tools genuinely cannot meet the requirement should custom code be recommended.

topics.question: How a BA positions Salesforce capabilities as potential solutions while deferring the final technical design to the architect or developer
topics.answer: The BA says things like, 'Salesforce has automation tools like Flow that could potentially handle this approval process—let's explore that with the team.' This positions a capability without locking in a design. The BA avoids saying 'We will use a trigger for this' or prescribing specific APIs. After capabilities are confirmed as viable, the architect decides the technical approach. This division of responsibility prevents the BA from inadvertently constraining the technical team's design options.

topics.question: Recommending a phased Salesforce solution when the business need exceeds the project's current scope or budget
topics.answer: When the full business need cannot be delivered in one project, the BA works with stakeholders to define phases based on business value and dependency order. Phase 1 delivers the must-have capabilities (MoSCoW: Must Have), Phase 2 delivers important but deferrable items (Should Have), and Phase 3 addresses nice-to-haves. The BA documents the phasing rationale and ensures Phase 1 is designed with future phases in mind to avoid costly re-work when the solution is extended.

objectives.title: Plan discovery activities based on the target stakeholders to perform a thorough analysis of business needs.

topics.question: Creating a discovery plan that sequences stakeholder engagements to build a complete picture of business needs
topics.answer: A discovery plan sequences sessions strategically: start with executive sponsors to understand goals and priorities, then move to process owners for operational detail, then to end users for ground-level insight. Starting top-down ensures the BA understands strategic context before diving into details, which helps frame user-level conversations. The plan documents each session's objective, format, duration, participants, and pre-reading materials.

topics.question: Identifying the right mix of discovery activities (surveys, interviews, job shadowing) for a complex multi-department rollout
topics.answer: For a multi-department rollout, the BA typically uses: surveys to gather broad input quickly from a large audience, interviews for deep dives with process owners and power users, workshops where cross-departmental alignment is needed, and job shadowing to observe actual workflows that stakeholders struggle to describe verbally. The mix depends on time constraints, stakeholder availability, and whether consensus-building or information-gathering is the primary objective.

topics.question: How a BA tailors discovery session formats (workshop, interview, observation) based on stakeholder role and availability
topics.answer: Executives: short (30-45 min), structured interviews focused on strategy and success criteria—they have limited time and want big-picture conversations. Process owners: workshops or longer interviews to map current-state processes. End users: observation/shadowing is most effective since they often struggle to articulate their process verbally. Remote or unavailable stakeholders: async surveys or document review as a substitute. The format should minimize friction for the stakeholder while maximizing the quality of information captured.

topics.question: How a BA prepares targeted questions for a discovery session based on the stakeholder's organizational level
topics.answer: Executive-level questions focus on strategy ('What does success look like? What are the top three business priorities this initiative must support?'). Manager-level questions focus on process and pain points ('Where does the current process break down? What reports do you wish you had?'). End-user questions focus on day-to-day tasks ('Walk me through what you do when a new lead comes in. What's the most frustrating part of your current tools?'). Tailoring prevents awkward mismatches where a VP is asked about data entry steps.

objectives.title: Identify key stakeholders and develop relationships with them as a trusted advisor to act as a liaison between business and technical teams.

topics.question: Techniques for identifying all relevant stakeholders including hidden or indirect stakeholders at the start of an engagement
topics.answer: Start with a stakeholder identification session with the project sponsor. Ask: 'Who else is affected by this process? Who provides inputs? Who consumes outputs? Who has regulatory or compliance involvement?' Review org charts, process documentation, and existing system user lists. Hidden stakeholders include IT security (for data access), finance (for reporting needs), and downstream teams who receive data from the system being implemented. Missing a key stakeholder early is a leading cause of late-stage requirement changes.

topics.question: The BA's role as a liaison translating business needs into technical language for developers and technical findings into business language for sponsors
topics.answer: When a business user says 'I need to see all my customers who haven't been contacted in 90 days,' the BA translates this into a technical requirement: 'A list view on the Account object filtered by Last Activity Date > 90 days ago, accessible to Sales users.' Conversely, when a developer says 'We need to respect governor limits on SOQL queries,' the BA translates: 'There's a system constraint that limits how many searches run at once—we need to restructure the report to work within those limits.' This translation prevents miscommunication.

topics.question: Using a stakeholder map to identify engagement strategies for each stakeholder group
topics.answer: A stakeholder map is a visual diagram showing all stakeholders positioned by their relationship to the project (internal/external, by department, by level). For each group, the BA documents: what they care about, their communication preferences, their level of Salesforce knowledge, and the appropriate engagement strategy. For example, end users may need hands-on demos, while executives need concise summary updates. The map ensures no stakeholder group is forgotten or under-engaged.

topics.question: Using the Power/Interest Grid to categorize stakeholders and determine the appropriate level of engagement for each category (manage closely, keep satisfied, keep informed, monitor)
topics.answer: The Power/Interest Grid plots stakeholders on two axes: Power (influence over the project) and Interest (degree of impact on them). High Power + High Interest: Manage Closely (frequent, detailed engagement—typically sponsors and key process owners). High Power + Low Interest: Keep Satisfied (periodic updates to maintain goodwill—e.g., senior executives not directly involved). Low Power + High Interest: Keep Informed (regular updates—e.g., end users). Low Power + Low Interest: Monitor (minimal engagement—e.g., peripheral departments). This prevents over-investing in low-impact relationships while under-serving critical ones.

topics.question: Using a RACI matrix to identify engagement strategies for each stakeholder group
topics.answer: RACI stands for Responsible (does the work), Accountable (owns the outcome), Consulted (provides input), Informed (receives updates). For BA activities: the BA is typically Responsible for requirements documentation; the business sponsor is Accountable for approving them; subject matter experts are Consulted; and the development team is Informed. RACI prevents engagement gaps (key people not consulted) and overload (too many people in the 'Responsible' column creating confusion).

topics.question: What the DACI framework roles mean (Driver, Approver, Contributor, Informed) in decision-making
topics.answer: DACI is a decision-making framework: Driver — the person who drives the decision process forward (typically the BA or PM), ensures the decision gets made. Approver — the single person with final decision authority (a sponsor or senior leader). Contributor — people who provide input and expertise to inform the decision (SMEs, developers). Informed — people who need to know the outcome but do not shape it. Unlike RACI, DACI is decision-specific—each major project decision has its own DACI assignment.

topics.question: Applying the DACI framework to clarify decision-making roles and resolve stakeholder conflicts on a Salesforce project
topics.answer: When stakeholders from two departments disagree on a requirement, the BA applies DACI: Who is the Approver for this decision? Is it the VP of Sales or the VP of Service? Once the Approver is identified and agreed, the BA facilitates input from Contributors, documents the decision with rationale, and informs everyone else. This removes the ambiguity of 'who decides' that often stalls projects. The BA acts as the Driver—not making the decision but ensuring it gets made with the right information.

topics.question: Creating a stakeholder communication plan that defines what information is communicated to whom, at what frequency, and through what channel
topics.answer: A stakeholder communication plan is a table/matrix that lists: each stakeholder group, the type of information they need (project status, milestone updates, requirement reviews), the frequency (weekly, bi-weekly, at key milestones), the channel (email, Slack, steering committee meeting, SharePoint), and the sender/owner. It prevents information gaps and ensures stakeholders are not surprised by decisions. The plan is reviewed and agreed at project kickoff and updated when stakeholder needs change.

topics.question: How a BA adapts communication style and content depth when presenting to executive sponsors versus end users versus technical developers
topics.answer: Executives: high-level, outcome-focused, use business metrics and risk language, limit to 5-10 minutes with a one-page summary. End users: concrete, scenario-based, show what it means for their daily tasks—use demos or visual mockups rather than text documents. Technical developers: detailed, precise, include data model specifics, field-level requirements, and edge cases. The same information must be packaged differently for each audience. A BA who pitches a developer's level of detail to an executive—or a high-level vision to a developer—loses credibility with both.

topics.question: How a BA builds credibility and trust with a skeptical senior stakeholder who resists the Salesforce initiative
topics.answer: Start by listening—understand why they are skeptical (past failed projects, loss of control, fear of change). Acknowledge their concerns genuinely. Bring evidence: data showing the problem that Salesforce will solve, and references to similar successful implementations. Involve them early: make them a Contributor in DACI so they feel ownership. Deliver on small commitments quickly to demonstrate reliability. Avoid overselling; be honest about limitations. Trust is earned through consistent honesty and follow-through, not by winning arguments.

topics.question: Recognizing when a BA should escalate a stakeholder conflict versus resolving it directly within the team
topics.answer: A BA should attempt direct resolution when: the conflict involves peer-level stakeholders, the disagreement is about requirements details rather than strategic priorities, and both parties are willing to collaborate. Escalation is appropriate when: the conflict involves competing priorities that require executive decision-making authority, a stakeholder is blocking progress and is not responding to facilitation, or the decision has significant budget or timeline implications. Escalate to the project sponsor or steering committee with a clear summary of the options and their trade-offs, not just the problem.

objectives.title: Given a scenario, choose the most effective technique for eliciting business needs from stakeholders.

topics.question: Choosing between interviews, workshops, observation, prototyping, and document analysis based on the elicitation goal and stakeholder context
topics.answer: Interviews: best for deep-dive with individuals, sensitive topics, or executives. Workshops: best when cross-functional alignment or group consensus is needed. Observation/shadowing: best when stakeholders cannot articulate their process verbally. Prototyping: best when stakeholders struggle to visualize requirements in abstract—showing a UI prompt more specific feedback. Document analysis: best when SMEs are unavailable or when existing materials (SOPs, reports) can substitute. Match the technique to the primary goal: information gathering (interviews/observation) vs. consensus building (workshops) vs. requirement validation (prototyping).

topics.question: The difference between open-ended and closed-ended questions and when to use each during requirements elicitation
topics.answer: Open-ended questions invite narrative responses and surface unexpected information ('Tell me about your current process for handling customer complaints'). Use them early in discovery to explore and learn. Closed-ended questions seek confirmation or specific data ('Does the system currently send an email when a case is closed?'). Use them to validate specifics or confirm understanding. A good elicitation session uses open-ended questions to explore, then closes with targeted questions to confirm what was heard.

topics.question: When facilitated workshops are preferable to one-on-one interviews for requirements elicitation
topics.answer: Workshops are preferable when: multiple stakeholders need to align on a shared process, conflicting requirements from different teams need to be resolved in real time, brainstorming benefits from group energy and cross-pollination of ideas, or time is limited and parallel input is needed. Interviews are better when: topics are sensitive or political, stakeholders need individual preparation time, or stakeholder seniority makes group dynamics awkward. Workshops save time but require skilled facilitation to prevent dominance by vocal participants.

topics.question: Timeboxing agenda items in workshops to achieve elicitation objectives
topics.answer: Timeboxing assigns a fixed time limit to each agenda item (e.g., 20 minutes to map the lead-to-opportunity process, 15 minutes for Q&A). It prevents one topic from consuming the entire session, ensures all agenda items are addressed, and creates a sense of urgency that keeps discussions focused. The BA communicates timeboxes upfront, uses a visible timer, and enforces them by moving off-topic items to a parking lot rather than letting discussions run over.

topics.question: Keeping workshop discussions on track to achieve elicitation objectives
topics.answer: Techniques include: stating the session objective clearly at the start ('Today's goal is to document the case escalation process'), referring back to the agenda when discussions drift, using a parking lot for off-topic but valid items, asking redirecting questions ('How does that relate to the process step we are mapping?'), and involving participants by calling on quieter members to balance dominant voices. The BA is both facilitator and timekeeper—quality outcomes require active session management.

topics.question: Managing a parking lot during facilitated workshops to capture off-topic items
topics.answer: A parking lot is a visible list (whiteboard, shared doc, or virtual sticky note board) where the BA captures valid but off-topic discussion items without letting them derail the session. When an item is parked, the BA acknowledges its value ('That's important—let me put it in the parking lot so we make sure it gets addressed'), preventing the contributor from feeling dismissed. At the end of the session, the BA reviews all parked items and assigns owners or schedules follow-up sessions.

topics.question: Using brainstorming to surface requirements from a large diverse stakeholder group
topics.answer: In a brainstorming session, all participants generate ideas freely without judgment. The BA facilitates with a clear prompt ('What capabilities does the new system need to support your team?'), collects responses rapidly (sticky notes, digital whiteboard, round-robin verbal sharing), and defers evaluation until the generation phase is complete. This prevents groupthink, surfaces diverse perspectives, and ensures quieter participants contribute. After generation, the BA groups and prioritizes the ideas with the group.

topics.question: Using affinity mapping to surface requirements from a large diverse stakeholder group
topics.answer: Affinity mapping (affinity diagramming) is used to organize a large volume of individual ideas into themed clusters. After a brainstorming session, the BA works with participants to group related sticky notes/ideas into categories (e.g., 'Reporting needs,' 'Automation needs,' 'Integration needs'). These clusters become natural requirement categories. Affinity mapping is especially useful when a diverse group has generated many disparate ideas that need to be structured before they can be prioritized or assigned.

topics.question: Using prototypes or wireframes as an elicitation tool to prompt more specific requirements from non-technical stakeholders
topics.answer: Abstract requirements ('We need a better dashboard') become concrete when a stakeholder sees a wireframe or Salesforce prototype. Seeing a visual representation triggers reactions ('This is close, but I also need to see the contract value' or 'This should only be visible to managers'). The prototype does not need to be fully functional—even a basic mockup in tools like Figma or a Salesforce sandbox drives much richer requirements conversations than blank-page interviews. It is especially effective with stakeholders who think visually.

topics.question: Selecting observation (shadowing) as the most appropriate elicitation technique when stakeholders cannot articulate their own processes
topics.answer: Many knowledge workers struggle to describe their own processes accurately because they have become automatic routines. Shadowing involves the BA sitting alongside a user during their actual work and observing in real time. The BA notes each step, tool used, decision made, and workaround employed. This surfaces the 'hidden' process that interviews miss. It is particularly valuable for call center agents, field reps, or data entry roles where the work is highly procedural and difficult to describe abstractly.

topics.question: Using document analysis (reviewing existing reports, SOPs, and process guides) as an elicitation technique when subject-matter experts are unavailable
topics.answer: Document analysis means reviewing existing artifacts—standard operating procedures, training manuals, existing system reports, org charts, data dictionaries, and meeting minutes—to extract requirements without needing live stakeholder time. It is ideal when SMEs are constrained or when the BA needs to pre-populate process maps before a workshop. Limitations: documents may be outdated or incomplete. The BA should validate document-derived requirements with a stakeholder before finalizing them.

objectives.title: Explain how to move from current state analysis to an agreed future state design.

topics.question: How a BA uses current-state process maps as a baseline for facilitating agreement on a future-state design
topics.answer: The BA presents the validated current-state process map to stakeholders and asks: 'Where does this process work well? Where does it break down?' Each identified pain point becomes a target for improvement in the future state. The BA facilitates a structured conversation where stakeholders propose improvements step by step, ensuring the future state is grounded in real problems rather than theoretical ideals. The current-state map prevents the group from designing a future state that forgets how things actually work today.

topics.question: Facilitating a gap analysis workshop to help stakeholders identify the delta between current state and desired future state
topics.answer: A gap analysis workshop places the current-state process map and the desired future-state vision side by side. The BA facilitates a comparison: what steps exist now that will be eliminated, changed, or kept? What new steps or capabilities are needed? Each gap is documented as a requirement or an issue that must be resolved. The output is a gap register that feeds directly into requirements documentation. This structured approach prevents the future state from being designed in isolation from current reality.

topics.question: Steps a BA follows to achieve stakeholder sign-off on the future state design before requirements are written
topics.answer: Steps: (1) Draft the future-state process map based on workshop outputs, (2) Share with participants for async review (typically 3-5 business days), (3) Incorporate feedback and version the document, (4) Schedule a review session to walk through the updated draft and resolve outstanding questions, (5) Obtain formal sign-off (email confirmation or signature on the document). Sign-off before requirements writing ensures that requirements are anchored to an agreed future state, not a moving target.

topics.question: Managing stakeholder disagreement about what the future state should look like and driving toward consensus
topics.answer: When stakeholders disagree, the BA first ensures both parties have heard each other's position by summarizing each view neutrally. Then the BA brings the discussion back to agreed business goals: 'Which option better supports our goal of reducing case resolution time?' If the disagreement cannot be resolved at the working level, the BA applies DACI to identify the Approver and escalates with a clear summary of both options and their trade-offs. The BA documents the outcome in a decision log regardless of which path is chosen.

objectives.title: Given a scenario, manage competing priorities to obtain stakeholder consensus.

topics.question: Techniques for facilitating consensus when stakeholders from different departments have conflicting requirements
topics.answer: Key techniques: (1) Bring stakeholders together in a joint session rather than managing conflicts bilaterally, (2) Anchor discussions to shared business goals ('We all agree the goal is to reduce time-to-close—which approach supports that better?'), (3) Use structured prioritization tools (MoSCoW, dot-voting) to make preferences explicit and objective, (4) Separate the people from the problem—frame disagreements as 'two valid options' rather than 'your view vs. their view,' (5) Document the agreed outcome in a decision log to prevent re-opening settled debates.

topics.question: How a BA uses MoSCoW prioritization to help a group of stakeholders prioritize a backlog of competing requirements
topics.answer: MoSCoW categorizes requirements as: Must Have (non-negotiable; the project fails without it), Should Have (important but could be deferred), Could Have (nice to have if time/budget allows), Won't Have this time (explicitly excluded for now). The BA facilitates the group through each requirement, asking 'If we could only deliver this one thing, would the project still have business value?' to test Must Have claims. MoSCoW creates a shared language for trade-offs and prevents every stakeholder from labeling their item as 'critical.'

topics.question: How a BA uses dot-voting to help a group of stakeholders prioritize competing requirements
topics.answer: Dot-voting (also called multi-voting) gives each participant a fixed number of votes (e.g., 5 dots) and asks them to place their votes on the requirements they feel are most important. Participants can split votes or stack them on one item. The BA counts votes and ranks requirements by total votes received. This technique is fast, visual, democratic, and surfaces genuine group preferences rather than allowing the loudest voice to dominate. It works best after requirements have been listed and briefly explained to all voters.

topics.question: What a RAID log tracks: Risks, Assumptions, Issues, and Dependencies
topics.answer: RAID log: Risks — potential future events that could negatively impact the project (with probability and impact ratings). Assumptions — conditions believed to be true; if they turn out false, they become risks or issues. Issues — problems that have already occurred and need resolution. Dependencies — tasks, decisions, or deliverables that must be completed before another can proceed. The RAID log is a living document maintained throughout the project. The BA contributes to it by surfacing risks and assumptions during discovery and requirements sessions.

topics.question: How a BA uses a RAID log to track and communicate project-level concerns that affect stakeholder decisions
topics.answer: The BA reviews the RAID log regularly (typically in sync with sprint cadence or weekly status meetings) and surfaces items that require stakeholder decisions: 'We have an assumption that the legacy system will be decommissioned before go-live—we need to confirm this with IT or it becomes a dependency risk.' Bringing RAID items to stakeholders proactively ensures decisions are made before they become critical blockers. The log also provides an audit trail of what was known, when, and what action was taken.

topics.question: Using a decision log to document agreed priorities and prevent scope debates from reopening during later project phases
topics.answer: A decision log records: the decision made, the date, who approved it, the alternatives considered, and the rationale. When a stakeholder tries to re-open a previously settled scope debate ('But I thought we were going to include the mobile app'), the BA refers to the decision log as the authoritative record. This prevents revisiting decisions already made and keeps the project moving forward. The decision log is distinct from meeting notes—it captures only formal decisions, not discussion.

topics.question: Identifying when competing stakeholder priorities should be escalated to an executive sponsor for resolution
topics.answer: Escalation to the executive sponsor is appropriate when: the conflict involves budget trade-offs or timeline changes, working-level stakeholders have genuinely irreconcilable priorities, a stakeholder refuses to participate in the consensus process, or the decision has strategic implications that are above the working team's authority level. The BA escalates with a clean summary: 'Here are two options, here are the trade-offs, and here is what we need decided by [date].' Escalating too early undermines the BA's credibility; escalating too late causes project delays.

topics.question: Strategies for maintaining project momentum when one key stakeholder repeatedly blocks consensus on requirements
topics.answer: Strategies: (1) Understand the root cause of resistance—is it fear, workload, or genuine disagreement? Address the root cause. (2) Involve the stakeholder's manager in setting expectations about their participation. (3) Use DACI to formally identify who the Approver is—if the blocker is not the Approver, their veto does not apply. (4) Time-box decisions: inform the stakeholder that if a decision is not received by a specific date, the project will proceed with a default option. (5) Escalate through the project sponsor if repeated blocking creates risk to the timeline.

objectives.title: Demonstrate how to define the scope of a complex business process and break it down into manageable steps.

topics.question: How a BA defines process boundaries (start event, end event, in-scope sub-processes) for a complex cross-functional workflow
topics.answer: Process boundaries define what is inside and outside the process being mapped. The start event is the trigger that initiates the process (e.g., 'Customer submits a support request'). The end event is the condition that marks the process as complete (e.g., 'Case is closed and customer is notified'). In-scope sub-processes are the intermediate steps included in the analysis. Boundary decisions are made with stakeholders to prevent scope from expanding indefinitely. Clearly stating 'This process begins when X and ends when Y' anchors the mapping effort.

topics.question: Decomposing a high-level business process into sub-processes and tasks to a level of detail appropriate for requirements elicitation
topics.answer: Process decomposition works hierarchically: Level 1 is the high-level process (e.g., Order to Cash). Level 2 breaks it into sub-processes (e.g., Order Entry, Credit Check, Fulfillment, Invoicing, Payment Collection). Level 3 breaks each sub-process into tasks (e.g., Order Entry: Receive order, validate product availability, confirm pricing, create order record). The BA stops decomposing when the level of detail is sufficient to write requirements or user stories. Over-decomposing wastes time; under-decomposing leaves gaps.

topics.question: Using swim-lane diagrams to delineate responsibilities and handoffs between departments in a business process
topics.answer: A swim-lane diagram (also called a cross-functional flowchart) assigns each department or role its own horizontal or vertical lane. Process steps are placed in the lane of the responsible party, and arrows crossing lanes represent handoffs. This makes it immediately visible who does what and where delays or miscommunications typically occur (at the handoffs). Swim lanes are especially useful for cross-departmental processes like quote-to-cash or case escalation, where accountability is often unclear.

topics.question: Identifying the correct level of process decomposition—knowing when a process map is detailed enough to drive requirements
topics.answer: A process map is detailed enough when: each task/step can be directly translated into a system requirement or user story, the performer, trigger, input, action, and output of each step are clear, exception paths and decision points are captured, and SMEs agree the map accurately represents the real process. Signs it is too high-level: steps are vague ('process request'), no decision points are shown. Signs it is too detailed: you are documenting keystrokes or menu clicks rather than business-level steps.

objectives.title: Analyze and document a business process to elicit requirements and engage stakeholders to visualize a future state.

topics.question: Selecting the appropriate process notation (BPMN, flowchart, swim lane, UPN) for communicating a process to different stakeholder audiences
topics.answer: BPMN (Business Process Model and Notation): formal, symbol-rich notation best for technical teams and architects who need precise process specifications. Flowchart: simple boxes and arrows, universally understood, good for simple linear processes and general audiences. Swim-lane diagram: flowchart with role/department lanes, best for cross-functional processes where accountability matters. UPN (Universal Process Notation): layered, plain-language notation designed for business users—best for non-technical stakeholders. Match the notation to the audience's literacy, not to what the BA prefers.

topics.question: The key characteristics of Universal Process Notation (UPN): who, what, when, why, how; and layered detail levels
topics.answer: UPN answers five questions for every process box: Who (the role responsible), What (the action performed), When (the trigger or timing), Why (the business reason), and How (the method or tool used). Each process box can be clicked to reveal the next level of detail—creating a layered, drillable view that allows executives to see the high-level view while end users can drill into task-level detail. UPN uses simple plain-language boxes rather than formal symbols, making it accessible to non-technical business users without training.

topics.question: How Universal Process Notation (UPN) differs from BPMN and basic flowcharts
topics.answer: UPN: designed for business users; uses plain-language activity boxes; supports layered detail (click to expand); answers who/what/when/why/how in each box. BPMN: designed for technical process architects; uses formal symbols (events, gateways, tasks, pools, lanes); supports complex parallel flows and exception handling; requires training to read. Basic flowchart: simple shapes (box, diamond, arrow); no formal standard; easy to read but limited in detail and scalability. Key differentiator: UPN is business-readable and layered; BPMN is technically precise but requires expertise.

topics.question: When to use UPN versus a swimlane diagram versus a value stream map when documenting a Salesforce business process
topics.answer: UPN: use when the primary audience is business stakeholders who need to understand and validate a process without process modeling training. Swim-lane diagram: use when the key question is 'who does what' and cross-functional handoffs need to be visible—ideal for showing where Salesforce will automate or facilitate a handoff. Value stream map: use when the focus is on identifying waste, delays, and non-value-added steps in an end-to-end process—more common in lean/operations contexts than typical Salesforce BA work.

topics.question: Facilitating a process mapping session with end users to capture the as-is workflow and identify pain points
topics.answer: Preparation: share a simple process map template and agenda in advance. During the session: start with the trigger ('What starts this process?'), walk through step by step using sticky notes or a digital whiteboard, ask 'What happens next? Who does it?' at each step. Actively probe for pain points: 'Where does this process slow down? What do you do when something goes wrong?' Document exceptions as branches. After the session: clean up and share the draft with participants for review. End users are the most reliable source of as-is process truth.

topics.question: Using a documented as-is process map to derive functional requirements for the to-be Salesforce solution
topics.answer: The BA walks through the as-is process map and for each step asks: 'Should Salesforce do this? Should it automate this? Should it notify someone? Should it capture data at this point?' Each answer generates a candidate requirement. Pain points in the as-is process become improvement requirements for the to-be solution. Steps that Salesforce should replace with automation become automation requirements. Steps that remain manual but need Salesforce data become reporting or visibility requirements. The as-is map is the seed from which to-be requirements grow.

topics.question: Validating a draft process map with stakeholders to confirm accuracy and surface missed steps or exceptions
topics.answer: Validation involves sharing the draft map with the stakeholders who participated in mapping, plus any SMEs who were not present. The BA walks through the map step by step in a review session, asking 'Does this accurately reflect how the process works today?' and 'What have we missed?' Common gaps found in validation: exception paths ('What if the customer doesn't respond?'), handoff steps between teams, and system-specific steps the BA did not observe. Validation must occur before the map is used as a requirements baseline.

topics.question: Identifying exception paths and edge cases in a business process that are not visible in the happy path
topics.answer: The happy path is the process flow when everything goes as expected. Exception paths are what happens when something goes wrong or an unusual condition occurs (e.g., 'What if the credit check fails? What if the product is out of stock? What if the customer disputes the invoice?'). BAs uncover exception paths by asking 'What could go wrong here? What do you do when X doesn't work?' during process mapping sessions. Exception paths often generate some of the most important requirements—and are frequently forgotten until UAT.

objectives.title: Document business processes in a version controlled repository to manage scope.

topics.question: Why process documents should be stored in a version-controlled repository and how this supports scope management
topics.answer: Version control gives every document a history: who changed it, when, and what changed. For scope management, this means: (1) The baseline version (the signed-off version) is always recoverable, (2) Scope changes are traceable—you can see exactly when and why a process step was added or removed, (3) Disputes about what was agreed are resolved by looking at the version that was signed off, not memory. Without version control, process documents become unreliable as they accumulate informal edits and stakeholders disagree about what the 'current' version says.

topics.question: How a BA uses version history of process documents to manage scope changes and communicate decisions
topics.answer: When a stakeholder requests a process change after sign-off, the BA updates the document with a new version number, documents what changed and why in a change log, and routes the updated version for approval. The version history shows the delta between the baseline and the proposed change, making the impact explicit. This is presented to the stakeholder as: 'Here is the original agreed process, here is the proposed change, and here is the impact on scope and timeline.' The decision and approval are recorded in the change log.

objectives.title: Understand the differences between scope, requirements and user stories.

topics.question: Distinguishing between project scope, a business requirement, a functional requirement, and a user story
topics.answer: Project scope: the boundaries of the entire engagement—what is included and excluded ('The project covers Sales Cloud for North America'). Business requirement: a statement of a business need or outcome ('Sales managers need visibility into pipeline health'). Functional requirement: a specific capability the system must provide to meet the business requirement ('The system must display a dashboard showing Opportunity stage distribution by owner'). User story: a development-ready description of a feature from the user's perspective ('As a Sales Manager, I want a pipeline dashboard so that I can identify at-risk deals'). Each level is progressively more specific.

topics.question: How scope, requirements, and user stories relate hierarchically and how changes to one affect the others
topics.answer: Scope defines the outer boundary; requirements describe what must be true within that scope; user stories are the development-ready decomposition of those requirements. A change to scope (expanding or contracting the project) requires reviewing all requirements and user stories to add, remove, or modify items accordingly. A change to a requirement ripples down to the user stories that implement it and potentially up to scope if it represents significantly new work. This hierarchy means changes must be impact-assessed at all levels.

topics.question: Distinguishing between functional requirements (what the system does) and non-functional requirements (how the system performs)
topics.answer: Functional requirements describe system behavior and capabilities: 'The system must automatically assign a new Lead to the territory manager based on zip code.' Non-functional requirements describe qualities of the system: performance ('The dashboard must load in under 3 seconds'), security ('Only Managers can view salary data'), scalability ('The solution must support 10,000 concurrent users'), usability ('The mobile interface must be navigable with one thumb'). Both types are essential—a functionally correct solution that is too slow or insecure fails to meet business needs.

topics.question: The main categories of non-functional requirements: performance, security, scalability, usability, and availability
topics.answer: Performance: how fast the system responds under expected load. Security: who can access what data, how data is encrypted and audited. Scalability: how the system behaves as data volumes or user counts grow. Usability: how easy and intuitive the interface is for the target users. Availability: what uptime/downtime windows are acceptable (e.g., '99.9% uptime during business hours'). In Salesforce, these often translate to: sharing rules and permission sets (security), Salesforce governor limits (scalability), report load times (performance), and page layout design (usability).

topics.question: Why both functional and non-functional requirements must be captured during elicitation
topics.answer: Functional requirements without non-functional requirements lead to solutions that work correctly in demo conditions but fail in production. For example, a Salesforce report that returns correct data but takes 45 seconds to load will be abandoned by users. Non-functional requirements set the quality bar that the solution must meet, not just the features it must have. Capturing both types during elicitation—rather than discovering performance or security gaps in UAT—prevents expensive late-stage rework and ensures the delivered solution is truly fit for purpose.

topics.question: Where each category of non-functional requirement surfaces in a Salesforce project
topics.answer: Performance: large report queries, Flow trigger volumes, API callout frequency. Security: field-level security, sharing rules, profiles/permission sets, encryption at rest. Scalability: data storage limits, API call limits, record-triggered automation volume. Usability: page layout design, mobile optimization, accessibility compliance. Availability: Salesforce's standard SLA is 99.9%—custom integrations or batch jobs may add downtime risk. The BA surfaces these during requirements discussions by probing: 'How many users will use this feature? Who should have access? How quickly do you need results?'

topics.question: Classifying a given artifact as scope statement, requirement, or user story based on its characteristics
topics.answer: Scope statement: describes project boundaries, not specific capabilities—'The project will implement Sales Cloud for the North America sales team, including Lead management and Opportunity tracking.'
