Dashboard components: gauge for current error rate vs SLA threshold, bar chart for volume by system, and a list of recent failures requiring attention. Share dashboards with business stakeholders via Salesforce access (no dev tools required). Schedule report emails for daily/weekly health summaries. Use Report Types to join log records to related Salesforce objects for context.

topics.question: Designing integration audit trail reports that capture message volumes, success/failure rates, and SLA compliance over time for stakeholder reporting
topics.answer: Audit trail report design: log each integration execution in a custom object with timestamps (start time, end time), volume processed, success count, failure count, and SLA target. Create Salesforce Report Types joining the log object to related records. Build matrix reports showing volume and error rates by day/week/month. SLA compliance: calculate processing time against the SLA threshold (e.g., percentage of records processed within 15 minutes). Schedule reports to run automatically and email to stakeholders. Archive older log records to Big Objects if long-term retention is required.

topics.question: Defining reporting requirements that distinguish transient failures (auto-recovered) from persistent failures (requiring business escalation) in integration monitoring dashboards
topics.answer: Transient failures: initially failed but successfully retried automatically. These should be logged with status 'Auto-Recovered' and tracked in a separate report metric (retry rate). Persistent failures: failed after all retry attempts and require human intervention. Log with status 'Failed - Pending Review' and trigger an automated alert. Dashboards should show: two separate gauges (transient vs persistent failure rates), a list of persistent failures pending review, and a trend line showing if the retry rate is increasing (early warning of a systemic issue). Distinguish these clearly so business stakeholders don't confuse auto-recovered events with true failures.

topics.question: Establishing integration governance reporting: tracking API consumer usage by connected app, enforcing rate limits per consumer, and providing capacity planning data to integration architects
topics.answer: Integration governance reporting: use the /limits REST endpoint and EventLogFile to extract API call counts per Connected App. Build a Salesforce Dashboard or external BI report showing: API consumption per Connected App as a percentage of daily limits, trends over 30/60/90 days for capacity planning, and Connected Apps approaching their fair-share threshold. Enforce rate limits: configure API gateway (MuleSoft API Manager) policies to throttle per Connected App. Provide monthly capacity planning reports to integration architects showing growth rates and projected limit exhaustion dates to inform licensing and architecture decisions.

reasoningengine.title: The Mental Model: What the Reasoning Engine Is

objectives.title: Understand what 'Daisy' is and how its three-layer architecture is the foundation for all Agentforce reasoning.

topics.question: What is 'Daisy' and what does it formally compile into when an agent is published?
topics.answer: 'Daisy' is the informal name for the Agentforce runtime planner — the engine that receives a user message, interprets the AgentScript file, and produces a response. According to Salesforce documentation, when you publish an agent via the CLI, Daisy formally compiles into the GenAiPlannerBundle metadata artifact. It is not a single large language model. It is a hybrid execution environment combining three layers: (1) a deterministic resolver that evaluates your authored logic before any LLM is involved, (2) an LLM reasoning loop where an underlying foundation model makes probabilistic decisions within the constraints the resolver has already enforced, and (3) the Einstein Trust Layer, a runtime security boundary that wraps every LLM call. Every reasoning behavior, every bug, and every optimization in Agentforce traces back to the interaction between these three layers.

topics.question: What is the fundamental split between the deterministic layer and the LLM layer, and what does each control?
topics.answer: Salesforce best practices describe a clear division of responsibility between the two primary layers. The deterministic layer handles: if/else condition evaluation, variable injection into prompt text, run @actions.X execution, available when filtering of tool schemas, transition to routing, and set variable capture. The LLM layer handles: which action to call, how to fill slot parameters, what to say to the user, whether to respond or call a tool, and how to phrase and sequence the response. The critical insight documented in Salesforce's Agentforce developer resources is that the LLM never sees raw AgentScript syntax — no if blocks, no run statements, no @variables.X references, and no available when guards. It only ever sees the output of the deterministic pass: a clean, resolved prompt string plus a filtered set of tool schemas. In summary: deterministic logic controls WHAT the agent knows; the LLM controls WHETHER and HOW to act on that knowledge.

topics.question: What is the Atlas engine, what is the Agent Graph, and what two mathematical structures underpin runtime execution?
topics.answer: A common misconception is that AgentScript is interpreted live, line-by-line, at runtime. Salesforce documentation clarifies that the Atlas engine employs a compilation phase when you publish an agent. The .agent file compiles into an Agent Graph that the runtime executes. This graph encodes two underlying mathematical structures. First, a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG): tool invocations, sequential dependencies, and deterministic actions are mapped as a DAG, which prevents infinite loops within automated workflows and guarantees that prerequisites are met before downstream actions occur. Second, a Finite State Machine (FSM): transitions between subagents and internal states are managed via an FSM that records 'backward arrows' indicating when the LLM must retry an action due to a failure, preventing catastrophic workflow degradation. The DAG/FSM duality explains why the runtime behaves with predictability in the deterministic path and with flexibility in the LLM path.

objectives.title: Understand the six operations Phase 1 performs and what it produces as output.

topics.question: What are the six operations Phase 1 performs, in order, and what does it produce?
topics.answer: Every reasoning iteration passes through Phase 1 before the LLM is ever involved. Per Salesforce's AgentScript documentation, the runtime reads reasoning.instructions: -> from top to bottom and performs these operations in sequence: (1) Evaluates if/else if/else conditions against the current values of all variables — only the matching branch's content proceeds; non-matching branches are discarded entirely. (2) Executes run @actions.X calls synchronously — the action runs and its outputs are immediately available. (3) Executes set @variables.X statements, updating variable state immediately. (4) Injects {!@variables.X} tokens by replacing them with current variable values in the pipe text. (5) Evaluates available when guards on each action in the reasoning.actions block — actions that fail their guard are completely removed from the tool schema and the LLM has no awareness they exist. (6) Fires 'transition to' immediately if one is reached, discarding the current prompt and starting fresh in the target subagent — the LLM is never called for this iteration. The output of Phase 1 is a resolved prompt string (only the pipe lines matching current state) and a filtered tool schema (only actions where available when evaluated to True).

topics.question: What does the LLM receive during Phase 2, and what three decisions can it make?
topics.answer: The resolved prompt string and filtered tool schemas from Phase 1 pass through the Einstein Trust Layer and are handed to the underlying foundation model. Per Salesforce's Agentforce developer documentation, the LLM receives exactly four things: (1) one system prompt — either the global system.instructions or the subagent-level system override, never both merged; (2) the full conversation history for the current session; (3) the resolved reasoning.instructions — only the pipe text matching the current variable state, with no conditionals, no run blocks, and no set statements; (4) tool schemas as JSON function schemas for only the actions that passed their available when guard. With this context, the LLM makes one of three decisions: call an action (selects one tool, fills its slot parameters using ellipsis extraction from conversation, and submits the call); produce a terminal response (writes a text reply to the user and ends the current reasoning loop); or delegate to a subagent (calls a subagent as a tool if one is available, which runs its own reasoning loop and returns control).

topics.question: How does the Phase 1 / Phase 2 split function as the primary diagnostic tool for unexpected agent behavior?
topics.answer: Salesforce best practices describe a binary diagnostic framework for unexpected agent behavior. If the wrong instructions reached the LLM, it is a Phase 1 problem: the cause is a wrong variable value, a wrong condition expression, or the use of pipe (|) mode instead of procedural (->) mode in the instructions block. If the right instructions reached the LLM but it acted incorrectly, it is a Phase 2 problem: the cause is a poor action description, ambiguous instructions text, a missing stop condition, or conflicting directives. This binary framing eliminates a large class of guesswork before a trace file is ever opened. Phase 1 problems are diagnosed by inspecting variable state and condition logic. Phase 2 problems are diagnosed by reviewing the LLMStep in the session trace, specifically the messages_sent field and the tool schemas that were made available.

objectives.title: Trace the full execution sequence for a single user message from arrival to turn end.

topics.question: What is the complete sequence of execution for a single user turn, from message arrival through turn end?
topics.answer: Per Salesforce's Agentforce documentation, a complete turn executes in this sequence. First, the user message arrives and triggers the before_reasoning hook (if present), which runs once per turn in deterministic-only mode. It can set variables, run actions, evaluate conditions, and fire transitions. If a transition fires here, the LLM is never called for this turn. Second, if no transition fired, the reasoning loop begins. The loop repeats until a terminal response is produced or the 3-4 iteration hard cap is reached. Each iteration runs Phase 1 (deterministic resolution), then the Einstein Trust Layer, then Phase 2 (LLM reasoning). If the LLM calls an action, the action executes, outputs are captured, the loop counter increments, and Phase 1 re-resolution begins immediately from the top with updated variable state. If the LLM produces a terminal response, the response is sent to the user and the loop exits. Third, after the reasoning loop exits, the after_reasoning hook fires once per turn, running deterministically. The turn then ends and the agent awaits the next user message.

topics.question: What is the re-resolution loop, and why must post-action checks be placed at the TOP of instructions: -> blocks?
topics.answer: The re-resolution loop is the single most misunderstood mechanic in Agentforce. Per Salesforce's AgentScript documentation, after every tool call the entire reasoning.instructions block is rebuilt from scratch using the updated variable state. This is not 'continue from where you left off' — it is a full re-evaluation of the entire instruction block, top to bottom, every time. The critical authoring consequence: post-action conditional checks MUST be placed at the TOP of instructions: -> blocks. When the loop re-evaluates after a tool call, it reads from the top. If a result-check is at the bottom, the LLM sees all prior instructions again (for example, 'please ask the user for their order number') before ever reaching the check, causing double-execution, confusion, and non-deterministic behavior. The correct pattern places the result-check first — for example, 'if @variables.order_status != "": transition to @subagent.show_status' at the very top — followed by the initial user-facing instruction below it, which only the LLM sees on first entry when no result yet exists.

topics.question: What is the backward arrow in FSM terms, and what does it represent in the context of a failed tool call?
topics.answer: The Atlas FSM records 'backward arrows' — a concept from Finite State Machine theory that describes what happens when the LLM attempts a tool call and receives an error payload. Rather than crashing, the FSM records the failure and the LLM reasons into an alternative approach. Salesforce's Agentforce tracing documentation describes these as the visual retry edges visible in trace tooling: they show exactly where the LLM pivoted and which alternative path it took after a failed invocation. The backward arrow mechanism is what prevents catastrophic workflow degradation when an action fails — instead of terminating, the agent has a structured recovery path. This retry logic also contributes to the 3-4 iteration cap concern, since failed retries still consume loop iterations.

topics.question: What does the LLM explicitly NOT see during a reasoning iteration, and what practical authoring rule follows from this?
topics.answer: Per Salesforce's Agentforce developer documentation, the LLM never sees: raw if or else keywords or the conditions they contain; run statements; set statements; available when conditions (failing actions simply do not appear in the tool schema); before_reasoning or after_reasoning block content; subagent names or the concept of subagents as a structural entity; the @variables.X syntax (it only sees the resolved value after {!@variables.X} injection); or any action invocations that fired deterministically during Phase 1. The practical authoring rule that follows directly: never write a reasoning instruction that tells the model to 'check @variables.X' or 'look at the active subagent.' The model cannot do this. Instructions must state the concrete operational task in plain English based on what Phase 1 has already resolved and injected into the prompt text. Any instruction that references AgentScript constructs directly is an authoring error.

objectives.title: Identify the five instruction surfaces, when each fires, who processes it, and whether it supports an instructions: wrapper.

topics.question: What are the five instruction surfaces in AgentScript, and how do they differ in lifecycle and processing?
topics.answer: Salesforce's AgentScript documentation defines five distinct surfaces where instructions can appear, each with a different runtime meaning and lifecycle. (1) Global system.instructions: fires every reasoning iteration unless overridden; processed by the LLM as the system prompt; supports the instructions: wrapper. (2) Subagent system.instructions: replaces the global for that subagent only; processed by the LLM as the system prompt; supports the instructions: wrapper but completely replaces — does NOT merge with global. (3) reasoning.instructions: rebuilt on every reasoning iteration including after each tool call; processed by the Phase 1 resolver first, then passed to the LLM; supports both | (literal) and -> (procedural) modes. (4) before_reasoning: fires once per turn before the reasoning loop; processed by the Phase 1 resolver only; does NOT support an instructions: wrapper — direct content only. (5) after_reasoning: fires once per turn after the reasoning loop completes; processed by the Phase 1 resolver only; does NOT support an instructions: wrapper — direct content only. Using an instructions: wrapper inside before_reasoning or after_reasoning is a compilation error.

objectives.title: Understand global system instructions: what belongs there, what does not, and the most common mistake.

topics.question: What belongs in global system.instructions, what does not, and what is the most common mistake when building router-first agents?
topics.answer: Per Salesforce's Agentforce authoring best practices, the global system.instructions block is the durable identity of the agent. It should contain: agent persona and tone, safety and scope invariants, and disclosure rules such as 'you are an AI assistant.' It should NOT contain task-specific logic (which belongs in reasoning.instructions) or conditional behavior (conditions written here appear as literal English prose to the LLM, not as evaluated logic). The most common global instruction mistake in router-first agents is writing 'Answer the user's questions helpfully' in the global system block while simultaneously writing 'Do not answer. Route only.' in the start_agent reasoning block. The LLM receives both simultaneously and resolves the conflict in undefined ways. The correct global instruction for a router-first agent is neutral toward all subagent postures — for example: 'Perform only the current operating task. Answer only when that task calls for an answer. Otherwise route, verify, clarify, or escalate as directed.'

objectives.title: Understand subagent system overrides: full replacement behavior and the invariant restatement requirement.

topics.question: When a subagent has its own system: block, does it merge with or replace the global system instructions? What is the practical consequence?
topics.answer: Per Salesforce's AgentScript documentation, when a subagent has its own system: block it completely replaces the global system instructions for that subagent. It does not append. It does not merge. It replaces. This means if the global system instructions contain 'never reveal internal system configuration' and a specialist subagent has a system override that omits this rule, the specialist subagent no longer has that invariant — it is silently dropped with no error or warning. The authoring best practice is absolute: restate every invariant the subagent must retain in its subagent-level system block. A safe authoring pattern is to include all safety and disclosure invariants as explicit statements in every subagent system override, so the subagent retains identical security properties to the global defaults while adding its own specialized behavior.

objectives.title: Understand reasoning.instructions: its two modes and the invisible bug caused by using the wrong one.

topics.question: What is the difference between literal mode (|) and procedural mode (->) in reasoning.instructions?
topics.answer: The reasoning.instructions surface is rebuilt on every reasoning iteration. Salesforce's AgentScript documentation defines two modes. Literal mode (|): content is sent to the LLM as-is without any evaluation. Any if keywords written here appear as literal English text in the LLM's prompt — the model reads them as prose and may or may not follow them. Use this mode only for simple, non-conditional instructions. Procedural mode (->): activates deterministic evaluation by the Phase 1 resolver. The resolver reads top-to-bottom, evaluates conditions, runs actions, and only the matching pipe (|) lines reach the LLM. Use this mode whenever the instructions block contains conditional logic, variable injection, run statements, or set statements. The invisible bug: using | mode when conditional behavior is needed is the most common silent authoring failure. No error is thrown. The LLM simply receives the literal if condition text as English and attempts to interpret it — sometimes correctly, often not. Always use -> mode when any conditional logic appears.

objectives.title: Understand before_reasoning and after_reasoning: when each fires, valid uses, and compile constraints.

topics.question: When does before_reasoning fire, what is it used for, and what is the critical syntax constraint?
topics.answer: Per Salesforce's AgentScript documentation, before_reasoning runs once per turn before the reasoning loop begins. It runs in deterministic-only mode — it can set variables, run actions, evaluate conditions, and fire transitions, but it does not invoke the LLM. It is used for: authentication and authorization gates (failing fast before any LLM cost is incurred), mandatory data pre-loading that every reasoning iteration will need, and early exits for invalid session states. The critical syntax constraint: before_reasoning does NOT use an instructions: wrapper. Content goes directly under the block as a direct child. Using 'instructions: ->' inside before_reasoning is a compilation error that produces no helpful error message. The correct syntax places transition, run, set, and if statements as direct children of the before_reasoning block.

topics.question: When does after_reasoning fire, what is it used for, and what two behavioral distinctions are critical to understand?
topics.answer: Per Salesforce's Agentforce documentation, after_reasoning runs once per turn after the reasoning loop produces a terminal response. The LLM has already spoken before after_reasoning executes. It is used for: state cleanup and logging, conditional transitions based on what the turn accomplished, and recording that a workflow step completed. Two critical behavioral distinctions: First, after_reasoning fires after the reasoning loop ends with a terminal response — it does NOT fire after each tool call within the loop. Second, if a subagent transitions mid-reasoning via @utils.transition to (LLM-driven handoff), the original subagent's after_reasoning does NOT run. Only a terminal text response triggers after_reasoning. Like before_reasoning, after_reasoning does not support an instructions: wrapper — direct content only. Using an instructions: wrapper is a compilation error.

reasoningengine.title: Variables and State in the Reasoning Loop

objectives.title: Distinguish mutable variables from linked variables: syntax, requirements, and constraints.

topics.question: What are mutable variables, what syntax do they require, and what is the boolean capitalization rule?
topics.answer: Per Salesforce's AgentScript language documentation, mutable variables are session-persistent values the agent can both read and write. They must have a default value declared at definition. Valid types include string, number, and boolean. Example declarations: customer_name as 'mutable string = ""', order_count as 'mutable number = 0', and is_verified as 'mutable boolean = False'. A critical and frequently misunderstood constraint: boolean default values must be capitalized — True or False. The AgentScript parser rejects lowercase true and false, producing a compile error. This boolean capitalization mistake is one of the most common compile errors in Agentforce development and does not always produce a clear error message indicating the exact cause.

topics.question: What are linked variables, what syntax do they require, and how do they differ from mutable variables?
topics.answer: Per Salesforce's AgentScript documentation, linked variables are read-only values populated from external session context. They must have a source declaration and must NOT have a default value — providing a default value on a linked variable is a compile error. Common linked variables include: EndUserId linked to @MessagingSession.MessagingEndUserId, RoutableId linked to @MessagingSession.RoutableId, and ContactId linked to @MessagingSession.ContactId. Linked variables expose the identity and session context that Salesforce establishes at session start. They are the primary mechanism for knowing who the user is without asking them. Service agents typically use MessagingSession-sourced linked variables, while employee agents use @session.sessionID as their primary source.

objectives.title: Master the three scope zones and understand the silent failure zone.

topics.question: What are the three scope zones in AgentScript and when is each valid?
topics.answer: Salesforce's AgentScript language documentation defines three distinct variable scope zones. @variables.X is session-persistent state — valid anywhere in AgentScript logic and injectable into pipe text via the {!@variables.X} syntax. @outputs.X holds action return values — valid ONLY in set and if statements immediately after the action's run block; the scope expires after those statements complete. @inputs.X holds action input values — valid ONLY in with clauses during action invocation, NOT valid in set statements or post-execution checks. Understanding these scope boundaries is essential because violations produce silent failures: the action executes successfully, the variable simply is not set, and no error is thrown or logged in a way that makes the cause obvious.

topics.question: What is the silent failure zone, and what does a correct versus incorrect @outputs usage look like?
topics.answer: Salesforce best practices flag @inputs and @outputs scope violations as the most dangerous bugs in AgentScript because they produce no error. The action executes successfully, the variable does not get set, and nothing in surface behavior reveals what happened. Example of an @inputs violation: writing 'set @variables.station = @inputs.station_name' after the action has already run — the @inputs scope has expired and the set silently does nothing. Example of an @outputs violation: referencing '{!@outputs.customer_location}' in a pipe line after the immediate set statements from the action block have completed — @outputs is gone at that point. The correct pattern captures ALL needed output values immediately in set statements directly under the run block, then uses @variables references everywhere else. In session traces, a FunctionStep that completes with no postVars diff is the diagnostic indicator of a scope violation.

topics.question: How do variables persist across subagent transitions, and why is this the primary data-passing mechanism in multi-subagent flows?
topics.answer: Per Salesforce's Agentforce documentation, @variables persist across subagent transitions. A variable set in Subagent A is fully available in Subagent B after the transition. This is the primary mechanism for passing state through a multi-subagent workflow without external storage or session middleware. A practical example: an identity verification subagent can set @variables.is_verified = True and @variables.customer_id after running a verification action, then transition to an order management subagent. The order management subagent's before_reasoning block can then check if @variables.is_verified == False and redirect back to the verification subagent if needed. This pattern creates a stateful, secure multi-step workflow entirely within the AgentScript session scope.

objectives.title: Understand the @utils.setVariables turn-end side effect and the correct alternative.

topics.question: What is the turn-end side effect of @utils.setVariables, and what is the correct pattern for capturing a value and immediately acting on it?
topics.answer: Per Salesforce's Agentforce documentation, @utils.setVariables is the LLM-driven slot-filling utility that lets the LLM extract values from conversation and populate variables. It has a non-obvious and frequently misunderstood behavior: it ends the turn after capturing values. Instructions do not re-evaluate in the same turn after setVariables runs. This means any action listed after setVariables in the same reasoning.actions block will NOT fire in the same turn — the turn has already ended. The correct pattern for 'capture then immediately act' is LLM slot-fill directly on the target action using the ellipsis operator: 'with order_id = ...' lets the LLM extract the order_id and call the action in one turn without the turn-ending side effect of setVariables. Use @utils.setVariables only when collecting variables across multiple turns is the explicit and intentional design goal.

objectives.title: Know the three input binding patterns and the security implications of choosing between them.

topics.question: What are the three ways to populate action parameters, who fills each, and when is each appropriate?
topics.answer: Salesforce's AgentScript documentation describes three input binding patterns with different runtime behavior. LLM slot-fill (syntax: 'with param = ...'): the LLM extracts the value from conversation context at Phase 2 reasoning time. If the value is absent from conversation, the LLM will prompt the user. Variable binding (syntax: 'with param = @variables.X'): the runtime reads the variable at Phase 1 resolution time, before the LLM is involved. If the variable is empty, the action receives an empty string with no user prompt. Literal value (syntax: 'with param = "fixed"'): a compiled constant resolved at Phase 1. The choice between ellipsis and @variables.X is security-critical: use @variables.X when the value has already been verified and should not be extractable from arbitrary user input; use the ellipsis only when the LLM legitimately needs to extract the value from conversation. Pinning a verified identifier (such as a customer ID confirmed through an auth gate) to @variables.X prevents a malicious user from substituting a different ID through natural language.

objectives.title: Distinguish deterministic action invocation from LLM-driven invocation.

topics.question: What is deterministic action invocation (run @actions.X), when does it fire, and what does the LLM see as a result?
topics.answer: Per Salesforce's AgentScript documentation, deterministic invocation uses the 'run @actions.X' syntax and fires during Phase 1 before the LLM is called. The action always executes when the code path is reached, regardless of what the LLM would think or decide. The LLM never sees the run statement — it only sees the resolved pipe text with injected variable values after the action has already completed. Deterministic invocation is appropriate for: pre-loading data that every reasoning iteration will need, security checks and authorization gates, mandatory logging, and chaining multiple actions in a guaranteed order. Because it fires every time the code path is reached, a run statement inside a reasoning.instructions block without a preceding condition guard can fire on every reasoning iteration, multiplying execution costs.

topics.question: What is LLM-driven action invocation (reasoning.actions block), and what makes a good action description?
topics.answer: LLM-driven invocation places actions in the reasoning.actions block and fires during Phase 2. The LLM decides whether and when to call the action based on the action's description field and the current conversation context. Per Salesforce's Agentforce authoring best practices, the description is the primary signal for tool selection — it must be specific enough for unambiguous selection. A vague description like 'Get data' is an anti-pattern; the LLM cannot reliably distinguish between tools with similar vague descriptions and will select incorrectly or hallucinate parameters. A correct description is specific and complete — for example: 'Look up the current status, estimated delivery date, and tracking number for a customer order by order ID.' The description should state what the action retrieves or does, what data it returns, and what parameter it requires.

objectives.title: Understand available when as a hard Phase 1 filter and how it differs from prose authorization.

topics.question: How does available when work, and why is it fundamentally different from a prose authorization instruction?
topics.answer: Per Salesforce's AgentScript documentation, available when is a hard Phase 1 compiler-level filter. When the condition evaluates to False during Phase 1, the action is completely absent from the tool schema handed to the LLM. The model has zero awareness the action exists. This is fundamentally different from a prose instruction like 'only call this action if the user is verified,' which is probabilistic — the LLM may or may not follow it depending on context, phrasing, and model behavior. available when makes unauthorized tool invocation impossible, not just unlikely. The Salesforce security best practice is clear: any action with financial impact, PII access, or irreversible effects MUST be gated with available when. Multiple available when clauses on a single action are evaluated as a logical AND — all conditions must be True for the action to appear in the tool schema.

objectives.title: Know the three transition mechanisms, where each is valid, and the consequences of using the wrong one.

topics.question: What are the three transition mechanisms, where is each valid, and what happens if you use the wrong one in the wrong context?
topics.answer: Salesforce's AgentScript documentation defines three transition mechanisms with distinct syntax and valid contexts. Bare 'transition to @subagent.X': valid in before_reasoning, after_reasoning, and inside run post-conditions. No LLM is involved — it is deterministic and one-way with no return. @utils.transition to @subagent.X: valid in reasoning.actions only. The LLM decides when to call it. One-way with no return — the caller does not resume. @subagent.X referenced in reasoning.actions (delegation): valid in reasoning.actions only. The LLM decides when to call it. Two-way — control returns to the caller after the child subagent completes its full reasoning loop, and the caller synthesizes the final response. This is the supervision pattern. Using the wrong syntax in the wrong context causes a compilation error that often produces an unhelpful error message with no clear indication of the cause.

topics.question: What is the difference between handoff and delegation/supervision?
topics.answer: Per Salesforce's Agentforce documentation, these two patterns represent fundamentally different control flow models. Handoff uses @utils.transition to: control transfers completely to the called subagent, which generates the final response. The caller never resumes. The original subagent's after_reasoning does not fire if the transition happens mid-reasoning. Delegation (supervision) uses @subagent.X as an action reference in reasoning.actions: the parent orchestrates, the child subagent runs its full reasoning loop and produces a result, and control returns to the parent, which synthesizes the final response. Supervision is the correct pattern when the parent needs to coordinate multiple child agents or synthesize results. Handoff is the correct pattern when the destination subagent should own the full response with no parent involvement.

objectives.title: Understand the zero-hallucination action pattern using filter_from_agent and is_used_by_planner.

topics.question: What are filter_from_agent and is_used_by_planner, and how do they combine to create a zero-hallucination routing pattern?
topics.answer: Salesforce's Agentforce documentation describes two output flags that control what the LLM can see and say about an action's outputs. filter_from_agent: True prevents the LLM from displaying the output value to the user — used for internal routing flags, risk scores, and system IDs that should never appear in agent responses. is_used_by_planner: True allows the LLM to reason about the output value for routing decisions — used for intent classification outputs and decision flags. Combining both flags creates the zero-hallucination routing pattern: the LLM must actually call the action to obtain the routing value (it cannot guess or hallucinate it based on conversation), and it can use the value for routing decisions but cannot expose it to the user. This is the recommended pattern for any intent classification action used in routing — it eliminates hallucinated routing by forcing the LLM to invoke the classifier before making a routing decision.

reasoningengine.title: The Posture Spectrum: Determinism vs. LLM Latitude

objectives.title: Understand the three posture types and when each is appropriate.

topics.question: What are the three posture types — Agentic, Mixed, and Scripted — and when is each appropriate?
topics.answer: Per Salesforce's Agentforce design documentation, posture defines the spectrum between agentic (LLM has latitude to decide) and deterministic (authored control structures govern). Agentic posture is the default: the LLM chooses which actions to call and when, extracts slot parameters from conversation, and determines response content and sequencing. Best for open-ended tasks, information retrieval, and conversational flows with no security or ordering requirements. Mixed posture applies selective determinism: some actions are gated with available when, some parameters are pinned to variable values instead of LLM extraction, and some conditional instructions restrict LLM behavior to matched branches. Best for tasks with security gates, irreversible actions, or external system ordering requirements. Scripted posture is fully deterministic: all transitions use bare 'transition to', all action invocations use 'run', and the LLM has zero discretion about what happens next. Best for regulated workflows, strict legal compliance, and zero-tolerance for variation in execution sequence.

objectives.title: Know the five justifications for adding determinism and the principle against adding it without justification.

topics.question: What are the five justifications for adding deterministic controls, and what happens when you add them without justification?
topics.answer: Salesforce's Agentforce design best practices specify that deterministic controls should be added only when justified by one of five concrete causes. First, regulatory requirement: a compliance rule mandates specific sequencing or disclosure. Second, trust gate: identity verification must complete before access is granted. Third, irreversible action: once fired, the action cannot be undone. Fourth, external system ordering: an external API or system requires operations in a specific sequence. Fifth, observed production failure: a specific behavior has failed in production and deterministic control is the proven fix. If the justification does not match one of these five, keep the posture agentic. Adding determinism for 'just in case' reasons increases brittleness without improving safety — it constrains the LLM's ability to handle natural variation in user input, produces more rigid failure modes when unexpected inputs arrive, and increases maintenance burden without a concrete benefit.

objectives.title: Know the three control primitives for implementing determinism.

topics.question: What are the three control primitives for implementing determinism and what does each one do?
topics.answer: Salesforce's AgentScript documentation defines three primitives for implementing deterministic control. available when: a hard Phase 1 filter that completely removes an action from the LLM's tool schema when the condition is False. Used for authorization gates and irreversible action guards. Parameter pinning: binding a parameter to @variables.X instead of the ellipsis operator forces a specific value at Phase 1 time and removes the LLM slot-fill decision entirely. Used for pre-filling verified data (such as a confirmed customer ID on a payment action) so the LLM cannot extract a different value from malicious user input. Conditional instructions: if/else blocks in 'reasoning.instructions: ->' mode ensure the LLM only sees the branch matching the current state. Used for security-state-dependent instruction sets — showing different instructions to verified versus unverified users. Each primitive operates at a different layer and can be combined for defense-in-depth.

objectives.title: Apply the minimal instructions principle.

topics.question: What is the minimal instructions principle and why do shorter instructions produce better LLM performance?
topics.answer: Per Salesforce's Agentforce authoring best practices, optimal LLM performance comes from concise, focused instructions. The principle is to push as much logic as possible out of AgentScript instructions and into actions — logic in actions is reusable across subagents and agents, and does not add context load to the LLM. Shorter instructions produce better reasoning because the model has fewer competing signals to resolve and a cleaner operational context. Every instruction that does not change behavior should be removed. Adding instructions without a concrete reason actively degrades LLM quality by introducing noise the model must filter. The minimal instructions principle is also directly connected to the 10,000-token architectural heuristic: every unnecessary instruction token brings the context budget closer to the threshold where latency and accuracy degrade measurably.

objectives.title: Understand what the Einstein Trust Layer is, when it operates, and how it differs from authoring-time safety review.

topics.question: What is the Einstein Trust Layer (ETL), when does it operate, and how is it different from the authoring-time safety review?
topics.answer: Per Salesforce's Einstein Trust Layer documentation, the ETL is the runtime security boundary that operates milliseconds before every LLM call, on every turn, for every user session. It sits between Phase 1 output and the LLM. This is distinct from the authoring-time safety review, which catches authoring-level risks once before deployment. The ETL operates continuously in every production session. The ETL processes every assembled context package before it exits the Salesforce trust boundary. The sequence: Phase 1 output (resolved prompt + tool schemas) flows through ETL sharing rule and field-level security enforcement, then ETL input toxicity and injection screening, then ETL zero-retention boundary establishment for the call, then into the LLM gateway and foundation model, then back through ETL output toxicity and grounding checks, then to the reasoning loop as the LLM response.

objectives.title: Understand the Zero-Retention Policy and what it guarantees for enterprise data.

topics.question: What does the Einstein Trust Layer Zero-Retention Policy guarantee, and what does it mean for enterprise CRM data?
topics.answer: Per Salesforce's Einstein Trust Layer documentation, the Zero-Retention Policy guarantees that customer CRM data used for grounding is never stored, logged, or used to train external public models by the underlying LLM providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and others). The data flows into the LLM gateway only for that specific inference call and is discarded immediately after the inference completes. This is a contractual and architectural guarantee from Salesforce, not a configuration option that can be accidentally disabled. The answer to the common enterprise question 'does our customer data train OpenAI's models if we use Agentforce?' is no — the mechanism is the ETL zero-retention policy enforced at the LLM gateway boundary.

objectives.title: Understand prompt guardrails, toxicity detection, and data boundary enforcement.

topics.question: What does the ETL screen for on input, and what does it enforce regarding Salesforce data permissions?
topics.answer: Per Salesforce's Einstein Trust Layer documentation, the ETL screens the assembled input context for malicious prompt injection attempts and inappropriate content before that context reaches the foundation model. It also screens outputs returned from the model before they are passed back to the reasoning loop — toxic or injection-carrying content in the model's response is intercepted at this layer. Regarding data permissions: Salesforce sharing rules and field-level security are enforced at every agent action. Grounding data pulled for an LLM call respects the same permission model as a direct SOQL query executed by the running user. The ETL extends this Salesforce governance model to the LLM boundary — the model cannot be given data the running user is not authorized to see, regardless of how the query or grounding call was constructed.

objectives.title: Understand the 3-4 loop iteration limit and its design implications.

topics.question: What is the 3-4 loop iteration limit, what enforces it, and what does it mean for workflow design?
topics.answer: Per Salesforce's Agentforce platform documentation, the reasoning loop has a hard guardrail of approximately 3-4 iterations before the runtime forces an exit. This is enforced by the Atlas FSM and protects against infinite loops. A reasoning iteration is one complete Phase 1 + Phase 2 cycle — each time the LLM calls an action and re-resolution begins, the iteration counter increments. The design implications are concrete: the engine cannot chain more than 3-4 LLM-driven action calls in a single user turn; workflows requiring more sequential decisions must be broken across multiple user turns; circular subagent references will hit this limit unpredictably and produce confusing failures; and counting the maximum possible loop iterations on every execution path is a required design validation step. When the cap is reached, the platform forces the turn to exit with an error response.

objectives.title: Understand the 10,000-token heuristic, what fills the token budget, and the three optimization levers.

topics.question: What is the 10,000-token heuristic, what fills the token budget, and how do you optimize against it?
topics.answer: Per Salesforce's Agentforce performance guidance, the reasoning engine operates with an effective architectural target of approximately 10,000 tokens per transaction payload. This is not a hard API limit — it is a performance and accuracy heuristic. Every token in the context window adds reasoning latency and creates interpretive load for the model. Beyond roughly 10,000 tokens, response quality degrades and latency spikes become measurable. The sources that fill the token budget and their controllability: global system instructions (100-500 tokens, controllable — keep concise); subagent system override (100-500 tokens, controllable — restate only required invariants); conversation history (grows per turn, partially controllable); resolved reasoning instructions (100-1,000 tokens, controllable — -> mode sends only matching branches); tool schemas for available actions (approximately 100 tokens per action, controllable — available when suppresses irrelevant tools). The three optimization levers: (1) Conciseness: remove any instruction that does not change behavior. (2) Consolidation: merge redundant actions. (3) Filtering: use available when aggressively — every suppressed action removes its schema from the budget. Critical distinction: token count drives latency and LLM accuracy, not credit billing. These are separate concerns with separate optimization levers.

objectives.title: Identify, understand, and remediate all ten documented reasoning anti-patterns.

topics.question: AP-1: | mode with conditional logic (the invisible bug) — what is it, why is it dangerous, and how do you fix it?
topics.answer: This anti-pattern occurs when a developer uses | (literal) mode in reasoning.instructions when the block contains if/else conditional logic. The result: the LLM receives the literal text 'if @variables.is_verified == True:' as English prose and attempts to interpret it as a natural language instruction. Sometimes it follows the intent; often it does not. No error is thrown and no compile warning is produced. This is the most common silent authoring failure in AgentScript development. Salesforce's AgentScript best practices are clear: always use -> (procedural) mode when the instructions block contains any conditional logic, variable checks, run statements, or set statements. The pipe character (|) then marks only the individual lines of text that should reach the LLM after conditions are evaluated by Phase 1.

topics.question: AP-2: Post-action check at the bottom (re-resolution trap) — what is it and how do you fix it?
topics.answer: This anti-pattern occurs when a post-action result check (such as 'if @variables.order_status != ""') is placed at the BOTTOM of a reasoning.instructions block rather than at the top. When re-resolution fires after a tool call, the resolver reads from the top. The LLM sees the initial instruction ('What is your order number?') again before reaching the result check — causing double-execution of initial prompts and non-deterministic behavior where the agent asks users for information it has already retrieved. Per Salesforce's AgentScript documentation and best practices, post-action conditional checks MUST be placed at the TOP of instructions: -> blocks so they fire first on every re-resolution. The initial user-facing instruction goes below the result check and is only visible to the LLM on first entry when no result yet exists.

topics.question: AP-3: Prose-based authorization (security failure) — what is it and why is it insufficient?
topics.answer: This anti-pattern uses a prose instruction in reasoning.instructions to restrict action access — for example, 'Only call the refund action if the customer is verified' — instead of using available when. Prose authorization is probabilistic: the LLM may or may not follow prose restrictions depending on context, phrasing, and model behavior. A sufficiently crafted user input can in some cases cause the LLM to disregard prose restrictions. Per Salesforce's Agentforce security best practices, always use 'available when @variables.is_verified == True' on any action with financial impact, PII access, or irreversible effects. available when is a hard Phase 1 filter — unauthorized tool invocation becomes structurally impossible, not just discouraged. Prose instructions and available when can coexist for defense-in-depth, but prose alone is never sufficient as a security control.

topics.question: AP-4: @inputs used after action execution (silent failure) — what is it and how do you fix it?
topics.answer: This anti-pattern involves using 'set @variables.X = @inputs.paramName' after the action's run block has completed. The @inputs scope expires immediately after the with clauses during action invocation. Any reference to @inputs.X in a set statement after the run block silently fails — the variable is not set, no error is thrown, and the FunctionStep trace shows no output capture in postVars. Per Salesforce's AgentScript scope documentation, use @outputs for post-action value capture (the action's return values). If the input value itself needs to be preserved, assign it to a @variables reference before the action call using a separate set statement, making it available via @variables throughout the subagent's scope.

topics.question: AP-5: instructions: wrapper in lifecycle hooks (compile error) — what is it and how do you fix it?
topics.answer: This anti-pattern involves wrapping before_reasoning or after_reasoning content in an 'instructions: ->' block. Per Salesforce's AgentScript documentation, these lifecycle hooks do not support the instructions: wrapper syntax. Using it causes a compilation error that typically does not produce a clear message identifying the exact cause. The correct pattern places transition, run, set, and if statements as direct children of the before_reasoning or after_reasoning block, with no instructions wrapper of any kind. The hooks support the same deterministic operations as procedural mode instructions — conditionals, run statements, set statements, and transitions — but the content is written as direct children of the hook block, not nested under an instructions: key.

topics.question: AP-6: Wrong transition syntax in wrong context (compile error) — what are the two invalid combinations?
topics.answer: This anti-pattern places @utils.transition to in a directive block (before_reasoning or after_reasoning) or places bare 'transition to' in a reasoning.actions block. Both combinations cause compilation errors with unhelpful error messages. Per Salesforce's AgentScript documentation, the correct pairings are strict: bare 'transition to @subagent.X' is valid only in before_reasoning, after_reasoning, and inside run post-conditions. '@utils.transition to @subagent.X' is valid only in reasoning.actions. Mixing these combinations — for example, writing '@utils.transition to' inside after_reasoning, or writing bare 'transition to' inside a reasoning.actions block — produces compile errors that can be difficult to diagnose without knowing this pairing rule explicitly.

topics.question: AP-7: Contradicting system and instructions (undefined behavior) — what is it and what is the correct fix?
topics.answer: This anti-pattern occurs when the global system.instructions says 'Answer the user's questions helpfully' while a router subagent's reasoning.instructions says 'Do not answer. Route only.' The LLM receives both simultaneously as part of the same system context and resolves the conflict in undefined ways — one instruction will win, but which one is unpredictable across turns and model updates. Per Salesforce's Agentforce authoring best practices, write global system instructions that are neutral toward all subagent postures: 'Perform only the current operating task. Answer only when the task calls for an answer. Otherwise route, verify, or escalate as directed.' This permits each subagent's reasoning.instructions to define the actual behavior without any contradiction at the system level.

topics.question: AP-8: Subagent system override dropping required invariants — what is it and how do you prevent it?
topics.answer: This anti-pattern occurs when a subagent-level system: block omits invariants that were defined in the global system instructions. Because the subagent system block completely replaces — not appends to — the global system instructions, any invariant not explicitly restated is silently dropped. This includes safety disclosures, data protection rules, persona constraints, and all behavioral guardrails defined globally. Per Salesforce's Agentforce security best practices, restate every invariant the subagent must retain in the subagent-level system block. A reliable pattern is to maintain a standard set of invariant statements that is explicitly included in every subagent system override, containing all non-negotiable safety and disclosure requirements that must apply regardless of subagent specialization.

topics.question: AP-9: @utils.setVariables followed by an immediate action (turn-end trap) — what is it and how do you fix it?
topics.answer: This anti-pattern lists @utils.setVariables and a target action in the same reasoning.actions block, expecting the action to fire in the same turn after the variables are collected. Per Salesforce's Agentforce documentation, @utils.setVariables ends the turn after capturing values. The action listed after setVariables never fires in the same turn. The correct pattern is to use the ellipsis slot-fill operator directly on the target action: 'with order_id = ...' causes the LLM to extract the value and call the action in a single turn, achieving capture-then-act without the turn-end side effect. This pattern is more efficient (one fewer turn per workflow step) and avoids the silent failure of the turn-end trap.

topics.question: AP-10: Vague action description leading to wrong tool selection — what is it and what does a correct description look like?
topics.answer: This anti-pattern uses generic descriptions such as 'Get data' or 'Look up information' for actions in the reasoning.actions block. Per Salesforce's Agentforce authoring best practices, the LLM uses the description as its primary signal for tool selection during Phase 2. Vague descriptions make it impossible to reliably distinguish between similar actions, leading to wrong tool invocation, hallucinated parameters, or the LLM asking the user to clarify something it should have already known. A correct description is specific enough for unambiguous LLM selection. It should include: what the action retrieves or does, the specific data it returns, the parameter it requires, and any relevant context about when to use it. Example of a correct description: 'Look up the current status, estimated delivery date, and tracking number for a customer order by order ID.'

objectives.title: Define and correctly use the precise Agentforce terminology required for developer and architect-level conversations.

topics.question: What is a Turn and what is a Reasoning Iteration, and how do they relate to each other?
topics.answer: Per Salesforce's Agentforce documentation: A Turn is one user message plus the agent's complete response cycle — everything from the moment a user message arrives to the moment the agent's response is delivered. A Reasoning Iteration is one complete Phase 1 (deterministic resolution) plus Phase 2 (LLM reasoning) cycle. Multiple reasoning iterations can occur within a single turn. Each time the LLM calls an action and re-resolution begins, a new reasoning iteration starts and the iteration counter increments toward the 3-4 hard cap. A turn with three sequential action calls before a terminal response would contain four reasoning iterations: one for each action call plus one for the final response. Understanding this distinction is critical for reasoning about the loop iteration limit and for reading session traces accurately.

topics.question: What is Deterministic Resolution, and what is Re-Resolution?
topics.answer: Per Salesforce's AgentScript documentation: Deterministic Resolution is Phase 1 — the process of evaluating all AgentScript constructs (conditions, run statements, variable injections, available when filters) before any LLM involvement occurs. It produces a resolved prompt string and a filtered tool schema. Re-Resolution is a specific mechanic within the reasoning loop: after every tool call (LLM-driven action execution), the entire reasoning.instructions block is rebuilt from scratch using the updated variable state. Re-resolution is a full re-evaluation from the top of the block, not a continuation from the position where the tool call was made. This distinction is the reason post-action checks must be placed at the top of instructions: -> blocks.

topics.question: What is Slot Filling, and what is Variable Binding?
topics.answer: Per Salesforce's AgentScript documentation: Slot Filling is the process by which the LLM extracts a parameter value from conversation context using the '...' (ellipsis) syntax. It is a Phase 2 probabilistic operation — the LLM decides what value from the conversation matches the parameter, and if the value is absent, the LLM prompts the user for it. Variable Binding is the process by which the runtime resolves '@variables.X' to its current stored value at Phase 1 time — before the LLM is involved. Variable binding is deterministic. The choice between slot filling (probabilistic, Phase 2) and variable binding (deterministic, Phase 1) is a security and reliability design decision with significant consequences for how the agent handles unexpected or malicious user input.

topics.question: What is a Tool Schema, what is | mode, and what is -> mode?
topics.answer: Per Salesforce's AgentScript and Agentforce documentation: A Tool Schema is the JSON function schema representation of an action that is handed to the LLM during Phase 2. The LLM uses tool schemas to understand what actions are available, what parameters they require, and what they return. Actions that fail their available when guard are completely excluded from the tool schema — they have no presence in what the LLM sees. | mode (literal mode) is the reasoning.instructions mode in which content is sent as-is to the LLM without any Phase 1 evaluation. Conditional logic written in | mode appears as literal English prose. -> mode (procedural mode) is the reasoning.instructions mode that activates Phase 1 deterministic evaluation: conditionals are evaluated, run statements execute, set statements capture values, and only the matching pipe (|) lines reach the LLM.

topics.question: What is Posture, what is Handoff, and what is Delegation/Supervision?
topics.answer: Per Salesforce's Agentforce documentation: Posture is the spectrum of LLM autonomy versus authored determinism configured for a subagent. Agentic posture gives the LLM maximum latitude. Scripted posture gives the LLM zero discretion. Mixed posture applies selective controls. Handoff is a one-way subagent transfer implemented via '@utils.transition to' — the calling subagent does not resume after the handoff and its after_reasoning does not fire if the handoff occurs mid-reasoning. Delegation (also called Supervision) is a two-way subagent call implemented by referencing '@subagent.X' as an action in reasoning.actions — the child subagent runs its full reasoning loop, produces a result, and control returns to the calling (parent) subagent, which synthesizes the final response. Handoff is appropriate when the destination should own the full response; delegation is appropriate when a parent needs to coordinate or synthesize across multiple child subagents.

topics.question: What is the DAG, what is the FSM, what is a Backward Arrow, and what is a GenAiPlannerBundle?
topics.answer: Per Salesforce's Agentforce and AtlasEngine documentation: A DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph) is the mathematical structure for tool invocations and sequential dependencies in the Agent Graph. The DAG prevents infinite loops within automated workflows and guarantees prerequisite ordering. An FSM (Finite State Machine) manages subagent transitions and retry logic within the Agent Graph. The FSM is enforced by the Atlas engine and is responsible for the 3-4 iteration hard cap. A Backward Arrow is an FSM term for a retry edge — the edge recorded when the LLM attempted a tool call, received an error payload, and reasoned into an alternative approach. Backward arrows are visible as literal visual edges in Agentforce trace visualization tooling. A GenAiPlannerBundle is the runtime metadata artifact created by the Salesforce platform when you publish an agent — it is the compiled output of the Atlas engine and is what actually executes in production. It is distinct from the AiAuthoringBundle, which is the authoring-domain artifact (.agent file) that developers create and maintain.

topics.question: What are @inputs, @outputs, and @variables, and what is the 10k Token Heuristic?
topics.answer: Per Salesforce's AgentScript scope documentation: @inputs holds action input values and is valid ONLY in with clauses during action invocation — it expires immediately after the with clause and cannot be used in set statements or post-execution checks. @outputs holds action return values and is valid ONLY in set and if statements immediately after the action's run block — it expires after those statements complete. @variables holds session-persistent state and is valid anywhere in AgentScript logic, including in pipe text via the {!@variables.X} injection syntax. Misusing @inputs or @outputs outside their valid scope produces a silent failure — the variable is not set and no error is thrown. The 10k Token Heuristic is the Salesforce-recommended architectural target of approximately 10,000 tokens per reasoning transaction payload. It governs latency and LLM reasoning accuracy, not credit billing. Credit billing is charged per action execution, not per token. These are completely separate optimization concerns.

topics.question: What is the Zero-Hallucination Pattern, and what is the Einstein Trust Layer (ETL)?
topics.answer: Per Salesforce's Agentforce documentation: The Zero-Hallucination Pattern is the combination of 'filter_from_agent: True' and 'is_used_by_planner: True' on an action output. Together these flags force the LLM to actually invoke the action to obtain a routing value rather than guessing or hallucinating it from conversation context, while also preventing the value from being exposed to the user. This pattern is the recommended approach for any intent classification action used in routing decisions. The Einstein Trust Layer (ETL) is the runtime security boundary between Phase 1 output and the LLM. It enforces zero-retention of CRM grounding data, screens inputs for prompt injection and toxicity, screens outputs for toxicity and grounding quality, and enforces Salesforce sharing rules and field-level security at the LLM boundary. The ETL operates on every turn, for every session, in every production deployment — it is not a configuration option but an architectural guarantee of the Agentforce platform.

rag.title: The Big Picture: What You Are Actually Selling

objectives.title: Understand the four foundational pillars of Agentforce RAG and how to position them to clients.

topics.question: What are the four foundational pillars of Agentforce RAG and what does each one mean?
topics.answer: The four pillars are: (1) Grounding — the agent answers from your proprietary data, not general LLM knowledge, eliminating hallucinations about your products, policies, and processes. (2) Trust — the Einstein Trust Layer ensures data never trains third-party LLMs, sensitive PII is masked before it leaves the org, and every AI interaction is audited. (3) Intelligence Infrastructure — Data 360 (formerly Data Cloud) is the vector database, identity engine, audit store, and analytics layer powering every enterprise-grade Agentforce feature. (4) Continuous Improvement — Agentforce Observability closes the loop between production conversations, content quality, and agent improvement. It is a product, not a project.

topics.question: How should a Success Architect position Agentforce RAG before a client meeting?
topics.answer: RAG with Agentforce is not a chatbot feature. It is a governed, enterprise-grade AI delivery system. Clients who understand the four pillars — Grounding, Trust, Intelligence Infrastructure, and Continuous Improvement — make better architecture decisions. The architect's job is to ensure the client understands all four pillars before signing the SOW, because each pillar shapes deployment decisions, Data 360 requirements, and long-term success metrics.

rag.title: Core Architectural Paradigms: Agents vs. Prompt Templates

objectives.title: Distinguish between Prompt Templates and Agentforce Agents and know when to recommend each.

topics.question: What are the key differences between a Prompt Template and an Agentforce Agent?
topics.answer: Prompt Templates are stateless (no memory across turns), execute a fixed template with no autonomous decision-making, are ideal for single-turn tasks such as summarizing a case or generating an email, have low complexity, integrate with RAG via a dynamic retriever in the template, and cost 2-16 credits per invocation. Agentforce Agents are stateful (maintain conversation history), make autonomous decisions about what to do next, are ideal for multi-turn conversations, have higher complexity involving subagents, actions, and routing logic, integrate with RAG via the knowledge: block and AnswerQuestionsWithKnowledge action, and cost 20 credits per action execution.

topics.question: When should you recommend a Prompt Template versus an Agentforce Agent to a client?
topics.answer: Recommend a Prompt Template when: the task is a single-turn operation triggered by a user or Flow; the output goes into a specific Salesforce field (Field Generation Template); multiple unrelated data objects need merging into one context window (Flex Template); or the client wants to start small and prove AI value quickly. Recommend an Agentforce Agent when: users need a conversational experience across multiple turns; the agent must make decisions based on user input such as routing, escalation, or data lookup; the use case involves multiple interdependent steps; or the client needs governed, audited AI interactions.

topics.question: What is the hybrid pattern combining Prompt Templates and Agentforce Agents, and when is it highest value?
topics.answer: The hybrid pattern uses an Agentforce Agent to manage the conversation, routing, and multi-turn context, while the agent calls Prompt Template actions for structured content generation tasks such as case summaries or proposal paragraphs. The Prompt Template uses RAG via a dynamic retriever to ground that content in proprietary data. This is the highest-value pattern for complex service and sales use cases because it combines the governance and multi-turn memory of an agent with the structured content generation strength of prompt templates.

rag.title: How Agentforce Reasons: The Engine Behind the Agent

objectives.title: Explain the ten-step reasoning loop and use it to diagnose agent behavior.

topics.question: What are the ten steps of the Agentforce reasoning loop and what happens at each step?
topics.answer: Step 1: Agent Invocation — the user sends a message and the agent session begins. Step 2: Classify Subagent — the reasoning engine reads the user's message. Step 3: Subagent Selection — the engine matches the message to a subagent based on its name and description fields. Step 4: Execute Scripted Logic — before_reasoning: hooks and deterministic run actions execute first, free with no LLM involved. Step 5: Build Prompt — resolved instructions, variable values, and conversation history are assembled into a prompt string. Step 6: Send to LLM — the prompt and available actions are sent to the LLM. Step 7: LLM Decision — the LLM decides to respond directly, ask for more information, or execute an action. Step 8: Action Execution — if an action is selected, the engine runs it such as Apex, Flow, or Prompt Template. Step 9: After-Action Logic — after_reasoning: hooks fire; deterministic transitions and guards evaluate results. Step 10: Grounding Check and Response — the response is validated against scope and grounding before reaching the user.

topics.question: What is the Grounding Check and why is it the most important step to explain to clients?
topics.answer: Before any response reaches the user, the reasoning engine verifies that: (1) the response is based on accurate information; (2) the response follows the agent's configured guidelines and instructions; (3) the response stays within the agent's defined scope and subagent boundaries. This is why a well-configured anti-hallucination instruction — telling the agent to refuse when retrieval is empty — is enforced at the engine level, not just at the LLM level. The Grounding Check is the platform's built-in safety net, and explaining it helps clients understand why proper instruction authoring is critical.

topics.question: What is the difference between Phase 1 (Deterministic) and Phase 2 (LLM) execution in Agent Script?
topics.answer: Phase 1 is Deterministic: the engine evaluates all conditionals against current variable values, runs any deterministic actions, and builds the final prompt string. No LLM is involved. This is instant and free. Phase 2 is LLM: the resolved prompt string is passed to the LLM with the list of available tools. The LLM reasons over the prompt and decides what to do. The critical implication: only the Phase 1 output reaches the LLM. If a conditional evaluates to false, the LLM never sees that branch. This is how deterministic authorization gates work — the agent user never knows what content was hidden from the LLM.

rag.title: Context Engineering: The Successor to Prompt Engineering

objectives.title: Define context engineering and apply its three levers and filter levels to agent design.

topics.question: What is context engineering and how does it differ from prompt engineering?
topics.answer: Context engineering is the discipline of designing systems that give an AI agent the exact information and boundaries it needs to succeed. It is not about writing clever prompts. It is about designing the entire information environment the agent operates in. Prompt engineering focuses narrowly on the text of a single prompt. Context engineering covers everything: which subagents exist, what instructions they carry, which actions are available, which data is retrieved, and which filters control access — all of which together determine what the LLM sees on every turn.

topics.question: What are the three levers of context engineering in Agentforce?
topics.answer: The three levers are: (1) Subagents — define specialized areas of expertise. Each subagent has a name and description that the routing engine uses to classify incoming messages. A well-written subagent description is the most important routing tool available. (2) Instructions — define the conversation flow, tone, and behavioral constraints within a subagent. These are the natural language directives the LLM receives in Phase 2. (3) Actions and Rules — execute real-world operations such as querying data, creating records, or calling APIs, and enforce deterministic business logic that the LLM cannot override.

topics.question: What is the Principle of Minimal Context and why does adding too much context harm agent performance?
topics.answer: The Principle of Minimal Context states: put only the information the agent needs for the current turn into the context window. Overly large context windows: (1) increase latency; (2) increase cost since each action execution is 20 credits; (3) dilute the signal-to-noise ratio, causing the LLM to anchor on irrelevant context. For RAG, this means retrieving 3-5 highly relevant chunks rather than dumping an entire knowledge base into context. More context does not mean better answers.

topics.question: What are the three levels at which filters control agent context, and what does each level control?
topics.answer: The three filter levels are: (1) Subagent-level filters — control which subagents are available to a given user. An internal HR subagent should only be visible to logged-in employees. (2) Action-level filters using the 'available when' guard — control which actions a subagent can call based on current variable values. A 'Process Refund' action should only be available when the customer has been verified. (3) Retriever-level filters — control which content is retrieved. Dynamic pre-filters restrict results based on runtime values such as the current user's region, account type, or product category. Per Salesforce documentation, enhanced retriever pre-filters support up to 10 dynamic filters per retriever, AND/OR logic, and LIKE operators for pattern matching.

rag.title: The RAG Lifecycle: Four Phases in Depth

objectives.title: Understand Phase 1: Ingestion — how structured and unstructured content enters Data 360.

topics.question: What are Data Model Objects (DMOs) and why do they matter for RAG?
topics.answer: DMOs are the harmonized, structured data layer in Data 360. They represent the final, clean source of truth after raw ingested data has been processed through Data Lake Objects (DLOs). For RAG, you configure which fields of a DMO are indexed. For example, you can semantically index the Answer__c and Summary__c fields of a Knowledge article, while using Title and ProductCategory__c as metadata for pre-filtering. This gives you semantic search on long-form content and deterministic filtering on categorical content — two fundamentally different capabilities applied to the same record.

topics.question: What are Unstructured Data Lake Objects (UDLOs) and how do they handle audio and video content?
topics.answer: UDLOs are directory tables that store structured metadata about unstructured assets such as location, file type, language, and creation date, while the actual content is processed by the indexing pipeline. PDFs, HTML pages, TXT files, and external documents are ingested into UDLOs. Audio and video files are a special case: the files remain at their external location using zero-copy file stores. They are submitted to a transcription service, and only the resulting text transcript is brought into Data 360 for indexing. The original files are never moved.

topics.question: What types of content should NOT be indexed in a RAG pipeline, and why?
topics.answer: Do not index categorical columns such as picklist values, boolean fields, or short label fields. These produce micro-chunks too short to carry semantic meaning. The vector search component of hybrid search becomes erratic when applied to micro-chunks. Also, do not over-index — only include fields that contain substantive information a user would actually ask about. Indexing metadata fields alongside content fields confuses the semantic model and degrades retrieval precision. Best practice for Knowledge articles: spread content across multiple fields — a question in one field, a detailed resolution in another, and related examples in a third — to give the chunker more material and reduce the risk of critical answers being split across a chunk boundary.

objectives.title: Understand Phase 2: Chunking — the most common source of RAG quality problems.

topics.question: What is the fundamental tension in chunking and how should architects approach chunk size decisions?
topics.answer: For retrieval: smaller chunks are better. A small chunk represents a single focused factoid and matches a specific user question precisely. For generation: larger chunks are better. The LLM needs enough surrounding context to generate a coherent, accurate answer. The practical approach: start with the platform default chunk size. Evaluate retrieval quality using debug mode in Prompt Builder. If answers are precise but contextually thin, increase chunk size. If there are retrieval misses on specific factoids, decrease it. Per Salesforce documentation, the maximum chunk size is 512 tokens, approximately 400-500 words in Latin-script languages.

topics.question: What is the Docling Parser, when should it be used, and how is it enabled?
topics.answer: The Docling Parser is a specialized, third-party intelligent document parsing framework built into Data 360. It combines open-source models to execute layout understanding, reading order detection, and advanced table extraction. Use it when the corpus contains: tabular data such as pricing grids, comparison tables, or specification sheets; multi-column layouts; documents with embedded figures and captions; or complex hierarchical structures. The default semantic extraction parser fails on tables — extracting text row by row and destroying column relationships. To enable it: in the Data 360 Setup, change the UDMO search index's parser setting to Docling. This is configured on the search index, not on the library.

topics.question: What is field prepending, what problem does it solve, and what are good candidates for prepending?
topics.answer: Field prepending solves the context loss problem: when a chunk is extracted from its parent document, it loses surrounding context. A chunk reading 'The maximum torque output is 450 Nm at 3,500 RPM' is meaningless without knowing which product it refers to. Field prepending prefixes each chunk with metadata fields at indexing time, producing: 'Product: Industrial Compressor Model X7. Section: Technical Specifications. The maximum torque output is 450 Nm at 3,500 RPM.' Good candidates for prepending include: product name or category, article title, document section header, last modified date, author or department, and applicable product version. Temporal prepending (adding last_modified_date) combined with a temporal pre-filter enables the agent to answer 'What changed in the November update?' queries, which pure vector search cannot handle alone.
