objectives.title: Understand Phase 3: Embedding — how semantic vectors are generated and managed.

topics.question: What is the 1:1 relationship between chunks and embeddings and how does cosine similarity enable semantic search?
topics.answer: One chunk produces exactly one embedding vector. The entire semantic content of that chunk is compressed into a fixed-length array of floating-point numbers. At query time, the user's question is embedded using the same model, and the engine computes cosine similarity between the query vector and every stored vector to find the most semantically similar chunks. This mathematical approach is what allows semantic search — a question about 'vehicle acceleration' can retrieve a chunk about 'engine torque output' even if those exact words are not shared between the query and the chunk.

topics.question: What role does Milvus play in Data 360 and why does an architect need to know it exists?
topics.answer: Milvus is the open-source vector database that Data 360 uses internally for unstructured data indexing and semantic search execution. It is purpose-built for storing and querying billions of high-dimensional embedding vectors at low latency. The architecture layers as follows: Apache Iceberg/Parquet (Lakehouse Layer) stores the original chunk text and metadata permanently; Milvus (Vector Store Layer) stores the embedding vectors and serves all similarity queries at query time; a Low-Latency NVMe Store provides sub-millisecond access to hot vector data. Architects do not configure Milvus directly — it is fully managed — but knowing it exists gives credibility with client data engineering teams and explains performance characteristics of semantic search at scale.

topics.question: What embedding models are available, when should each be selected, and what is the cost of changing models?
topics.answer: The default model is E5-Large-V2, which performs well on English-language enterprise content and is the right default for monolingual English corpora. For multilingual corpora, explicitly select the multilingual-e5-large model. Even a subtle language variant mismatch — indexing in en_US and querying in en_GB — can cause retrieval degradation. The multilingual model maintains cross-lingual synonymity, meaning a Spanish query can retrieve a semantically equivalent English chunk without any translation step. The cost of model mismatch is severe: if you index content with one embedding model and later change it, all existing embeddings become incompatible and you must re-index the entire corpus. Finalize model selection before indexing production content.

objectives.title: Understand Phase 4: Retrieval — how retrievers bridge the vector index and the agent.

topics.question: What is an ensemble retriever and when should it be used?
topics.answer: An ensemble retriever bundles multiple individual retrievers into one. It is used when a client has content in multiple sources — such as Knowledge articles, PDFs, and external documents — and users ask questions that span those domains. At query time, it: (1) runs the query against each individual retriever simultaneously; (2) collects result sets from each retriever; (3) applies a reranking algorithm to merge and score the combined results; (4) returns the top N results drawn from across all sources. This is the correct architecture when users cannot be expected to know which source contains the answer to their question.

topics.question: What is the difference between static and dynamic pre-filters on a retriever, and why are dynamic pre-filters architecturally stronger than prompt-level instructions?
topics.answer: Static pre-filters are set at configuration time. Example: 'Only retrieve chunks where PublishStatus = Online.' Dynamic pre-filters are passed at runtime from conversation context or prompt inputs. Example: 'Only retrieve chunks where ProductLine = the current user's assigned product line.' Dynamic pre-filters are machine-enforceable data access controls — they prevent content from even entering the candidate pool before vector similarity is calculated. This is fundamentally stronger than a prompt-level instruction telling the LLM to not reveal confidential information, because the LLM never sees the restricted content at all.

topics.question: What is Advanced Retrieval Mode and when does it significantly improve performance?
topics.answer: Advanced Retrieval Mode combines iterative retrieval with LLM-based query rewriting: (1) the user asks an imprecise or complex question; (2) the system runs an initial retrieval; (3) an LLM summarizes the retrieved results; (4) the LLM rewrites the original query using the retrieved context to form a better-targeted query; (5) the system runs a second retrieval with the improved query; (6) the second retrieval's results are used for the final response. This pattern dramatically improves performance on complex, multi-part questions where the initial query phrasing is not optimal. It is not needed for straightforward factual queries.

rag.title: Search Indexing and Retrieval Strategies

objectives.title: Compare search strategies and make data-driven recommendations about when to use hybrid search.

topics.question: What are the three search strategies available in Data 360 and what are the best use cases for each?
topics.answer: Vector (Semantic) search converts query and chunks to embeddings and finds results by cosine similarity. Best for long-form prose, narrative articles, and cross-lingual content. Limitation: can miss highly specific keywords, SKUs, and product codes. Keyword (BM25) search uses classic lexical matching on exact and stemmed terms. Best for short specific queries, product codes, and domain jargon. Limitation: no semantic understanding — 'car' does not match 'automobile.' Hybrid search combines vector and BM25, then reranks the merged results. Best for corpora with both narrative content and domain-specific terminology. Limitation: approximately 2x credit cost, higher latency, and unstable on micro-chunks.

topics.question: When should hybrid search be used and when should it explicitly NOT be used?
topics.answer: Use hybrid search when: the corpus contains product names, SKUs, order numbers, or technical codes that vector search consistently fails to retrieve; testing shows a 10-15% or greater recall improvement over pure vector search; the client can absorb approximately 2x the Data Cloud services credit consumption; and latency is not a primary constraint. Do NOT use hybrid search when: the corpus is primarily categorical — short labels, picklist values, brief descriptions — because the keyword component destabilizes retrieval on micro-chunks; response time is critical; or the content is all narrative prose with no domain-specific terminology that vector search cannot handle on its own.

topics.question: Why does hybrid search fail on categorical content corpora and what is the fix?
topics.answer: The vector component of hybrid search requires chunks with enough semantic scope to produce meaningful embeddings. A chunk containing only 'Gold Tier Warranty' has near-zero semantic scope. The vector component produces a near-random similarity score. The reranking algorithm then combines a meaningful keyword score with a near-random vector score, producing unpredictable results. When clients ask why the agent is giving wrong answers on simple category questions, the root cause is often hybrid search applied to a corpus of short categorical content. The fix: use pure vector search for categorical corpora and rely on dynamic pre-filters to enforce categorical constraints deterministically.

rag.title: ADL vs. Manual Setup: Choosing the Right Architecture

objectives.title: Know when to use ADL (Agentforce Data Library) versus manual configuration.

topics.question: What does the ADL automatically provision and when is it the recommended approach?
topics.answer: When you create an ADL, the platform automatically provisions the entire RAG pipeline: a data stream (connection to source data), a Data Lake Object (DLO), a Data Model Object or Unstructured Data Model Object (DMO/UDMO), a search index with embedding model and chunking configuration, a retriever that bridges the index to the agent, and a prompt template using AnswerQuestionsWithKnowledge. The entire pipeline is created from a single CLI command or Setup UI interaction. ADL is strictly recommended when: the source data is Salesforce Knowledge articles (KAV objects), the source data is files such as PDFs, HTML, or TXT stored in a Salesforce-managed file store, or the client has an existing active Custom Retriever to wire in.

topics.question: When is ADL insufficient and manual configuration required?
topics.answer: ADL is not sufficient when: you need to retrieve from long-text fields on standard or custom Salesforce objects that are not Knowledge articles; you need complex multi-source merging with custom reranking logic the ensemble retriever does not support; or access control requirements demand procedural, runtime logic that pre-filters cannot express. Manual configuration gives full control over every component of the RAG pipeline — data streams, DLOs, DMOs/UDMOs, search indexes, custom retrievers, and ensemble retrievers. It is also required when the client's content lives in long-text fields on non-KAV Salesforce objects or when external systems require custom data streams.

topics.question: Walk through the ADL scoping decision tree to determine the correct architecture for a client's content.
topics.answer: Start by asking: does the client have content to ground the agent? If No: build the agent without RAG using topics and actions. If Yes: where does the content live? Salesforce Knowledge articles (KAV) — use the ADL KNOWLEDGE source type. Files such as PDF, HTML, or TXT — use the ADL SFDRIVE source type. An existing Custom Retriever — use the ADL RETRIEVER source type. Public web or client website — use the General Web Search action, which is a separate feature and not an ADL source type. An external system with data residency constraints — use MuleSoft with a Custom Retriever. Long-text fields on non-KAV Salesforce objects — use Manual Configuration. Multiple heterogeneous sources — use Manual Configuration with an Ensemble Retriever.

rag.title: ADL Source Types: Deep Technical Walkthrough

objectives.title: Know the three ADL source types and the unique technical requirements of each.

topics.question: What are the three ADL source types and when is each used?
topics.answer: Per Salesforce documentation, the ADL CLI command 'sf agent adl create' accepts exactly three source type values: (1) sfdrive — use when the client has PDF, HTML, or TXT files to upload. Provisioning time: 2-10 minutes per file via JIT indexing. Readiness signal: retrieverId non-null AND file status = INDEXED. (2) knowledge — use when the org has Salesforce Knowledge articles (KAV objects). Provisioning time: 2-10 minutes async, can race. Readiness signal: retrieverId non-null AND a live test query returns non-empty knowledgeSummary. (3) retriever — use when the client has an existing active Custom Retriever. Provisioning time: immediately READY. Readiness signal: retrieverId non-null, same as the provided retriever ID. When client intent is ambiguous, always ask — 'knowledge base' could mean SFDRIVE (upload PDFs) or KNOWLEDGE (use existing KAV articles). Never guess.

topics.question: How does SFDRIVE JIT indexing work and what are the possible file status states?
topics.answer: SFDRIVE uses a Just-in-Time (JIT) indexing pipeline — each file is indexed individually as it is uploaded. The library becomes READY when at least one file has reached INDEXED status. The top-level library status can show READY while individual files are still processing, so always check per-file status. File states are: UPLOADED (file landed in storage, indexing not yet started — wait), INDEXING (JIT pipeline is processing the file — wait), INDEXED (file is chunked and searchable — success state), INDEX_FAILED (indexing failed — delete and re-add the file to retry), DELETING (file removal in progress — wait), DELETE_FAILED (removal failed — retry deletion). Per Salesforce documentation, limits are: max 100 MB per file, max 1,000 files per library, supported types: PDF, TXT, HTML.

topics.question: What is the --index-mode flag for SFDRIVE and when should each mode be used?
topics.answer: The --index-mode flag controls how files are processed during indexing. 'basic' (UI label: Text Only) uses standard semantic extraction at standard credit cost — correct for corpora of pure, continuous prose. 'enhanced' (UI label: Intelligent Context) uses LLM-based processing for tables, images, and complex layouts at substantially higher per-file cost — use when the corpus contains tables, embedded images, infographics, multi-column layouts, or any content where spatial relationships carry meaning. Do not apply enhanced mode universally. The cost differential is material for large corpora. Test both modes on representative documents if in doubt.

topics.question: What is the KNOWLEDGE library Day 0 race condition, how does it manifest, and how is it resolved?
topics.answer: The Day 0 race condition is the most common cause of early-stage KNOWLEDGE library failures. It works as follows: (1) the library is created and the CRM Connector is triggered; (2) the Day 0 chunking job fires almost immediately; (3) the CRM Connector has not yet committed article data to the lakehouse, which has approximately a 17-second visibility window; (4) the chunking job sees 0 rows, skips processing, and emits a READY status anyway; (5) the library shows READY with a non-null retrieverId but contains 0 indexed chunks. Do not declare success based on retrieverId alone for KNOWLEDGE libraries. Wait approximately 10 minutes, then send a live test query and verify that the returned knowledgeSummary is non-empty. If still empty, force a re-index by running: sf agent adl update with the library ID, target org, and content fields flags.

topics.question: What is the KNOWLEDGE library primaryIndexField constraint and what happens if the wrong fields are chosen?
topics.answer: Two primary index fields must be specified at KNOWLEDGE library creation time. These fields are immutable after the library is created. Common choices are ArticleNumber and Title. If you choose the wrong fields, you must delete the library and recreate it — there is no in-place update for primary index fields. This makes the initial field selection a critical, irreversible architectural decision that should be confirmed with the client's Knowledge team before running the create command.

topics.question: What is the ARFPC_ prefix requirement and what error does omitting it cause?
topics.answer: The value in the .agent file's knowledge: block is NOT the raw libraryId. It is the libraryId prefixed with ARFPC_. The correct format is: rag_feature_config_id: 'ARFPC_1JDg7000001hilBGAQ'. Omitting the ARFPC_ prefix causes a validation failure during sf agent validate. The error message points to the knowledge: block but does not explain the prefix requirement, making this one of the most common and confusing implementation mistakes. Always verify the prefix is present when wiring a library into the .agent file.

topics.question: What is the KNOWLEDGE library language alignment requirement and how does a mismatch manifest?
topics.answer: The retriever filters chunks by language at query time. The agent user's LanguageLocaleKey must match the language of the indexed Knowledge articles. Even subtle mismatches such as en_US vs. en_GB cause the retriever to silently return 0 results. The failure mode is completely silent — the retriever applies the language filter, finds no matching chunks, and returns an empty result with no error logged that connects the empty result to the language filter. Pre-launch verification: run a SOQL query grouping Knowledge__kav records by Language where PublishStatus = 'Online' and compare the results to the agent user's LanguageLocaleKey.

rag.title: Web Search Grounding: The Public Knowledge Pattern

objectives.title: Distinguish web search grounding from ADL RAG and know when each is appropriate.

topics.question: How is web search grounding architecturally different from ADL RAG?
topics.answer: Web search grounding is NOT an ADL source type. The three ADL source types are sfdrive, knowledge, and retriever. Web search is implemented through a separate feature: the General Web Search Topic and Action, configured directly on an Agentforce agent independently of the ADL pipeline. Key differences: ADL RAG uses your proprietary content ingested and indexed in Data 360, has an audit trail, and gives full citation and compliance control. General Web Search queries the public internet at runtime, has an external dependency, cannot guarantee content is on-brand, and is not appropriate for regulated industries. Confusing these two is a common mistake with completely different security and cost implications.

topics.question: When is web search grounding appropriate and when is it explicitly NOT appropriate?
topics.answer: Web search IS appropriate when: the agent's scope includes general public information too volatile to maintain in a managed corpus such as current news or publicly available product announcements; a client website is the authoritative source for public-facing content and maintaining it in SFDRIVE would create version drift; or the agent is explicitly positioned as a general assistant with broad scope. Web search is NOT appropriate when: the content is proprietary such as internal policies, pricing, customer data, or processes; the use case has compliance or regulatory requirements that demand fully auditable grounding; the client needs to prevent the agent from surfacing competitor or off-brand content; or data residency requirements restrict processing of content from arbitrary external sources.

topics.question: What is the Knowledge-First with Web Search Fallback pattern and how is it implemented?
topics.answer: This pattern uses AnswerQuestionsWithKnowledge as the primary grounding source and the General Web Search action as a fallback when the proprietary corpus returns an empty result. How it works: (1) the agent calls AnswerQuestionsWithKnowledge for every substantive question; (2) if knowledgeSummary is non-empty, the agent answers from the proprietary corpus; (3) if knowledgeSummary is empty, the agent invokes the General Web Search action; (4) the agent answers from web search results, clearly labeling the source as publicly available information. Instructions must: call AnswerQuestionsWithKnowledge first, answer from the knowledge summary when non-empty including citations, call GeneralWebSearch when the summary is empty while informing the user of the source shift, and never combine content from both sources in the same response without clear labeling.

topics.question: When should the refuse/escalate fallback be used versus the web search fallback?
topics.answer: Refuse/escalate fallback: use for compliance-governed agents in regulated industries such as financial services, healthcare, government, and legal, and for agents with proprietary-only scope. Risk profile: low risk, full control. Web search fallback: use for general assistants, public-information agents, and broad-scope use cases where the compliance team has approved the use of public web content as a grounding source. Risk profile: higher risk, external dependency, content not controlled. Never recommend the web search fallback to a client in a regulated industry without first confirming compliance team review and approval. Domain scoping on the General Web Search action should always be configured to prevent surfacing competitor or off-brand content.

rag.title: Wiring RAG into Agent Script

objectives.title: Configure RAG in Agent Script using the knowledge: block and AnswerQuestionsWithKnowledge action correctly.

topics.question: How is the knowledge: block structured in an .agent file and what does each property do?
topics.answer: The knowledge: block is placed between the connection: block (if present) and the language: block. Block ordering is enforced by the Agent Script compiler. Structure: the knowledge: block contains rag_feature_config_id set to the ARFPC_-prefixed library ID, citations_enabled set to True to render inline citations, and an optional citations_url base URL prepended to citation links. The rag_feature_config_id is the most common source of errors when the ARFPC_ prefix is omitted.

topics.question: What does the AnswerQuestionsWithKnowledge action do at runtime?
topics.answer: The reasoning engine auto-instantiates this action when a knowledge: block is present. At runtime it: (1) takes the current user query as input; (2) vectorizes the query using the configured embedding model; (3) runs a similarity search against the configured search index via Milvus; (4) returns the top N retrieved chunks as knowledgeSummary; (5) returns citation metadata alongside the summary. This action costs 20 credits per call. If retrieval fails or the knowledge base contains no matching content, knowledgeSummary is empty — which must be handled by explicit instructions.

topics.question: What is the Anti-Hallucination Guard Pattern and what are its four non-negotiable duties?
topics.answer: The Anti-Hallucination Guard Pattern is the most critical instruction block to get right. When retrieval fails, the knowledgeSummary output is empty. Without an explicit guard, the LLM may fabricate an answer from its pre-training data. The four non-negotiable duties are: (1) Call before answering — explicitly instruct the agent to call AnswerQuestionsWithKnowledge before generating any response. (2) Ground only in returned content — base the response only on the content returned in the knowledge summary. (3) Decline gracefully when retrieval is empty — provide a specific, helpful fallback message such as a support email, phone number, or escalation path. (4) Cite only returned sources — do not fabricate citations or add external links not returned alongside the knowledge summary.

topics.question: How should refuse messages be tailored by domain, and what are examples for compliance, technical support, and HR agents?
topics.answer: Tailor the refuse message to the agent's specific domain so users get actionable next steps rather than a generic 'I don't know.' Compliance agent: 'I don't have that in our current Policy Manual. Please contact the Compliance team directly at compliance@example.com for guidance.' Technical support agent: 'That issue is not documented in our knowledge base yet. I will create a case so our Level 2 team can investigate and document a resolution.' HR agent: 'I could not find that in our HR policies. Please contact HR directly through the employee portal.' The domain-specific message maintains trust and gives users a clear path forward.

rag.title: The Einstein Trust Layer: Security Architecture for RAG

objectives.title: Explain the Einstein Trust Layer's security features and know which require Data 360.

topics.question: What is the Einstein Trust Layer and what is its role relative to external LLM providers?
topics.answer: The Einstein Trust Layer is a set of technical agreements, security controls, and data governance policies built directly into the Salesforce platform. It sits between your org and any external LLM provider. All AI-powered features, including Agentforce and RAG, route through the Trust Layer. It is not optional, configurable middleware. It is mandatory, always-on security infrastructure that ensures no customer data leaks to, trains, or is retained by external LLM providers.

topics.question: What is Zero Data Retention and how should it be positioned with clients concerned about data privacy?
topics.answer: Salesforce maintains contractual zero-data retention agreements with all external LLM providers, including OpenAI and Azure OpenAI. Under these agreements: no data sent to the LLM is retained by the third-party provider after the API call completes; no customer data is used to train or improve the external LLM models; no human at the LLM provider organization has access to your data during or after the transaction. Client positioning: 'Your data goes in, the answer comes out, and nothing stays. Your proprietary content, customer data, and business logic cannot leak into a shared model that your competitors might also use.'

topics.question: How does the Trust Layer enforce pattern-based data masking and what types of data are detected?
topics.answer: Before the augmented prompt leaves Salesforce and reaches the external LLM, the Trust Layer scans the entire prompt — including retrieved content — for sensitive data patterns and masks them. Standard patterns detected and masked include: credit card numbers for PCI DSS compliance, Social Security Numbers and National ID numbers, healthcare identifiers for HIPAA compliance, bank account numbers, and passport numbers. Custom patterns can also be configured. Masking works by replacing detected patterns with placeholder tokens such as [MASKED_CC] before transmission. The LLM sees and processes the masked version only. Architect responsibility: configure and test masking rules before go-live by running test prompts with intentionally seeded PII to verify masking fires correctly.

topics.question: What does the Trust Layer Audit Trail capture and why does it matter for architects?
topics.answer: The Audit Trail captures: every prompt sent to the LLM and every response received; the trust signals applied to each interaction including masking events, toxicity scores, and grounding sources used; and user feedback on AI responses. All audit data is stored in Data 360 — this is why Data Cloud/Data 360 is required for full Trust Layer functionality. For architects, the Audit Trail is also a quality improvement data source: analyzing patterns of negative user feedback across the audit trail reveals content gaps in the RAG corpus, and analyzing masking events reveals where the data ingestion pipeline is inadvertently pulling sensitive content into the index.

topics.question: Which Agentforce features require Data 360 and which do not?
topics.answer: Does NOT require Data 360: a basic conversational agent with no RAG. DOES require Data 360: RAG via Agentforce Data Library, full Audit Trail and compliance reporting, toxicity scoring data storage, Trust Layer Dashboards, Agentforce Analytics, Agent Observability including session tracing and quality scores, Bring Your Own LLM, External Data Sources for grounding, and Unstructured Data such as files and PDFs. The practical answer for enterprise clients: if they want the features that make Agentforce enterprise-grade — RAG, compliance, analytics, and observability — they need Data 360. Frame it as: 'Data 360 is the intelligence infrastructure that makes your agent trustworthy, measurable, and improvable.'

rag.title: Data 360 Architecture: The Intelligence Infrastructure

objectives.title: Understand the Data 360 storage model, federation capabilities, and identity resolution pipeline.

topics.question: What are the eight design principles of Data 360?
topics.answer: 1. Openness and Interoperability — federates with Snowflake, Databricks, BigQuery, and Redshift without data duplication. 2. Storage-Compute Separation — storage and processing scale independently. 3. Multi-Model Storage — supports structured data (DMOs), unstructured data (UDMOs), and vector embeddings in one platform. 4. Metadata-Driven Design — all configuration is metadata that can be version-controlled and deployed via Salesforce CLI. 5. Real-Time Hybrid Processing — supports both low-latency retrieval for agent queries and batch processing for content ingestion and index refresh. 6. Intelligent and Active Data — continuously ingests, analyzes, and pushes insights into business workflows. 7. Governance and Privacy by Design — data lineage, access control, residency rules, encryption, and compliance are built in at the storage layer. 8. One-to-Many Tenancy — a single Data 360 org can serve as source of truth for multiple Salesforce orgs.

topics.question: What are the three integrated storage layers in Data 360 and what role does each play?
topics.answer: Layer 1: The Lakehouse (Apache Iceberg + Parquet) — the permanent storage layer. All ingested content, structured records, and metadata live here. Provides ACID transactions, schema evolution, time travel, and high-volume batch processing. Chunk text and document metadata are stored permanently here. Layer 2: Milvus (Vector Store) — after chunks are embedded, the resulting high-dimensional vectors are managed by Milvus. At query time, the retriever converts the user's query into a vector and queries Milvus for the most similar chunk vectors. Milvus is managed by the Data Processing Center (DPC). Layer 3: Low-Latency NVMe Store — an NVMe SSD-based layer providing millisecond-level access to frequently queried data. Hot vector data, customer profiles, and real-time engagement signals live here. The retriever accesses embeddings from this layer at query time, not from the Lakehouse directly, which is why RAG retrieval is fast even for large corpora.

topics.question: What is zero-copy federation, how does it work, and what is the latency warning architects must give clients?
topics.answer: Zero-copy federation allows Agentforce to retrieve from data that physically lives in an external system — such as Snowflake, Databricks, or BigQuery — without moving that data into Salesforce storage. How it works: Data 360's query federation layer connects to external data warehouses via JDBC, translating Data 360 queries into the target system's SQL dialect using query pushdown. For file-based federation, external data must be in Apache Parquet format using the Apache Iceberg tabular format. For RAG, a client with a massive product catalog in Snowflake can create a search index backed by federated data without an ETL pipeline. Latency warning: federated data sources have higher retrieval latency than native Data 360 storage because each query crosses a network boundary. Always benchmark retrieval response times for federated sources before committing to this architecture.

topics.question: What is identity resolution in Data 360 and how does it enable personalized RAG grounding?
topics.answer: Identity resolution unifies customer records across disparate source systems — CRM, commerce, marketing, support — into a single Unified Individual profile. This enables Agentforce agents to ground on a holistic, unified view of the customer. The identity resolution pipeline: (1) Matching — blocking keys and Locality Sensitive Hashing (LSH) identify candidate record pairs; (2) Deep Matching — AI models calculate probabilistic match scores; (3) Clustering — matched records are grouped using transitive closure; (4) Reconciliation — reconciliation rules such as Most Frequent, Most Recent, or Source Priority populate the Unified Profile. Per Salesforce documentation, processing occurs in near-real-time, processing small batches of changes as often as every 15 minutes.

topics.question: What are Data Spaces, what are they used for, and what is the critical gotcha regarding their configuration?
topics.answer: Data Spaces are logical partitions within a Data 360 org used to enforce governance boundaries. Use cases: separating data by business unit or region, separating by sensitivity level such as public-facing vs. internal-only content preventing cross-domain retrieval between unrelated agents. Critical gotcha: the Data Space scope must be configured on the Einstein Agent User's permission set in Setup UI. This is a UI-only configuration — it cannot be deployed via metadata XML. Automated deployment pipelines must include this as a documented manual post-deployment step. If this step is missed, all other permission layers can be perfectly configured but grounded queries will still return empty results.

rag.title: Permission Model: The Four Layers That Cause Silent Failures

objectives.title: Identify and resolve all four permission layers that cause silent RAG failures.

topics.question: What is Layer 1 of the RAG permission model and what happens when it is missing?
topics.answer: Layer 1: Data Cloud Permission Set on the Agent User. The Einstein Agent User must hold a Data Cloud permission set or permission set license. Assignment priority: (1) GenieDataPlatformStarterPsl (PSL) if found; (2) GenieUserEnhancedSecurity (PS); (3) DataCloudUser (PS); (4) DataCloudArchitect (PS) — last resort, over-privileged but functional. What happens when missing: AnswerQuestionsWithKnowledge returns an empty knowledgeSummary for every query. The agent refuses every question with no error message indicating the root cause.

topics.question: What is Layer 2 of the RAG permission model (KNOWLEDGE source type) and what is the deployment template?
topics.answer: Layer 2: Knowledge Object and FLS, applicable to KNOWLEDGE source type only. The Einstein Agent User must have: object-level Read on Knowledge__kav, and field-level Read on every field configured in the library — both primary index fields and all content fields. Custom fields such as Answer__c and Summary__c require explicit grants. What happens when missing: the runtime returns an access error visible only in server-side logs; the user sees no error. Deployment template: Permission Set XML with objectPermissions allowing Read on Knowledge__kav, plus fieldPermissions entries for each custom field with readable set to true.

topics.question: What is Layer 3 of the RAG permission model and how is language alignment verified before go-live?
topics.answer: Layer 3: Language Alignment, applicable to KNOWLEDGE source type only. The retriever filters chunks by language at query time. The agent user's LanguageLocaleKey must match the language of the indexed Knowledge articles. Even en_US vs. en_GB is treated as a mismatch, causing the retriever to silently return 0 results. No error is logged in a way that connects the empty result to the language filter. Pre-launch verification SOQL: SELECT Language, COUNT(Id) ct FROM Knowledge__kav WHERE PublishStatus = 'Online' GROUP BY Language. Compare results to the agent user's LanguageLocaleKey. This check should be a standard item in every pre-launch checklist.

topics.question: What is Layer 4 of the RAG permission model and why can it not be automated?
topics.answer: Layer 4: Data Space Scope. The Data Space scope grant on the agent user's permission set is a separate configuration from the permission set assignment itself. It must be set through Setup UI by navigating to Permission Sets, clicking the assigned Data Cloud permission set, opening Data Cloud Data Space Management, editing the enabled Data Spaces list to add the ADL's data space (typically 'default'), and saving. This cannot be deployed via metadata XML. Any automated deployment pipeline must include this as a documented manual post-deployment step. All other layers can be perfectly configured, but grounded queries will still return empty results if this step is missed.

rag.title: Prompt Engineering for RAG Grounding

objectives.title: Select the right template type, design effective grounding instructions, and debug without consuming credits.

topics.question: What is the difference between Flex Templates and Field Generation Templates and when should each be used?
topics.answer: Flex Templates are used when you need to combine multiple disparate data objects into a single context window — for example, combining a customer's case history, recent Knowledge article views, and a retrieved knowledge summary into one prompt. They are the right choice for complex, multi-source grounding scenarios. Field Generation Templates generate a structured summary directly into a specific Salesforce record field. The target field must be placed on the Lightning page layout in App Builder. Ideal for AI-generated content such as case summaries, opportunity summaries, or product descriptions triggered directly on a record page, where the output is always written to a defined field.

topics.question: What are the four prompt instruction design principles for RAG grounding?
topics.answer: (1) Be explicit about the call order — tell the LLM to call the retriever action before responding. Without explicit instruction, the default LLM behavior may attempt to respond from general knowledge first. (2) Be explicit about what 'no result' means — the LLM will try to be helpful and will fabricate an answer when retrieval is empty without an explicit instruction to decline. (3) Be explicit about citations — tell the LLM which citations it is and is not allowed to use, and explicitly prohibit any citation not returned by the retriever. (4) Avoid over-constraining — instructions that are too long or too specific reduce the LLM's ability to handle edge cases gracefully. Aim for the minimum set of directives that prevent the behaviors you want to prevent.

topics.question: What is the dynamic retriever reference syntax for manual Prompt Templates and how is it placed?
topics.answer: When building Prompt Templates manually without ADL, the retrieved content enters the prompt via a dynamic retriever reference using the EinsteinSearch sfdc_ai__DynamicRetriever results placeholder. This placeholder is resolved at runtime by executing the configured retriever query and injecting the results into the prompt string. Place it immediately before the instruction block that tells the LLM to use it. This positioning ensures the LLM receives the retrieved content in context immediately before the instruction directing it to use that content.

topics.question: How can architects debug retrieval quality without spending any credits?
topics.answer: Append &c__debug=1 to the URL of any Prompt Builder page to enable debug mode. In debug mode: the retrieval step executes normally, the retrieved content is displayed in the UI, the LLM generation step does NOT execute, and no credits are consumed. This allows architects to verify retrieval quality — which chunks are being returned and why — completely independently from generation quality. This is the correct first step when troubleshooting a RAG quality problem: diagnose retrieval before blaming generation.

rag.title: Agentforce Observability: Governing Agents in Production

objectives.title: Use Agentforce Observability tools to monitor, diagnose, and continuously improve deployed agents.

topics.question: What does session tracing capture and how do architects use it?
topics.answer: Every agent conversation is logged with a full waterfall trace of each step in the reasoning loop: which subagent handled the message and why; which actions were invoked and in what order; what content was retrieved, meaning the actual chunks returned by the retriever; where the agent escalated or ended the conversation; and the exact prompt sent to the LLM and the response received. Architects use session tracing to diagnose routing failures, retrieval gaps, and action errors with exact diagnostic data rather than relying on user reports. Session traces are stored in the .sfdx/agents/ directory during preview testing.

topics.question: What are Conversation Clusters and how are they used to identify gaps?
topics.answer: Conversation Clusters use AI classification to group production conversations by user intent without requiring manual labeling. This creates a real-time view of what users are actually asking the agent, not what was assumed during design. Using clusters operationally: which intent clusters have the highest escalation rate? These are content gaps. Which intent clusters have the highest session length? These are efficiency gaps. Which intent clusters were not anticipated in the original design? These reveal new use cases and expansion opportunities. Clusters make it possible to prioritize improvement work based on volume and impact rather than anecdotal feedback.

topics.question: What are Quality Scores and how should they be used operationally?
topics.answer: Quality Scores are AI-generated assessments of each interaction's relevance and helpfulness. They surface agent misinterpretations, inefficient subagent flows, and generation failures automatically. Operational use: set a threshold — for example, Quality Score below 60 flags for review — and review flagged conversations weekly. This creates a structured, systematic improvement cadence rather than relying on anecdotal user complaints. Quality Scores are generated per interaction and stored in Data 360, making them queryable for trend analysis.

topics.question: What is the Agentforce Testing Center and what best practice applies to knowledge corpus updates?
topics.answer: The Agentforce Testing Center allows architects to upload a synthetic Q&A test set — question and expected answer pairs — and run a bulk evaluation before deploying changes. The platform measures recall, precision, and faithfulness metrics across the full test set. Best practice: treat synthetic test sets as unit tests for your RAG pipeline. Generate them using an LLM from your document corpus. Run them every time a significant content update is made. Only deploy to production if the quality threshold passes. This prevents regression — a content update that improves coverage for new questions may inadvertently degrade coverage for existing ones.

topics.question: What is the Continuous Improvement Loop and what are its stages?
topics.answer: The Continuous Improvement Loop stages are: (1) Content Added or Updated; (2) Index Refresh — automatic for KNOWLEDGE libraries, manually triggered for SFDRIVE; (3) Testing Center — run synthetic test set evaluation; (4) Deploy to Production only if the quality threshold passes; (5) Observability — monitor session traces, quality scores, and conversation clusters; (6) Weekly review — identify content gaps, routing failures, and efficiency opportunities; (7) Content team addresses identified gaps; (8) Cycle repeats. This positions the agent as a living product rather than a one-time project delivery. The architect's role is to embed this loop into the client's operational model before go-live.

rag.title: Pro-Code RAG: Apex and the Connect API

objectives.title: Know when to use Apex-based retrieval and how to implement it correctly.

topics.question: In what four scenarios is pro-code Apex retrieval appropriate instead of no-code ADL retrievers?
topics.answer: (1) Procedural access control — retrieval results must be filtered based on dynamic runtime user attributes that cannot be expressed as static pre-filter conditions. (2) Multi-corpus merging with custom ranking — you need to merge results from multiple search indexes using custom ranking logic the ensemble retriever does not support. (3) External vector database integration — the data lives in an external vector database such as Pinecone, Weaviate, or Chroma, exposed via a MuleSoft API or external service. (4) Custom reranking models — you want to apply a fine-tuned reranking model to retrieval results before they enter the LLM context window.

topics.question: What are the vector_search and hybrid_search SQL functions in the Data Cloud Connect API?
topics.answer: vector_search executes pure semantic search using a SQL function that accepts the search index name, query text, and number of results, returning chunk text and similarity scores. A similarity score threshold filter (e.g., > 0.75) should be applied to eliminate low-quality matches. hybrid_search executes semantic combined with keyword search using a similar SQL function that additionally accepts a hybrid_weight parameter ranging from 0.0 to 1.0. A value of 0.0 is pure keyword search, 1.0 is pure vector search, and 0.5 is equal weighting. Both functions return chunks with scores for downstream processing in the Apex class.

topics.question: What are the key architectural requirements for an Apex class implementing pro-code RAG?
topics.answer: The Apex class should: (1) accept the user query as an @InvocableVariable input; (2) apply runtime access control logic to determine pre-filter values; (3) build the SQL query string with the appropriate pre-filters; (4) call the Data Cloud Connect API; (5) process and format the returned chunks; (6) return the formatted context as an @InvocableVariable output; (7) return citation metadata such as source names and URLs as separate output fields. Governor limit awareness: Data Cloud Connect API calls count against callout limits — 100 callouts per transaction per Salesforce documentation. Design the Apex class to batch multiple queries into a single API call where possible.

rag.title: MuleSoft as the RAG Extension Layer

objectives.title: Know when MuleSoft extends Agentforce RAG and how Agent-to-Agent retrieval works.

topics.question: What use cases require MuleSoft as the RAG extension layer?
topics.answer: MuleSoft enables Agentforce to retrieve from external systems that ADL and standard Data 360 retrievers cannot reach natively: (1) External knowledge systems such as Confluence, SharePoint, and ServiceNow, where content cannot be uploaded to SFDRIVE due to licensing or data residency constraints. (2) External vector databases such as Pinecone, Weaviate, and Chroma, exposed as a standardized REST endpoint. (3) Legacy content repositories including mainframe-era document stores or proprietary CMS platforms via MuleSoft's connector ecosystem. In all cases, MuleSoft acts as the integration and protocol translation layer between Agentforce and the external system.

topics.question: What is Agent-to-Agent (A2A) retrieval via MuleSoft and when is it used?
topics.answer: A2A retrieval allows a central Agentforce orchestrator to hand off a retrieval-heavy subtask to a specialized external agent. Examples include: a Legal RAG Agent grounded on legal documents and contracts that are too sensitive to mix with general customer service content; a Finance RAG Agent grounded on financial reports, pricing models, and financial policies; a Technical Documentation Agent grounded on deep technical content too large and specialized for the general service agent corpus. MuleSoft manages the handoff, receives structured results from the specialized agent, and returns them to the orchestrating Agentforce agent. This pattern keeps sensitive or large-scale corpora isolated while still making their content available to the main agent.

topics.question: What is MCP integration between MuleSoft and Agentforce and what observability benefit does it provide?
topics.answer: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) integration between MuleSoft and Agentforce enables retrieval telemetry from external RAG sources to flow into enterprise observability platforms such as Splunk, Datadog, and Dynatrace. This gives operations teams a unified view of AI agent performance across Salesforce-native and externally-integrated data sources. Without MCP integration, external retrieval hops are invisible to Agentforce Observability, making it impossible to diagnose whether a quality issue originates in the Agentforce pipeline or in the external retrieval source.

rag.title: Cost Model: RAG Consumes Credits

objectives.title: Understand the Agentforce credit model and apply optimization strategies to reduce consumption.

topics.question: What operations are free and what operations consume credits in Agentforce?
topics.answer: FREE operations: routing and transitions (@utils.transition), variable management (@utils.setVariables), escalation (@utils.escalate), conditional logic, before_reasoning: and after_reasoning: hooks, and LLM reasoning turns. CREDIT-CONSUMING operations: Prompt Template invocation (2-16 credits, varying by template complexity), Flow action execution (20 credits per execution), Apex action execution (20 credits per execution), External Service action (20 credits per execution), AnswerQuestionsWithKnowledge (20 credits per call — it is an action), and General Web Search action (20 credits per call). Key insight: LLM reasoning is free. Actions cost credits. A user who asks 5 questions in one session costs 100 credits for AnswerQuestionsWithKnowledge alone.

topics.question: What is the hybrid search credit premium and when does it justify the cost?
topics.answer: Hybrid search consumes approximately twice as many Data Cloud services credits as pure vector search because it executes two parallel operations — vector and BM25 — and runs a reranking operation over the merged results. Recommendation: start with pure vector search. Establish a quality baseline. Upgrade to hybrid only if there is a measurable 10-15% or greater recall improvement that justifies the credit premium. Hybrid search should be a measurement-driven architectural decision, not a default upgrade applied universally.

topics.question: What is the web search fallback credit implication and why is corpus quality always more cost-effective?
topics.answer: When using the knowledge-first with web search fallback pattern, a session where retrieval misses result in web search fallback incurs credits for both the AnswerQuestionsWithKnowledge action (20 credits, empty result) and the General Web Search action (20 credits, search executed). High miss rates in the proprietary corpus effectively double the retrieval cost for affected queries. This reinforces why improving corpus quality is always more cost-effective than relying on web search fallback at scale — better content reduces misses and eliminates the double-billing scenario.

topics.question: What is the loop iteration limit and how should agents be designed around it?
topics.answer: Per Salesforce documentation, Agentforce enforces a hard limit of approximately 3-4 loop iterations per agent session. Do not design agents that rely on retry loops. Always build explicit fallback branches. For example: call AnswerQuestionsWithKnowledge once. If knowledgeSummary is empty, transition immediately to the escalation subagent — do not retry. In production, an agent that works in preview can fail after 3-4 turns with a generic error if retry loops or circular references are present. Map all execution paths and eliminate any circular references before go-live.

topics.question: What are the three main credit optimization strategies in Agentforce?
topics.answer: (1) Preemptive action execution in before_reasoning: — actions that must always run, such as identity verification or session initialization, run deterministically before the LLM, eliminating unnecessary multi-turn loops that would otherwise consume extra action credits. (2) Filter retrieval by pre-conditions — use 'available when' guards on the AnswerQuestionsWithKnowledge action to prevent it from being called when the query is too vague, saving 20 credits per avoided call. (3) Cache context in variables — store retrieved data such as account tier or customer type in session variables after the first retrieval. Do not call the retrieval action again for the same data within the same session.

rag.title: Troubleshooting and Quality Metrics

objectives.title: Apply the 7-layer diagnostic ladder and interpret RAG quality metric patterns.

topics.question: What are the seven layers of the diagnostic ladder for 'agent is not answering correctly' issues?
topics.answer: Layer 1: Content Existence — does the answer actually exist in the corpus? Search the raw source content before diagnosing the retrieval pipeline. Layer 2: Content Quality — is the content written in a way that supports semantic retrieval? Short, categorical, or overly technical content without explanatory context retrieves poorly. Layer 3: Chunking — is the answer split across a chunk boundary? Adjust chunk size or rethink content structure. Layer 4: Retrieval — are the right chunks being retrieved? Use Prompt Builder debug mode by appending &c__debug=1 to the URL to inspect exact chunks returned. Layer 5: Context Window — is enough relevant context being returned? Increase num_results on the retriever and re-test. Layer 6: Generation — is the LLM ignoring the retrieved context? Strengthen the grounding directive in the instructions. Layer 7: Permissions — is the agent user blocked from accessing the content? Check all four permission layers (Data Cloud Permission Set, Knowledge Object/FLS, Language Alignment, and Data Space Scope).

topics.question: What are the three RAG quality metrics and what does each measure?
topics.answer: Faithfulness: measures whether the generated answer is grounded in the retrieved context. A low score indicates the LLM is fabricating or paraphrasing beyond retrieved content. Context Relevance: measures whether the retrieved context is relevant to the user's query. A low score indicates the retriever is returning wrong or off-topic chunks. Answer Relevance: measures whether the final answer addresses the user's question. A low score indicates a content gap or context window size issue. All three metrics must be measured together — high scores on some dimensions while others are low reveal specific, diagnosable failure modes.

topics.question: What do the three RAG quality metric pattern combinations diagnose?
topics.answer: Pattern 1: Low Faithfulness combined with High Context Relevance — the right content was retrieved but the LLM is not using it correctly. Fix: strengthen the grounding directive in instructions. Pattern 2: Low Context Relevance combined with any Faithfulness score — the wrong content is being retrieved. Fix: check embedding model selection, search strategy, or content quality and structure. Pattern 3: High Faithfulness combined with High Context Relevance but Low Answer Relevance — the agent is accurately grounded in retrieved content but that content does not fully answer the question. Fix: this is a content gap. Add the missing information to the corpus. There is no prompt-level fix for a content gap.

rag.title: Known Platform Issues and Production Gotchas

objectives.title: Know the most common production gotchas, their symptoms, and their fixes.

topics.question: What is the KNOWLEDGE library race condition symptom and fix?
topics.answer: Symptom: the library shows READY with retrieverId populated, but every grounded query returns empty knowledgeSummary. Fix: wait 10 minutes, send a live test query. If still empty, force a re-index by running the sf agent adl update command with the library ID, target org, and content fields specified. Do not declare success based on retrieverId alone for KNOWLEDGE libraries. Always verify with a live test query that returns non-empty knowledgeSummary before declaring the library ready for production.

topics.question: What is the language filtering silent failure symptom and fix?
topics.answer: Symptom: KNOWLEDGE library shows READY and permissions are correct, but grounded queries return empty results with no error message. Fix: align the agent user's LanguageLocaleKey with the article language in Salesforce. Even en_US vs. en_GB is treated as a mismatch. Verify via SOQL by querying Knowledge__kav grouped by Language where PublishStatus = 'Online' and comparing the results to the agent user's LanguageLocaleKey.

topics.question: What is the Data Space Scope UI-only gotcha and why does it block automated deployments?
topics.answer: Symptom: all permissions are assigned correctly but grounded queries still return empty results. Fix: set the Data Space scope in Setup UI on the agent user's Data Cloud permission set — this step cannot be performed via metadata XML deployment. Navigate to Setup, open Permission Sets, click the assigned Data Cloud permission set, open Data Cloud Data Space Management, edit the list, add the ADL's data space (typically 'default') to the Enabled Data Spaces list, and save. Every automated deployment pipeline must document this as a required manual post-deployment step that cannot be skipped.

topics.question: What is the ARFPC_ prefix gotcha and what error does it produce?
topics.answer: Symptom: sf agent validate fails with an unresolved reference error pointing to the knowledge: block. Fix: prepend ARFPC_ to the library ID in the rag_feature_config_id field. Correct format: rag_feature_config_id: 'ARFPC_1JDg7000001hilBGAQ'. The error message points to the knowledge: block but does not explain the prefix requirement, making this one of the most confusing implementation errors. Always include the ARFPC_ prefix when wiring a library into the .agent file.

topics.question: What is the reserved @InvocableVariable keywords gotcha?
topics.answer: Symptom: Apex compiles successfully but the agent fails at runtime with errors such as 'SyntaxError: Unexpected model' or similar messages referencing field names. Fix: rename reserved field names in the Apex @InvocableVariable class. Use vehicle_model instead of model, and issue_description instead of description. The reserved keyword list includes: model, description, label, and other Agent Script built-in identifiers. Always review @InvocableVariable field names for conflicts with Agent Script reserved words before deployment.

topics.question: What is the @inputs scope violation silent drop and how is it fixed?
topics.answer: Symptom: an action executes successfully but a variable set from @inputs shows its default value rather than the action's output. Fix: use @outputs to capture action results. @inputs is only valid during action invocation inside the 'with' directive — it is not a general-purpose storage mechanism. Attempting to read @inputs outside of the specific context where it is valid causes a silent drop where the variable retains its default value. This is one of the most insidious bugs because there is no error message, only wrong data at runtime.

topics.question: What is the web search fallback content control risk and how is it mitigated?
topics.answer: Symptom (operational, not technical): the web search fallback surfaces competitor information or off-brand content in agent responses. Fix: scope the General Web Search action to a specific domain or set of domains. If domain scoping is not sufficient to prevent unacceptable content, remove the web search fallback entirely and use the refuse/escalate pattern instead. This is an operational risk that must be evaluated before enabling web search for any customer-facing agent, particularly in competitive industries.

rag.title: Success Architect Client Conversation Frameworks

objectives.title: Apply structured conversation frameworks to scope, diagnose, and recommend Agentforce RAG solutions.

topics.question: What are the five discovery questions a Success Architect should answer before scoping any Agentforce RAG solution?
topics.answer: (1) What is the business outcome? 'Reduce Tier 1 support tickets' is an outcome. 'Build a chatbot' is not. (2) Where does the content live today? Salesforce Knowledge, SharePoint, PDFs, public website? (3) Who is the audience? Customer-facing service agent, internal employee agent, or sales productivity agent? (4) What does success look like in 90 days? This drives metric selection and scope boundaries. (5) Is Data Cloud already provisioned? This determines whether RAG is in scope for initial delivery and what the timeline will be.

topics.question: How should a Success Architect lead the 'Is Data Cloud Required?' conversation with a client?
topics.answer: Lead with: 'It depends on what you need the agent to do.' If the client wants a basic conversational agent that routes to human agents and executes Salesforce actions, Data Cloud is not required. If the client wants the agent to answer questions from their knowledge base, produce compliance audit trails, use their preferred LLM, or measure agent performance with analytics, Data Cloud is required. The practical reality for most enterprise clients: they want at least one of those features. Position Data 360 proactively as the intelligence infrastructure that makes the investment enterprise-grade rather than presenting it as an add-on cost.

topics.question: How should a Success Architect frame the 'Why Is the Agent Not Answering Correctly?' conversation?
topics.answer: Use the 7-layer diagnostic ladder covered in the Troubleshooting and Quality Metrics section. Client framing: 'When an agent gives a wrong or incomplete answer, the root cause is always in one of seven places. Let us go through them in order, because fixing the wrong layer wastes time and budget.' This positions the architect as methodical and expert. It prevents the client from jumping to 'rewrite the prompt' as a first response to every quality issue. Walk through the layers in order: content existence, content quality, chunking, retrieval, context window, generation, and permissions.

topics.question: How should a Success Architect frame the 'When Do We Need Hybrid Search?' conversation?
topics.answer: Default recommendation: start with pure vector search. Upgrade trigger: when the client reports that the agent is not finding answers to questions involving specific product names, order numbers, policy codes, or other exact-match terminology. Frame the upgrade decision as measurement-driven: 'Let us run a test set of 20 failing queries and compare vector-only retrieval against hybrid. If hybrid delivers 10% or more recall improvement, it is worth the cost increase.' Never recommend hybrid search without first establishing a quality baseline and quantifying the improvement.

topics.question: What is the six-step Architecture Recommendation Framework for presenting solutions to clients?
topics.answer: (1) State the requirements — what specific capabilities does this solution need? (2) State the constraints — data residency, existing licenses, content location, and timeline. (3) Apply the decision tree — walk through the ADL scoping decision tree explicitly and visibly. (4) Recommend the pattern — name the architecture pattern that fits and explain why it was selected. (5) Identify the risks — name the two or three most likely failure modes and your mitigation approach for each. (6) Define success metrics — name the specific Agentforce Observability metrics you will use to declare the solution successful. This structure demonstrates rigor and builds client trust.

rag.title: Architecture Pattern Reference

objectives.title: Select and explain the correct architecture pattern for each Agentforce RAG use case.

topics.question: What is Pattern 1: Simplest Viable RAG, when is it used, and what are its key risks?
topics.answer: Pattern: ADL with the KNOWLEDGE source type. Use when: the client has existing, well-maintained Salesforce Knowledge articles. This is the fastest time-to-value path. Flow: Published Knowledge articles are ingested via the ADL KNOWLEDGE source type, which auto-provisions the full pipeline through a Search Index and Milvus Vector Store to a Retriever. The .agent file uses the knowledge: block and AnswerQuestionsWithKnowledge action. At runtime, a user query is embedded, Milvus similarity search runs, and a grounded response with citations is returned. Key risks: (1) language alignment failure causing silent empty results; (2) the Day 0 race condition causing READY status with 0 indexed chunks; (3) Knowledge article quality not optimized for semantic retrieval — articles written for human browsing may not chunk or retrieve well for AI.

topics.question: What is Pattern 2: Document Library RAG, when is it used, and what is the key risk?
topics.answer: Pattern: ADL with the SFDRIVE source type. Use when: the client has knowledge in PDF, HTML, or TXT files with no existing Salesforce Knowledge setup. Flow: client files are uploaded using 'sf agent adl upload', triggering JIT indexing in either basic or enhanced mode. The Docling or default parser processes the content into chunks, which are embedded and stored in Milvus via the ADL SFDRIVE library and retriever. At runtime, grounded responses with citations are returned. Key decisions: basic vs. enhanced index mode, chunk size tuning, and per-file INDEXED status verification. Key risk: files with tables fail silently with the default parser. Always test with representative documents — including any tables or multi-column layouts — before bulk upload.

topics.question: What is Pattern 3: Multi-Source Ensemble RAG, when is it used, and what is its key risk?
topics.answer: Pattern: Ensemble Retriever combining multiple ADL sources. Use when: the client has content in multiple formats — such as Knowledge articles and PDFs — and users ask questions that span those formats. Flow: Source A (Knowledge Articles) flows through an ADL KNOWLEDGE library to Retriever A. Source B (Product PDFs) flows through an ADL SFDRIVE library to Retriever B. Both retrievers feed into an Ensemble Retriever, which merges and reranks results across both sources. A Prompt Template with dynamic retriever binding passes the merged context to the Agentforce Agent, which returns a grounded response with citations drawn from both sources. Key risk: source overlap creates noisy context windows. Content governance must be consistent across both sources to prevent contradictory information from appearing in the same response.

topics.question: What is Pattern 4: Knowledge-First with Web Search Fallback, when is it used, and when is it NOT appropriate?
topics.answer: Pattern: AnswerQuestionsWithKnowledge as primary, General Web Search as fallback when knowledgeSummary is empty. Use when: the agent's scope includes both proprietary knowledge and general public information, and the compliance team has approved public web grounding. Flow: User question triggers AnswerQuestionsWithKnowledge. If knowledgeSummary is non-empty, the agent answers from the proprietary corpus with citations. If knowledgeSummary is empty, the General Web Search action runs and the agent answers from web results labeled as 'from public sources.' Key decisions: domain scoping on the General Web Search action, compliance review before deployment, and credit model implications of double-action miss scenarios. NOT appropriate for: regulated industries, compliance-governed agents, or proprietary-only scope.

topics.question: What is Pattern 5: Pro-Code RAG with Access Control, when is it used, and what are its key risks?
topics.answer: Pattern: Apex @InvocableMethod implementing custom retrieval with runtime user-specific filtering. Use when: retrieval results must enforce dynamic, runtime user-specific access rules that cannot be expressed as static pre-filters. Flow: the Agent calls an Apex @InvocableMethod action. At runtime, the Apex class queries the user's role or clearance level from Salesforce objects, builds a dynamic SQL query with user-specific pre-filters, and calls the Data Cloud Connect API using vector_search() or hybrid_search(). Milvus returns filtered, ranked chunks. The Apex class formats chunks into a structured context string that the LLM uses to generate a response grounded in the access-controlled content. Key risks: governor limit exposure from the 100 callout limit per transaction, Apex errors that fail the entire action, and the need for thorough Apex test coverage with realistic @InvocableVariable inputs.

topics.question: What is Pattern 6: External RAG via MuleSoft, when is it used, and what is its key risk?
topics.answer: Pattern: MuleSoft API as the retrieval endpoint for external systems. Use when: the grounding data cannot be ingested into Salesforce due to data residency restrictions, licensing constraints, or volume constraints. Flow: an external system such as Confluence, SharePoint, or an external vector database connects to a MuleSoft API that serves as the retrieval endpoint with authentication and scoping. The Agentforce agent calls the MuleSoft API via an External Service action. MuleSoft executes retrieval against the external system and returns structured chunks with citation metadata. The agent formats the results into a grounding context and the LLM generates a response. Key decisions: MuleSoft API authentication, error handling if MuleSoft is unavailable, and latency benchmarking. Key risk: external system availability becomes an agent dependency. The Trust Layer masking still applies to returned content even though the data lives externally.

uxdesigner.title: Provided with a set of business requirements, determine which research methodology and tools should be used to design a solution.

objectives.title: Provided with a set of business requirements, determine which research methodology and tools should be used to design a solution.

topics.question: Selecting the correct research approach (generative vs. evaluative) depending on whether the team is exploring a problem space or validating a proposed solution.
topics.answer: Generative research is used when the team does not yet know what problem to solve. Methods include interviews, ethnographic observation, and diary studies. The output is insights and problem definitions. Evaluative research is used when a solution already exists (even as a prototype) and the team needs to assess how well it works. Methods include usability testing and A/B testing. Key rule: if the team is asking 'What should we build?' use generative. If asking 'Does this work?' use evaluative.

topics.question: Choosing between qualitative research methods (contextual inquiry, interviews, diary studies) vs. quantitative methods (surveys, analytics) given a specific business constraint such as limited access to users or need for statistical confidence.
topics.answer: Qualitative methods (interviews, contextual inquiry, diary studies) reveal the 'why' behind behaviors. They require fewer participants (5-10) but need direct user access. Use them to uncover motivations, mental models, and pain points. Quantitative methods (surveys, analytics) reveal the 'what' and 'how many.' They require larger samples for statistical significance and can be run without live user access. If you have limited user access, analytics and surveys are practical alternatives. If you need to understand root causes, qualitative methods are essential even with access constraints.

topics.question: Defining research objectives and writing a discussion guide for a stakeholder or user interview, including how to structure open-ended questions to avoid leading the participant.
topics.answer: A research objective defines what you need to learn (e.g., 'Understand how sales reps currently track follow-up activities'). A discussion guide is a structured but flexible script with warm-up questions, core topic questions, and wrap-up. Open-ended questions begin with 'Tell me about...', 'Walk me through...', or 'How do you...'. Avoid leading questions like 'Don't you find it hard to...?' or binary yes/no questions. Probing follow-ups such as 'Can you say more about that?' surface deeper insights without steering the participant.

topics.question: Selecting the appropriate discovery tool (empathy maps, journey maps, stakeholder maps, affinity diagrams) based on the research goal and available inputs.
topics.answer: Empathy maps (Think/Feel/Say/Do) synthesize interview data into a shared understanding of a user's mindset. Journey maps visualize the end-to-end experience across touchpoints and reveal moments of friction. Stakeholder maps identify who influences the project and their level of interest/power. Affinity diagrams cluster raw research observations into themes to surface patterns. Choose based on what you have: raw interview notes -> affinity diagram; need to understand a user's emotional experience -> empathy map; need to see the full flow of a process -> journey map.

topics.question: Determining appropriate participant screening criteria and recruitment strategies when end users are difficult to access directly (e.g., using proxy users, SMEs, or customer success managers as substitutes).
topics.answer: Screening criteria define who qualifies as a valid research participant (e.g., role, tenure, usage frequency). When direct end-user access is blocked, proxy users, subject matter experts (SMEs), or customer success managers who interact with users daily can serve as substitutes. Proxies provide second-hand insights, so triangulate their input with any available analytics data. Always document proxy limitations in your research findings so stakeholders understand the gap.

topics.question: Using competitive analysis or benchmarking against industry-standard UX patterns to establish baseline design requirements when no direct user access is available.
topics.answer: Competitive analysis reviews how similar products solve the same problem, revealing industry norms users may already expect. Benchmarking compares a proposed design against established UX heuristics or recognized pattern libraries (e.g., Nielsen Norman Group, SLDS component blueprints). Both are useful when you cannot recruit users: they give you a defensible baseline for design decisions grounded in existing user expectations rather than assumptions.

topics.question: Determining when to use card sorting vs. tree testing for evaluating information architecture decisions.
topics.answer: Card sorting asks participants to group content cards into categories that make sense to them. It is used early, when you are designing or redesigning a navigation structure, to understand users' mental models. Tree testing (also called 'reverse card sorting') asks participants to find items within an existing hierarchy. It validates whether a proposed navigation structure is intuitive. Use card sorting to create IA; use tree testing to validate it.

topics.question: Identifying the appropriate use of usability testing vs. A/B testing given constraints around sample size, development phase, and decision type.
topics.answer: Usability testing observes users completing tasks and identifies why problems occur. It requires fewer participants (5-8), works at any fidelity level, and surfaces qualitative insight. A/B testing compares two live variants with a large audience to determine which performs better on a measurable metric. Use usability testing in discovery or design phases to find and fix problems. Use A/B testing in production when you need statistically significant data on which of two working solutions drives better outcomes.

uxdesigner.title: Given a scenario, demonstrate how to gather requirements and plan strategy given current user experiences.

objectives.title: Given a scenario, demonstrate how to gather requirements and plan strategy given current user experiences.

topics.question: Using stakeholder interviews and contextual observation to surface hidden pain points that stakeholders cannot articulate in written requirements.
topics.answer: Stakeholders often describe solutions ('we need a button here') rather than problems. Interviews using open-ended questions reveal the underlying need. Contextual observation (watching users work in their actual environment) uncovers workarounds, shortcuts, and frustrations that users have normalized and would never mention in a meeting. Together, these methods surface the real requirements behind stated ones.

topics.question: Identifying when existing analytics data (page views, drop-off rates, click paths) is sufficient to define design requirements vs. when primary research is still required.
topics.answer: Analytics data is sufficient when it clearly answers 'what is happening' and the decision is straightforward (e.g., a page with a 90% drop-off rate clearly needs redesign). Primary research is still required when analytics shows a problem but not the cause (e.g., users abandon a form, but you don't know why). The rule: analytics defines the 'what'; interviews and observation reveal the 'why.' Use both together for the strongest requirements base.

topics.question: Synthesizing research findings using affinity mapping to cluster themes and identify the most impactful problem areas to address in a Salesforce solution.
topics.answer: Affinity mapping involves writing individual observations, quotes, or data points on sticky notes (physical or digital) and grouping them by similarity. Clusters that emerge represent recurring themes. In a Salesforce context, common themes might be around data entry friction, navigation confusion, or lack of visibility into related records. Once clustered, themes are ranked by frequency and severity to prioritize the Salesforce configuration or design changes that will have the most impact.

topics.question: Building an as-is journey map from interview and observation data to identify moments of friction in the current user experience.
topics.answer: An as-is journey map documents what users actually do today, step by step, including the systems they use, their actions, their emotional highs and lows, and their pain points at each stage. It is built from interview quotes and observation notes. In Salesforce projects, this reveals where users switch between systems, perform manual workarounds, or duplicate data entry, which then become the targets for declarative or process improvements.

topics.question: Translating raw user research findings into a prioritized problem statement (How Might We statement) to guide design strategy.
topics.answer: A How Might We (HMW) statement reframes a user pain point as a design opportunity. Format: 'How might we [help user] [achieve goal] [given constraint]?' Example: 'How might we help service agents find related case history without leaving the active case record?' HMWs are derived from affinity-mapped research themes and serve as the design brief. They are broad enough to allow creative solutions but specific enough to stay grounded in the real user problem.

topics.question: Aligning stakeholders around research findings by presenting evidence (quotes, observations, data) in a compelling format that builds organizational support for a UX-centered approach.
topics.answer: Stakeholders respond to evidence, not opinions. Present findings using a mix of direct user quotes, video clips (if available), behavioral data, and journey maps. Frame issues in terms of business impact (e.g., 'Users spend 12 minutes per case switching systems, translating to X hours per week across the team'). Use a structured readout with themes, supporting evidence, and prioritized recommendations. This transforms research into a shared organizational understanding that justifies UX investment.

topics.question: Conducting a heuristic evaluation against Nielsen's 10 heuristics to identify UX deficiencies in an existing Salesforce implementation.
topics.answer: Nielsen's 10 heuristics are expert-review criteria: (1) Visibility of system status, (2) Match between system and real world, (3) User control and freedom, (4) Consistency and standards, (5) Error prevention, (6) Recognition over recall, (7) Flexibility and efficiency, (8) Aesthetic and minimalist design, (9) Help users recognize and recover from errors, (10) Help and documentation. Evaluators walk through a Salesforce implementation and flag violations per heuristic with a severity rating. No user recruitment is needed, making it fast and cost-effective for identifying obvious problems.

uxdesigner.title: Describe key Salesforce UX personas and which processes they normally do.

objectives.title: Describe key Salesforce UX personas and which processes they normally do.

topics.question: Differentiating the responsibilities and platform behaviors of the Salesforce Admin, End User, and Executive personas in the context of UX design.
