topics.question: Sharing rules can only open access beyond OWD — they can never restrict access that has already been granted by OWD or another mechanism; understanding this unidirectional nature when diagnosing unexpected access
topics.answer: Sharing rules are additive only. If a user already has Read/Write via OWD or role hierarchy, a sharing rule granting Read Only to that same user has no effect — it cannot reduce their access. When diagnosing a case where a user has "too much" access, sharing rules are never the culprit. The problem will always be OWD being too open, or the role hierarchy or another grant providing broader access than intended.

topics.question: Criteria-based sharing rules vs. owner-based sharing rules: which triggers automatically when record data changes vs. when record ownership changes
topics.answer:
- Owner-based sharing rules fire automatically when a record's owner changes. They share records owned by members of one group with members of another group.

- Criteria-based sharing rules fire automatically when a record's field values change and match the rule's criteria (e.g., Industry = "Technology"). If a field value changes so the record now meets the criteria, the share is granted. If it no longer meets criteria, the share is revoked.

Key distinction: criteria-based rules respond to data; owner-based rules respond to ownership.

topics.question: Public Groups in sharing rules: how a public group can include users, roles, roles and subordinates, and other public groups, and why using a public group in a sharing rule is more maintainable than adding individual users directly
topics.answer: A Public Group can contain any mix of: individual users, roles, roles and subordinates, and other public groups. When used as the target of a sharing rule, adding or removing a user from the group automatically updates their record access without touching the sharing rule itself. This is far more maintainable than building sharing rules around individual users, which would require rule changes every time someone joins or leaves a team.

topics.question: Field-Level Security vs. page layout visibility: which one is the authoritative security control that prevents a user from reading a field value via API
topics.answer: Field-Level Security (FLS) is the authoritative control. If a field is set to Hidden or Read Only via FLS on a profile or permission set, the user cannot see or access that field value through the UI, API, or reports — regardless of whether the field appears on a page layout. Page layout visibility only controls what is shown on the screen in the UI. A field hidden on a page layout but not restricted by FLS is still fully accessible via API. For true security, FLS must be configured.

topics.question: When a record's OWD is set to 'Controlled by Parent' on a child object and the parent is Private, determining what access a user without an explicit share on the parent record has to the child record
topics.answer: "Controlled by Parent" means the child record's access is entirely determined by the user's access to the parent record. If the parent object's OWD is Private and a user has no share on the parent, they have no access to the parent record. As a result, they also have no access to any child records tied to that parent, even if they know the child record exists. Access to the child requires access to the parent first.

topics.question: Grant Access Using Hierarchies setting on custom objects: how disabling this setting prevents the role hierarchy from granting access upward and the implications for manager access to subordinates' records
topics.answer: By default, users above a record owner in the role hierarchy inherit at least the same access the owner has. On custom objects, an admin can disable "Grant Access Using Hierarchies." When disabled, the role hierarchy is no longer used to grant access for that object — a manager will not automatically see their subordinate's records. The only ways to access those records are via OWD (if not Private), sharing rules, or explicit manual shares. This setting cannot be disabled on standard objects.

topics.question: Manual sharing behavior on ownership transfer: when a record owner changes, which sharing grants are automatically removed
topics.answer: When a record's owner changes, all manual shares (shares created via the Sharing button) on that record are automatically deleted. Shares granted via OWD, role hierarchy, sharing rules, or territory management are unaffected and recalculated based on the new owner. The practical implication: if a user manually shared a record with someone, and ownership is then transferred, that manual share is gone and must be re-created if still needed.

topics.question: Report folder and email template folder sharing: which user types (public groups, roles, roles and subordinates) can be granted access
topics.answer: Report and email template folders can be shared with: individual users, public groups, roles, and roles and subordinates. Access levels for report folders are: Viewer (can run), Editor (can run and save), and Manager (can manage the folder). Sharing folders with roles and subordinates is especially useful for giving an entire sales hierarchy access to a set of reports without managing individual users. Guest users cannot access shared folders.

topics.question: Dashboard folder sharing: the access levels available (Viewer, Editor, Manager) and which level allows a user to save a dashboard back to a shared folder
topics.answer:
Dashboard folders have three access levels:

- Viewer: Can view and run dashboards in the folder, but cannot save changes.

- Editor: Can view, run, and edit dashboards, and save them back to the folder.

- Manager: Can do everything Editors can, plus manage folder membership and delete the folder.

To save a modified dashboard back to a shared folder, a user needs at minimum Editor access on that folder.

topics.question: Territory Management 2.0 model states (Planning, Active, Archived) and what actions are allowed in each state
topics.answer:
| State | What You Can Do |

|---|---|

| Planning | Create/edit territory types, models, hierarchy, and rules. Cannot run assignment rules org-wide. |

| Active | Run assignment rules, associate users to territories, connect to forecasting. Only one model can be Active at a time. |

| Archived | Read-only. No edits, no rule execution. Used for historical reference. |

You must activate a model before its territories affect record access or forecasting.

topics.question: How Territory Management 2.0 assignment rules determine which territories are assigned to an account and how that propagates access to related opportunities and contacts
topics.answer: Territory assignment rules evaluate account field values (e.g., State, Industry, Annual Revenue) and assign matching accounts to territories. When an account is saved, Salesforce runs all active rules in the active model and assigns the account to every matching territory. Users assigned to those territories then gain access to the account. Opportunities associated with the account are also accessible to territory users. Contacts associated with the account gain the same territory-based access through the account relationship.

topics.question: Given a multi-mechanism scenario (Private OWD + role hierarchy + criteria-based sharing rule + Territory Management), identifying which mechanism grants a specific user Read/Write access to an account record
topics.answer: Work through each mechanism in turn and take the highest access granted:

topics.question: **OWD Private**: grants nothing by default.
**Role Hierarchy**: does the user sit above the record owner? If yes, grants at least the owner's access.
**Criteria-based sharing rule**: does the account's field data match the rule criteria and is the user in the target group? Grants the access level defined on the rule.
**Territory Management**: is the user assigned to a territory that covers this account? Grants access per territory settings.
topics.answer: The user's effective access is the highest level from any single mechanism. To determine *which* one granted it, identify the first mechanism that produces the access level in question.

admin2.title: Compare and contrast the capabilities of custom profiles, permission sets, and delegated administration.

objectives.title: Compare and contrast the capabilities of custom profiles, permission sets, and delegated administration.

topics.question: Permission sets vs. profiles: which object-level permissions can be granted via permission set but NOT removed via permission set
topics.answer: Permission sets can only add permissions on top of what a profile grants — they cannot take permissions away. For example, if a user's profile grants Read on Accounts, a permission set cannot remove that Read access. The only way to remove an object permission is to edit the profile directly. This means profiles still define the minimum permission baseline, and permission sets are purely additive grants layered on top.

topics.question: Custom profiles: limitations on deletion (cannot delete a profile assigned to a user) and cloning behavior when the source profile has a permission not available in the target edition
topics.answer: You cannot delete a custom profile if any user is currently assigned to it. You must first reassign all those users to a different profile. When cloning a profile, if the source profile contains permissions that are not available in the current edition (e.g., a feature only in Enterprise), those permissions are silently dropped from the clone. Always review the cloned profile to confirm all expected permissions carried over correctly.

topics.question: Delegated administration: what a delegated administrator CAN do (manage users in specified roles/subordinates, assign specified profiles and permission sets, unlock users) vs. what they CANNOT do (change OWDs, create or clone profiles)
topics.answer:
Can do:

- Create and edit users in specified roles and their subordinates.

- Assign only the profiles and permission sets explicitly listed in their delegation group.

- Unlock user accounts and reset passwords for users in their scope.

Cannot do:

- Change Organization-Wide Defaults.

- Create, clone, or delete profiles.

- Manage users outside their delegated scope.

- Change system-level settings or org security.

Delegated admins are scoped helpers, not full system administrators.

topics.question: Delegated administrator scope: a delegated admin is restricted to managing users within which roles relative to their defined delegation group
topics.answer: A delegated administrator can manage users in the roles explicitly listed in their delegation group AND all subordinate roles below those roles in the hierarchy. They cannot manage peers, users in roles above their scope, or users in entirely separate role branches. The scope is always downward from the specified roles.

topics.question: Permission set groups: how stacking multiple permission sets into a group differs from assigning each permission set individually
topics.answer: A Permission Set Group bundles multiple permission sets into a single unit for assignment. The result is the union of all permissions across every permission set in the group. Functionally, assigning a group or assigning each constituent permission set individually produces the same net permissions. The advantage of a group is operational: you assign one thing to a user instead of many, and adding or removing a permission set from the group instantly updates all users assigned to the group.

topics.question: Permission set groups: the role of muting permission sets within a group and when muting is appropriate
topics.answer: A Muting Permission Set is a special permission set that can only exist inside a Permission Set Group. It selectively removes specific permissions that one of the group's constituent permission sets would otherwise grant. Use muting when you want to use a broad permission set (e.g., "Sales Rep Full Access") but need to suppress one specific permission (e.g., Delete on Opportunities) without creating an entirely new permission set. Muting avoids the overhead of maintaining duplicated permission sets with minor variations.

topics.question: Permission Set License (PSL): the concept of a license-based permission set that grants access to features available only in add-on licenses (e.g., Einstein Analytics, Salesforce Maps) and how PSLs differ from standard permission sets
topics.answer: A Permission Set License (PSL) is a license entitlement that must be assigned to a user before any permission set granting the related feature can be assigned. For example, to grant a user access to Einstein Analytics, they must first have the Einstein Analytics PSL assigned, and then a permission set enabling specific Analytics features. PSLs are tied to purchased add-on licenses — they are not configuration objects you create. Standard permission sets grant feature access within the org's existing license; PSLs unlock entirely separate licensed feature sets.

admin2.title: Given a scenario, determine the implications of user authentication.

objectives.title: Given a scenario, determine the implications of user authentication.

topics.question: My Domain requirement: which Salesforce features require My Domain to be enabled before they can be configured (SSO, Lightning components, etc.)
topics.answer:
My Domain must be enabled before you can configure:

- Single Sign-On (SSO) with external identity providers.

- Lightning components (Aura and LWC) deployed to the org.

- Social Sign-On (login via Google, Facebook, etc.).

- Canvas apps.

- Named Credentials that reference the org's domain.

My Domain gives the org a unique URL (e.g., `yourcompany.my.salesforce.com`), which is required for these features to function correctly and securely.

topics.question: Login IP Ranges (on profiles) vs. Trusted IP Ranges (org-wide): which setting prevents login entirely vs. which triggers an email verification challenge when outside the range
topics.answer:
- Login IP Ranges (profile-level): If a user's IP is outside the configured range, login is completely blocked. No workaround via email challenge. The user simply cannot log in.

- Trusted IP Ranges (org-wide, in Security Controls): If a user's IP is outside this range, Salesforce sends an email verification challenge (an activation link). The user can still log in after clicking the link. This is a friction-add, not a hard block.

The profile-level setting is the stricter enforcement mechanism.

topics.question: Login Hours: how the profile-level restriction blocks access outside configured hours and how it differs from IP-based restrictions
topics.answer: Login Hours restrict when users on a specific profile can log in. Outside configured hours, login is blocked entirely. If a user is already logged in when their allowed window closes, their session expires and they are logged out at the next page load. Unlike IP restrictions, Login Hours are time-based only and have nothing to do with network location. Both restrictions can apply simultaneously to the same profile — a user must be in both the right IP range and within the allowed hours to log in.

topics.question: Session Settings: session timeout values and how idle sessions are terminated
topics.answer: Session Settings (under Security Controls) control how long an authenticated session remains valid. The timeout value defines the maximum idle time before a session is automatically invalidated (options range from 15 minutes to 8 hours, default is 2 hours). When the idle timeout is reached, the user's session is terminated and they are redirected to the login page on their next action. Admins can also set an absolute session timeout regardless of activity and enforce re-authentication after the session expires.

topics.question: SAML-based SSO: the role of the Identity Provider (IdP), the Service Provider (SP), and the assertion consumer service URL in the login flow
topics.answer:
- Identity Provider (IdP): The system that authenticates the user and issues the SAML assertion (e.g., Okta, Azure AD, ADFS). It is the "trust source."

- Service Provider (SP): Salesforce. It receives and validates the SAML assertion but relies on the IdP to do the actual authentication.

- Assertion Consumer Service (ACS) URL: The Salesforce endpoint that receives the SAML response from the IdP after a successful authentication. The IdP posts the assertion to this URL to complete the login flow.

Flow: User attempts to access Salesforce → redirected to IdP → user authenticates at IdP → IdP posts SAML assertion to ACS URL → Salesforce validates assertion → user is logged in.

topics.question: MFA enforcement: the difference between enabling MFA in Session Settings vs. using a Permission Set vs. org-wide enforcement
topics.answer:
- Session Settings (profile-level): Enables MFA for users on a specific profile. Granular control but requires per-profile configuration.

- Permission Set: A "Multi-Factor Authentication for User Interface Logins" permission can be added to a permission set and assigned to specific users, regardless of their profile.

- Org-wide enforcement: Via the "Require MFA for All Direct UI Logins" setting in Session Settings or by enabling the Salesforce MFA requirement, it applies to every user in the org with no exceptions at the profile level.

Org-wide enforcement is the most comprehensive and least granular. Salesforce requires MFA for all orgs.

topics.question: MFA enforcement: what happens to existing user sessions when MFA is newly enabled or enforced
topics.answer: Existing active sessions are not immediately terminated when MFA is newly enabled. Users currently logged in can continue their session. However, the next time they log in (after their current session expires or they log out), they will be required to complete MFA. There is no forced re-authentication of live sessions at the moment MFA is switched on.

topics.question: Connected App OAuth flow: when an admin must pre-authorize a connected app for all users vs. requiring user-level authorization
topics.answer:
- Admin pre-authorization ("Admin approved users are pre-authorized"): The admin enables the connected app for all users and approves it centrally. Individual users are not prompted for OAuth consent. Use this for internal integrations where you do not want users to see or manage OAuth prompts.

- User-level authorization ("All users may self-authorize"): Each user must individually approve the connected app's access to their account the first time they authenticate. Use this for apps where individual user consent is appropriate or required.

The Connected App's OAuth Policies setting controls this behavior.

admin2.title: Compare and contrast the capabilities of a complex business model (...)

objectives.title: Compare and contrast the capabilities of a complex business model (...)

topics.question: Person Accounts: the record types they merge (Account + Contact into one record) and which standard Contact features are unavailable (e.g., cannot relate a Person Account contact to multiple accounts)
topics.answer:
A Person Account is a single record that combines Account and Contact fields, designed for B2C scenarios where your customers are individuals rather than businesses. Because the Contact is merged into the Account record, the following standard Contact features are not available for Person Accounts:

- Cannot be related to multiple accounts (Contacts to Multiple Accounts).

- Cannot have a Reports To relationship.

- Cannot be the primary contact on a separate Account record.

- Do not appear in the standard Contacts list view.

Person Accounts behave like Accounts in sharing and like Contacts in some Service Cloud features.

topics.question: Person Accounts enablement: once Person Accounts are enabled, what change is irreversible and what prerequisite record type setup is required
topics.answer: Enabling Person Accounts is irreversible — you cannot disable it once turned on. Before enabling, Salesforce requires that at least one record type exists on both the Account and Contact objects. This is a hard prerequisite; the feature will not activate without it. Because it is permanent, Salesforce Support must assist with enablement. Plan carefully: existing data models, integrations, and AppExchange apps may behave differently after Person Accounts are enabled.

topics.question: Person Accounts OWD implications: how the sharing model differs for Person Account records compared to standard Account-Contact relationships
topics.answer: Person Account records follow the Account OWD for sharing purposes, not the Contact OWD. In a standard Account-Contact model, Contact sharing is governed by the Contact OWD and the parent Account's sharing. With Person Accounts, there is no separate Contact record, so the Account sharing model entirely controls visibility. This simplifies sharing in some ways but means the Contact OWD setting has no effect on Person Account visibility.

topics.question: Contacts to Multiple Accounts: how an indirect account–contact relationship differs from the direct (primary) relationship, and which account's sharing rules govern the contact's visibility
topics.answer: Every Contact has one primary (direct) Account, stored in the Account Name field, which governs the Contact's OWD-based access and whose sharing rules control visibility of the Contact. A Contact can also be indirectly related to other Accounts via the Account Contact Relationship object — these are secondary relationships. However, the sharing rules, OWD, and role hierarchy of indirect accounts do not grant access to the Contact. Only the primary account's sharing model does. Users who can see an indirect account do not automatically see the related contacts unless they can also see those contacts through the primary account path.

topics.question: Given a scenario with both business accounts and person accounts in the same org, identifying which standard Salesforce features behave differently or are restricted for person account records
topics.answer:
When both coexist in the same org:

- Campaigns: Person Accounts can be added as campaign members; standard business account contacts can too, but you must handle them separately.

- Cases: Person Accounts can be the contact on a case, but the relationship lookup behaves differently.

- Duplicate Management: Matching rules must account for the fact that Person Accounts are queried differently from Contacts.

- Reports: You must use specific Person Account report types, as standard Contact reports do not include Person Accounts.

- Partner/Customer Community: Person Accounts can be enabled as community users, but certain portal features behave differently.

- Contacts to Multiple Accounts: Unavailable for Person Accounts.

admin2.title: Given a scenario, determine the appropriate solution to enhance or extend objects (...)

objectives.title: Given a scenario, determine the appropriate solution to enhance or extend objects (...)

topics.question: Master-detail vs. lookup relationship: which relationship type rolls up summary fields, enforces cascade delete, and controls the child record's OWD
topics.answer:
| Feature | Master-Detail | Lookup |

|---|---|---|

| Roll-Up Summary Fields | Yes | No |

| Cascade Delete | Yes (child deleted with parent) | No (child remains, field nulled or blocked) |

| Child OWD | Controlled by Parent | Independent |

| Required parent field | Yes | Optional |

| Max per object | 2 | 25 |

Master-detail is a tighter, more dependent relationship. Lookup is looser and more flexible.

topics.question: Lookup filter on a lookup field: how a lookup filter restricts the records a user can select in a lookup and the difference between a required vs. optional lookup filter behavior
topics.answer:
A lookup filter narrows the records available in the lookup search dialog based on field criteria (e.g., only show Accounts where Type = "Customer").

- Required filter: The user cannot select or save a record that does not meet the filter criteria. An error is shown if they try.

- Optional filter: The filter is applied by default to pre-filter results, but the user can click "Search Without Filter" to see all records and select one that does not match the criteria. No error is thrown on save.

topics.question: Junction objects: how to model a many-to-many relationship between two standard objects and the implications for OWD on the junction object
topics.answer: A junction object is a custom object with two master-detail relationships, one to each of the two objects in the many-to-many relationship (e.g., Campaign Member joining Campaign and Contact). The junction object's OWD is set to Controlled by Parent, meaning it inherits access from whichever parent gives the user the most access. There is no independent OWD for the junction record itself. Cascade delete applies from both parents: deleting either parent deletes the junction records related to it.

topics.question: Roll-up summary fields: which aggregate functions are supported (COUNT, SUM, MIN, MAX) and which child relationship types allow them
topics.answer:
Supported aggregate functions: COUNT, SUM, MIN, MAX.

- COUNT: Counts child records (any field type).

- SUM: Sums a numeric field on child records.

- MIN / MAX: Returns the minimum or maximum value of a numeric, currency, date, or date/time field on child records.

Roll-up summary fields are only supported on the master object in a master-detail relationship. They cannot be created on lookup relationships.

topics.question: Roll-up summary fields: whether filter criteria can be applied to restrict which child records are included in the aggregate
topics.answer: Yes. When creating a roll-up summary field, you can optionally add filter criteria to restrict which child records are included in the calculation. For example, a SUM roll-up on Opportunity Amount could filter to only include child records where Stage = "Closed Won." Child records that do not match the filter are excluded from the aggregate. This makes roll-up summaries very flexible for targeted calculations.

topics.question: Converting a lookup relationship to master-detail: which pre-conditions must be met (all existing child records must have a parent value, no existing validation or default field rules on the field)
topics.answer: To convert a lookup to master-detail:

topics.question: **All existing child records must have a value in the lookup field** (no blank/null parent values allowed, since master-detail requires a parent).
The lookup field cannot have any **default field values** set.
The object cannot exceed the **limit of 2 master-detail relationships** per object.
The relationship must not be **self-referential**.
topics.answer: If any child records have a null parent, the conversion will fail until those records are updated.

topics.question: Record types: how they control picklist values and page layout assignments, and the distinction between the Record Type and the page layout
topics.answer: A record type controls two things:

topics.question: **Picklist values**: Which values from a picklist field's global value set are available when a user with that record type creates or edits a record.
**Page layout assignment**: Which page layout is shown to which profile when viewing a record of that type.
topics.answer: The record type and page layout are separate objects. The record type does not contain layout fields itself — it simply maps a profile to a layout. You can assign the same layout to multiple record types, or different layouts per profile within the same record type.

topics.question: Record types: how they control business process assignments (e.g., opportunity stages, case stages)
topics.answer: Record types are linked to Sales Processes (for Opportunities), Lead Processes (for Leads), and Support Processes (for Cases). These processes define which Stage or Status picklist values are available for that process. When a record type is tied to a specific process, only the stages in that process are available to users assigned that record type. This is how orgs can give different sales teams different sets of Opportunity stages using the same Opportunity object.

topics.question: Object Creator vs. Object Manager: when to use Object Creator for guided end-to-end custom object creation vs. Object Manager for modifying existing objects
topics.answer:
- Object Creator: A guided, wizard-style tool for creating a brand-new custom object from scratch. It walks through naming, fields, relationships, and page layouts in a step-by-step flow. Best for first-time object creation.

- Object Manager: The central hub for managing all objects (standard and custom). Use it to modify existing objects — adding fields, editing relationships, managing page layouts, record types, triggers, and more.

Object Creator is creation-only. Object Manager is the ongoing management interface.

topics.question: Schema Builder: capabilities it provides beyond Object Manager (visualizing cross-object relationships, creating new fields and objects in a single canvas)
topics.answer:
Schema Builder provides a visual, drag-and-drop canvas showing objects and their relationships as a connected diagram. Capabilities beyond Object Manager:

- Visually see how multiple objects relate to each other at once.

- Create new custom objects, fields, and relationships directly on the canvas without navigating away.

- Drag fields from the palette onto objects on the canvas.

It is especially useful for understanding and designing complex data models with many cross-object relationships.

topics.question: Schema Builder limitations: which operations it cannot perform (e.g., cannot delete objects or fields)
topics.answer:
Schema Builder cannot:

- Delete custom objects or fields.

- Modify existing field properties in detail (e.g., formula syntax, complex field options).

- Manage page layouts, record types, or validation rules.

- Deploy or package metadata.

For deletion or detailed field editing, you must use Object Manager directly.

admin2.title: Given a scenario, determine the appropriate solution to enhance or extend the UI/UX with applications (...)

objectives.title: Given a scenario, determine the appropriate solution to enhance or extend the UI/UX with applications (...)

topics.question: App Manager: differences between a Classic app and a Lightning app — which settings are available only in Lightning apps (navigation items, utility bar, app options like 'Enable header' in console context)
topics.answer:
| Feature | Classic App | Lightning App |

|---|---|---|

| Navigation items | Basic tab bar | Dynamic navigation with standard & custom items |

| Utility bar | No | Yes |

| Console navigation | No | Yes (configurable) |

| App branding (logo, color) | Limited | Full |

| Form factor targeting | No | Yes (desktop, phone) |

Lightning apps also support the Service Console style with workspace tabs and split view. Classic apps are legacy and offer no utility bar or console configuration.

topics.question: Lightning App Builder page types (App Page, Record Page, Home Page) and which assignment mechanisms (app, record type, profile) are available for each type
topics.answer:
| Page Type | Assignment Options |

|---|---|

| App Page | Assign to specific Lightning apps |

| Record Page | Assign by app, record type, and/or profile |

| Home Page | Assign by app and/or profile |

Record Pages have the most granular assignment options, allowing you to tailor the layout per profile and record type combination. Home Pages can be app-specific or profile-specific. App Pages are simply added to one or more apps' navigation.

topics.question: Standard Lightning page components: which components are available on a standard Record Page by default vs. must be added from the component palette in Lightning App Builder
topics.answer:
Available by default (already on the standard record page): Record Detail (fields), Related Lists, Chatter Feed, Activity Timeline, Highlights Panel (for standard objects).

Must be added from the palette: Report Charts, Flow components, custom LWC components, Knowledge components, Recent Items, List Views, Milestones, and any third-party components from AppExchange.

The default page gives a functional layout; customization adds richness.

topics.question: Component visibility filters in Lightning App Builder: how filter conditions (field values, record type, user permission, form factor) can conditionally show or hide a component on a Lightning record page without Dynamic Forms
topics.answer:
Component Visibility Filters allow you to add one or more conditions to any component on a Lightning record page. The component only renders if all conditions are met. Filter types include:

- Field value (e.g., show component only when Status = "Open").

- Record type (show only for a specific record type).

- User permission (show only if user has a specific permission).

- Form factor (show only on desktop or mobile).

These filters work at the component level and do not require Dynamic Forms. Multiple conditions use AND logic by default.

topics.question: Dynamic Forms vs. page layouts: how Dynamic Forms allows field-level and section-level visibility rules directly on the Lightning record page, replacing the need for multiple page layouts for the same record type
topics.answer:
With traditional page layouts, field visibility is static per layout. To show different fields to different users or in different contexts, you need multiple layouts and profile/record type combinations.

Dynamic Forms moves individual fields and sections directly onto the Lightning record page as independent components. Each field or section can have its own visibility conditions (field value, user permission, profile, etc.). One record page with Dynamic Forms can replace many traditional page layouts, reducing layout sprawl significantly. This is only available in Lightning Experience.

topics.question: Dynamic Forms eligibility: which object types support Dynamic Forms (custom objects and select standard objects in Lightning Experience) and which standard objects have limited or no Dynamic Forms support (e.g., Opportunity, Case, Lead, Contact may have limited support depending on release)
topics.answer:
Dynamic Forms is fully supported for custom objects. Support for standard objects has been expanding with each Salesforce release. As of recent releases:

- Supported: Account, Contact, Lead, Opportunity, Case (generally available but check the latest release notes for any remaining limitations).

- Not supported: Person Accounts (limited), some Service Cloud objects.

Always verify in the current release notes, as Salesforce has been rolling out standard object support incrementally. In the exam context, know that custom objects have full support and some standard objects are still gaining it.

topics.question: Service Cloud Console app: the difference between split view and workspace tabs, and how keyboard shortcuts reduce agent handle time in the console
topics.answer:
- Workspace tabs: Each case/record opens as its own tab at the top of the console. Sub-tabs (e.g., related records) appear below the main tab. Agents can work on multiple records without losing context.

- Split view: A collapsible panel on the left side of the console displaying a list view. Agents can click through records in the list without opening new tabs, keeping the list visible alongside the record.

Keyboard shortcuts allow agents to perform common actions (next/previous record, open macros, focus chatter, etc.) without using the mouse, directly reducing average handle time.

topics.question: In-App Guidance: how prompt types (targeted prompts, walkthroughs, floating prompts) are configured to guide users on a Lightning page, and which user license is required to create in-app guidance
topics.answer:
Prompt types:

- Floating prompt: A small popup that appears anywhere on the screen. Not anchored to a specific element.

- Targeted prompt: Anchored to a specific UI element on the page (button, field, component). Highlights the element.

- Walkthrough: A series of sequential prompts guiding users through a multi-step process on the page.

In-App Guidance is created via Setup > In-App Guidance. Creating and editing prompts requires a user with the "Manage In-App Guidance" permission, typically a System Administrator. No special add-on license is required — it is available in Lightning Experience for Enterprise Edition and above.

topics.question: Lightning page Analyze button: what the performance analysis surfaces (slow-loading components, components with errors) and when an admin should use it vs. Debug Mode
topics.answer:
The Analyze button in Lightning App Builder scans the page and surfaces:

- Components that are slow to load (identified as performance bottlenecks).

- Components that have errors (configuration issues or missing dependencies).

- Recommendations to improve page performance (e.g., move slow components below the fold).

Use Analyze when users report slow page load times or when you want to proactively audit a complex record page.

Debug Mode (enabled per user in Setup) gives developers full, un-minified JavaScript and detailed console logs for LWC and Aura component debugging. Use Debug Mode for component-level code issues, not for general page performance.

admin2.title: Given a scenario, determine the appropriate tools for monitoring and troubleshooting system activity (...)

objectives.title: Given a scenario, determine the appropriate tools for monitoring and troubleshooting system activity (...)

topics.question: Setup Audit Trail: what categories of changes it captures vs. what it does NOT track
topics.answer:
Captures: Changes made in Setup — creating/modifying profiles, permission sets, custom fields, page layouts, flows, custom objects, sharing rules, company settings, installed packages, user creation/deactivation, and more.

Does NOT track:

- Changes to record data (field value changes on business records).

- Running of reports or dashboards.

- Data exports or imports.

- Changes made by the Salesforce system itself (e.g., automated system upgrades).

- Viewing of records (read activity).

Setup Audit Trail is specifically for configuration changes in Setup, not data-level activity.

topics.question: Setup Audit Trail: the retention period for audit entries (last 180 days viewable in UI, up to 6 months downloadable as CSV)
topics.answer: The Setup Audit Trail shows the last 180 days of changes directly in the UI (up to 20 recent entries on the page). You can download a CSV of the full 6 months of history. Anything older than 6 months is not retained by Salesforce. For longer retention, export the CSV regularly and store it in an external system as part of your compliance strategy.

topics.question: Field History Tracking: the maximum number of tracked fields per object (20) and the UI retention period (18 months)
topics.answer:
- Max tracked fields per object: 20.

- UI retention: The related list on a record shows field history for the last 18 months.

- Field History Tracking records: who changed a field, when, what the old value was, and what the new value is.

- Once you enable tracking on a field, history is only captured going forward, not retroactively.

topics.question: Field History Tracking: how to access data older than 18 months (Data Loader or API query on FieldHistory objects)
topics.answer:
Field history older than 18 months is no longer visible in the UI, but Salesforce retains it for up to 18 months total in the database (accessible via API). To access historical data approaching or at the limit:

- Use Data Loader or a SOQL query via API against the relevant `__History` object (e.g., `AccountHistory`, `OpportunityFieldHistory`).

- For long-term retention beyond 18 months, export field history records regularly to an external data store or use Salesforce Shield Field Audit Trail, which extends retention up to 10 years.

topics.question: Login History: what information is captured, how long it is retained (6 months), and how to query it for compliance investigations
topics.answer:
Captured data: Username, login date/time, source IP address, login type (UI, API, SSO, etc.), browser/platform, login status (Success, Failed, etc.), and the geographic location (when available).

Retention: 6 months.

Querying: Viewable in Setup > Login History, filterable by user and date. For programmatic access, query the `LoginHistory` object via SOQL or export via Data Loader. For compliance investigations, filter by user, date range, and status to identify unauthorized access attempts or anomalous login patterns.

topics.question: Health Check: what the score represents (percentage of security settings meeting Salesforce Baseline Standard) and what specific security settings it evaluates
topics.answer:
The Health Check score is a percentage (0–100) representing how many of your org's security settings meet or exceed the Salesforce Baseline Standard. A higher score means more settings are configured to Salesforce's recommended security posture.

Evaluated settings include:

- Password policies (length, complexity, expiration, lockout threshold).

- Session security settings (timeout, secure connections, clickjack protection).

- Certificate and network access settings.

- Guest user access settings.

- Login IP ranges and trusted IPs.

topics.question: Health Check: which settings reduce the score and how to improve it
topics.answer:
Settings that most commonly reduce the score:

- Short session timeouts or very long ones (allowing extended idle sessions).

- Weak password policies (short minimum length, no complexity requirements, no expiration).

- No lockout after failed attempts.

- Guest user access that is too permissive.

- HTTP connections allowed (instead of HTTPS-only).

To improve the score: Click any failing setting in Health Check to navigate directly to the configuration page and apply the recommended value. Salesforce shows the current value, the recommended value, and the risk level (High, Medium, Low).

admin2.title: Explain how to ensure sensitive data is set up to support a business/legal/compliance use case in production and sandbox environments.

objectives.title: Explain how to ensure sensitive data is set up to support a business/legal/compliance use case in production and sandbox environments.

topics.question: Shield Platform Encryption vs. Classic Encryption: which fields can be encrypted with each
topics.answer:
| | Classic Encryption | Shield Platform Encryption |

|---|---|---|

| Field types | Custom text fields only (adds a "masking" encryption) | Standard and custom fields: text, text area, date, date/time, email, phone, URL, number, and more |

| File encryption | No | Yes (files and attachments) |

| Standard fields | No | Yes |

Shield Platform Encryption is the enterprise-grade solution. Classic Encryption is a limited, legacy feature that only masks a custom text field.

topics.question: Shield Platform Encryption vs. Classic Encryption: whether encrypted fields are searchable/filterable and which one encrypts data at rest in the database
topics.answer:
- Classic Encryption: Fields are not searchable via SOQL or standard search. They display as masked values (asterisks) in the UI.

- Shield Platform Encryption: Encrypts data at rest in the database using AES-256. With Deterministic Encryption, fields can be used in exact-match filters and SOQL WHERE clauses. With Probabilistic Encryption (the default), fields are not searchable/filterable.

Only Shield Platform Encryption truly encrypts data at rest. Classic Encryption is UI masking, not true at-rest encryption.

topics.question: Full Copy sandbox: the only sandbox type that replicates all production data; why it is used for compliance testing and what its refresh interval restriction is (29-day minimum)
topics.answer:
A Full Copy sandbox is an exact replica of production — all metadata AND all data records. It is used for:

- Compliance testing: Testing with real (or real-volume) production data.

- Performance testing: Load testing with production data volumes.

- Disaster recovery drills.

Refresh interval: Minimum 29 days between refreshes. This is the longest refresh restriction of all sandbox types, reflecting the cost and time of copying an entire production org. Because it holds real data, access must be carefully controlled to meet compliance requirements.

topics.question: Sandbox data masking: how to prevent sensitive production data (SSNs, credit card numbers) from appearing in non-full sandboxes, including the use of data mask tools and sandbox templates
topics.answer: For Partial Copy sandboxes, use sandbox templates to control which objects are included in the copy and limit the volume of sensitive data. Beyond templates, use Data Mask (a Salesforce-native tool) or third-party data anonymization tools to scramble or replace sensitive field values (SSNs, credit card numbers, email addresses) after refresh. For Developer and Developer Pro sandboxes, no production data is included by default. Establish a process where any sandbox refresh that includes production data triggers an automated masking job before granting developer access.

admin2.title: Explain how to review and troubleshoot security settings including pending updates that may change system access.

objectives.title: Explain how to review and troubleshoot security settings including pending updates that may change system access.

topics.question: Critical Updates: how to review and activate/deactivate pending critical updates before their auto-activation date, and the risk of not testing them in a sandbox first
topics.answer:
Critical Updates (now called Release Updates in newer Salesforce versions) are changes Salesforce plans to auto-activate in a future release to improve security, performance, or compliance. Admins can review them in Setup > Release Updates.

- Activate early: Test in a sandbox, then activate in production before the auto-activation date to control timing.

- Deactivate temporarily: Some updates can be deactivated to buy more time, but they will auto-activate eventually.

- Risk of not testing: Auto-activation in production without sandbox testing can break flows, integrations, page layouts, or sharing behavior. Always test in a sandbox first to identify impact.

topics.question: Security Health Check high-risk settings: identifying which specific configuration changes (e.g., session timeout, password complexity, IP restrictions) most significantly improve the Health Check score
topics.answer:
High-risk settings (those that most impact the score when misconfigured):

- Session timeout: Setting it too long (e.g., 8 hours) is flagged as high-risk. Recommended: 2 hours or less.

- Password minimum length: Shorter than 8 characters is high-risk. Recommended: 8+ characters.

- Password complexity: Not requiring uppercase, numbers, or special characters is high-risk.

- Maximum invalid login attempts: Setting it too high (or no lockout) is high-risk. Recommended: 5 or fewer attempts.

- Require secure connections (HTTPS): Not requiring HTTPS is high-risk.

- Guest user access: Granting excessive object permissions to guest users is flagged.

Fixing high-risk items yields the greatest score improvement.

admin2.title: Describe the features of Salesforce which enable Sales users to conduct the sale process, including products, price books, schedules, orders, and quotes.

objectives.title: Describe the features of Salesforce which enable Sales users to conduct the sale process, including products, price books, schedules, orders, and quotes.

topics.question: Products and Price Books: how a product must be added to at least one price book before it can be added to an opportunity, and the role of the Standard Price Book vs. custom price books
topics.answer: Every product must have an entry in at least one price book (as a Price Book Entry) before it can be added to an opportunity. The Standard Price Book is the system-default price book. Every org has exactly one. A product's entry in the Standard Price Book is its "list price." Custom price books allow different pricing for different markets, regions, or customer segments. A product must first be added to the Standard Price Book, and then it can be added to a custom price book with a different price. When adding products to an opportunity, the user selects a price book first, then chooses products from that book.

topics.question: Product Schedules: the difference between quantity schedules, revenue schedules, and combined schedules, and which object stores the schedule data
topics.answer:
- Quantity schedules: Define when and how much of a product is delivered (e.g., 10 units in January, 10 in February). Used for physical goods.

- Revenue schedules: Define when revenue is recognized (e.g., $500/month over 12 months). Used for services or subscriptions.

- Combined schedules: Track both quantity delivery and revenue recognition independently on the same product.

Schedule data is stored on the Opportunity Product (OpportunityLineItem) object and its child schedule records (`OpportunityLineItemSchedule`). Schedules do not affect the Opportunity Amount directly unless the schedule amounts are configured to do so.

topics.question: Quotes: the sync behavior between a quote and its parent opportunity (only one quote can be synced at a time; syncing a new quote unsyncs the previous), and what fields sync between the objects
topics.answer: Only one quote can be synced to an opportunity at a time. When you sync a quote, changes to the quote's line items and totals sync back to the opportunity's products and amounts (and vice versa). Syncing a second quote automatically unsyncs the first. Fields that sync include: opportunity Amount, Close Date, and products/line items. To prevent the quote from being edited independently while synced, the opportunity and quote stay in lockstep. To stop syncing, click "Unsynce" on the quote.

topics.question: Orders: how orders are created from contracts or opportunities, the status lifecycle (Draft → Activated), and restrictions on editing an activated order
topics.answer:
Orders can be created from Contracts or directly from Opportunities (depending on configuration). Status lifecycle: Draft → Activated.

- In Draft state: order products can be added, edited, or removed.

- Once Activated: the order is locked. Products cannot be added or removed, and most fields cannot be edited. To make changes, you would need to create a Reduction Order.

Orders require the product to be in a price book matching the account's currency. Activation signals that the order is committed and ready for fulfillment.

topics.question: Account Teams: default team templates, the access level granted to team members, and whether Account Team access overrides OWD restrictions on related opportunities and cases
topics.answer:
Account Teams allow multiple users to collaborate on an account. Each member is assigned a Team Role and an access level (Read Only or Read/Write) to the Account, and optionally to related Contacts, Opportunities, and Cases.

Default team templates can be created so that users' personal default teams are automatically added to new accounts they own.

OWD interaction: Account Team membership does grant access to related Opportunities and Cases, even if OWD for those objects is Private. The access level is whatever is configured on the team membership, not exceeding Read/Write. This is one of the few declarative ways to grant access to related records beyond OWD without sharing rules.

topics.question: Opportunity Teams: how they differ from Account Teams in terms of member roles and split percentages, and how Opportunity Team sharing interacts with the base OWD
topics.answer: Opportunity Teams are specific to a single opportunity. Each team member has a Role (e.g., Account Executive, Sales Engineer) and an access level. Opportunity Teams also support split percentages for tracking each member's contribution to a deal (used in overlay or split forecasting). Account Teams are account-wide; Opportunity Teams are deal-specific. Opportunity Team membership grants access to that specific opportunity regardless of OWD, similar to how Account Teams work. The access granted is the level set on the membership record.

admin2.title: Distinguish and understand the implications and capabilities of Forecasting and Territory Management.

objectives.title: Distinguish and understand the implications and capabilities of Forecasting and Territory Management.

topics.question: Collaborative Forecasting: the forecast hierarchy vs. the role hierarchy, how forecast adjustments work (manager can adjust subordinate's forecast without changing the subordinate's own number), and the effect of including opportunity from a forecast
topics.answer:
Forecast hierarchy: Separate from the role hierarchy. It must be explicitly configured and maps to managers and their direct reports for forecasting purposes.

Forecast adjustments: A manager can adjust a subordinate's forecast number upward or downward. This adjustment is additive to the rollup — the subordinate's own forecast number is unchanged. The manager's view shows their adjustment separately from the subordinate's submitted amount.

Include/Exclude from forecast: Setting an opportunity's Forecast Category to "Omitted" removes it from the forecast rollup entirely. Moving it back to any other category re-includes it.

topics.question: Forecast categories: the mapping from Opportunity Stage to forecast category (Pipeline, Best Case, Commit, Closed, Omitted) and how a custom stage maps to a forecast category
topics.answer:
Standard mapping:

| Forecast Category | Typical Stage Mapping |

|---|---|

| Pipeline | Early stages (e.g., Prospecting, Qualification) |

| Best Case | Mid-probability stages (e.g., Proposal) |

| Commit | High-probability stages (e.g., Negotiation) |

| Closed | Closed Won |

| Omitted | Closed Lost, or explicitly excluded |

When creating a custom opportunity stage, the admin must manually map it to one of these forecast categories. The mapping is done in the Stage picklist configuration. The forecast category determines how the opportunity appears in the forecast rollup.

topics.question: Forecasting types (opportunity revenue, opportunity quantity, product family, overlay): how each type differs and when product family forecasting is enabled
topics.answer:
- Opportunity Revenue: Forecast based on the opportunity's Amount field. Most common type.

- Opportunity Quantity: Forecast based on the total quantity of products on the opportunity.

- Product Family: Forecast rolls up by product family, allowing separate forecast amounts for each family (e.g., Hardware vs. Software). Requires product families to be defined and products categorized.

- Overlay: Tracks overlay/split revenue where multiple reps share credit for a deal. Uses split percentages from Opportunity Teams.

Multiple forecast types can be active simultaneously. Product family forecasting requires enabling product schedules or product families in the org settings.

topics.question: Forecast rollup behavior: how forecasts roll up from the bottom of the forecast hierarchy to the top, what 'cumulative forecast rollup' means vs. standard rollup, and whether closed/won amounts are always included
topics.answer:
Forecasts roll from individual reps up through managers in the forecast hierarchy. Each manager's total includes their own pipeline plus their direct and indirect reports' amounts.

- Standard rollup: Each category (Pipeline, Best Case, Commit, Closed) is shown separately and does not include higher-probability categories.

- Cumulative forecast rollup: Higher categories include the amounts from lower (more likely) categories. For example, "Best Case" includes Commit and Closed amounts in addition to Best Case-only deals.

Closed Won amounts are always included in every forecast category rollup (except Omitted) because closed deals are certain revenue.

topics.question: Territory Management 2.0: territory types, territory models, territory hierarchy, and how territory assignment rules fire when an account record is saved
topics.answer:
- Territory Types: Organizational categories for territories (e.g., "Geographic," "Named Account"). Used to classify territories, not for access control.

- Territory Models: The container for an entire territory structure. Only one model can be Active at a time.

- Territory Hierarchy: The tree of territories within a model (parent/child relationships, e.g., North America > West > California).

- Assignment rules: Each territory has filter criteria. When an account is saved, Salesforce evaluates all active assignment rules in the active model and assigns the account to every territory whose rules it matches. Rules can be run manually for all accounts or fire automatically on account save (if configured).

topics.question: Territory model states (Planning, Active, Archived): which actions (running assignment rules, associating territories to users) require the model to be in Active state
topics.answer:
- Planning: Design mode. You can build the hierarchy, create territories, configure rules, and preview assignments. You cannot run rules org-wide or affect record access.

- Active: The model is live and controls record access. Running assignment rules on all accounts requires the model to be Active. Users are associated to territories only in the Active model (or in Planning for preview/testing purposes, but it has no access effect).

- Archived: Read-only. No changes or rule execution. Used for historical auditing.

Only one model can be Active at any time. Activating a new model automatically archives the previous one.

topics.question: Territory Management 2.0 and opportunities: how an opportunity appears in a territory forecast and the difference between opportunity territory assignment (manual vs. filter-based)
topics.answer:
An opportunity appears in a territory's forecast when it is assigned to that territory. Assignment can happen two ways:

- Filter-based (automatic): A territory assignment rule on the Opportunity object (separate from Account rules) automatically assigns the opportunity based on field criteria (e.g., close date, revenue range). Requires enabling opportunity filters in territory settings.

- Manual: A user (or admin) directly assigns a territory to the opportunity from the opportunity record.

The assigned territory determines which territory's forecast the opportunity rolls into. If no territory is assigned, the opportunity does not appear in territory-based forecasting.

admin2.title: Explain how to create and maintain Salesforce Knowledge (...)

objectives.title: Explain how to create and maintain Salesforce Knowledge (...)

topics.question: Knowledge article record types: how they control the article's page layout, fields, and which Lightning record page is displayed to agents and customers
topics.answer:
Knowledge article record types work similarly to record types on other objects. Each record type:

- Controls which fields appear on the article (via page layout assignment).

- Controls which page layout is shown to users.

- In Lightning, determines which Lightning record page is assigned for that article type.

- Can control which channels the article is visible in (internal app, customer portal, partner portal, public knowledge base).

Common practice is to create separate record types for different article categories (e.g., FAQs, How-To Guides, Known Issues), each with its own layout and channel settings.

topics.question: Knowledge article lifecycle: Draft → Review → Published → Archived, and who has permission to publish vs. archive an article based on the Knowledge User profile permission
topics.answer:
| State | Description |

|---|---|

| Draft | Article is being written/edited. Not visible to end users. |

| Review | Article is pending approval/review. |

| Published | Visible to users in configured channels. |

| Archived | Removed from active channels. Not deleted, but no longer visible. |

- Publishing: Requires the "Publish Articles" permission (Knowledge User with publish permission or a profile/permission set granting it).

- Archiving: Requires the "Archive Articles" permission. Admins and designated content managers typically have this.

Standard users cannot publish or archive unless explicitly granted the permission.

topics.question: Knowledge article versioning: when a published article is edited, a draft version is created while the published version remains live; the relationship between article versions and how publishing the new draft replaces the previous version
topics.answer: When a published article is edited, Salesforce creates a new draft version while the current published version remains live and visible to users. The two versions coexist until the draft is published. When the new draft is published, it replaces the previous published version, which is then moved to an archived state (as a previous version, not deleted). Salesforce maintains a version history so previous versions can be referenced. This ensures users always see the current published content while editing is in progress.

topics.question: Data categories in Knowledge: how category groups and categories control article visibility for internal users, partner users, and customer portal users
topics.answer:
Data Category Groups are top-level containers (e.g., "Products," "Geography"). Within each group are categories in a hierarchy (e.g., Products > Hardware > Laptops).

Articles are tagged with categories. Visibility is controlled by assigning data category visibility to user profiles:

- Internal users: Can be granted visibility to all or specific categories.

- Partner users: Visibility configured per portal profile.

- Customer users: Visibility configured per community/portal profile.

Users only see articles tagged with categories they have visibility to. This allows fine-grained content access control without duplicating articles.

admin2.title: Explain how to create and maintain service entitlements and entitlement processes.

objectives.title: Explain how to create and maintain service entitlements and entitlement processes.

topics.question: Entitlements vs. entitlement processes: an entitlement defines what support a customer is eligible for; an entitlement process defines the SLA timeline with milestones and automated actions
topics.answer:
- Entitlement: A record that defines what support a customer is entitled to — for example, "Phone Support," "24/7 Support," or "Email Only." Entitlements link to Accounts, Contacts, or Assets. They answer: does this customer have support, and what kind?

- Entitlement Process: A timeline of SLA milestones attached to an entitlement. It defines how long an agent has to respond, resolve, or escalate a case — and what automated actions fire (emails, field updates) when milestones are hit or missed.

Think of entitlements as the contract and the entitlement process as the SLA clock.

topics.question: Entitlement lookup on a case: how the entitlement lookup on a case is auto-populated based on Account or Contact matching and what the 'Set Default Entitlement' entitlement setting does
topics.answer: When a case is created or an Account/Contact is set on a case, Salesforce can auto-populate the Entitlement field by matching the Account or Contact to an active entitlement for that customer. The "Set Default Entitlement" option on an entitlement record marks it as the one to auto-apply when a matching case is created for that account or contact. If multiple entitlements exist for a customer, the one marked as default is chosen automatically. Without this setting, agents must manually select the entitlement.

topics.question: Entitlement milestones: how milestone actions (warning and violation) fire before and after the milestone completion time, and what happens to milestone timers when a case is closed
topics.answer:
Milestones are required steps in an entitlement process (e.g., "First Response within 2 hours," "Resolution within 8 hours"). Each milestone has:

- Warning actions: Fire a set time before the milestone deadline (e.g., email the agent 30 minutes before the 2-hour mark).

- Violation actions: Fire if the milestone is not completed by the deadline (e.g., escalate the case, notify a manager).

When a case is closed, all milestone timers stop. If a case is reopened, timers may resume depending on configuration. Completed milestones are not affected by case closure.

topics.question: Entitlement processes and business hours: how associating business hours with an entitlement process affects milestone completion time calculations (only business hours count)
topics.answer: When business hours are associated with an entitlement process, milestone timers only count time during configured business hours. For example, if business hours are 9 AM to 5 PM Monday-Friday, and a case is opened at 4 PM Friday, a 4-hour response milestone deadline would be 10 AM Monday (not 8 PM Friday). This ensures SLA calculations reflect actual working time. Entitlement processes without business hours count 24/7 clock time. Each entitlement process can reference a specific set of business hours.

admin2.title: Describe the features of Salesforce which enable interaction between support agents and customers (...)

objectives.title: Describe the features of Salesforce which enable interaction between support agents and customers (...)

topics.question: Case Feed: which publisher actions are available by default (Log a Call, Send Email, Change Status) and how to add custom quick actions to the Case Feed publisher
topics.answer:
Default publisher actions in Case Feed: Log a Call, Send Email, Change Status.

To add custom actions: Create a quick action on the Case object (object-specific action), then add it to the Case Feed's publisher layout (Case Feed Layout or Global Publisher Layout, depending on org setup). In Lightning, actions added to the Case page layout's "Highlights Panel" and "Quick Actions in the Salesforce Classic Publisher" section appear in the Case Feed action bar. Custom quick actions can trigger flows, create records, or update fields.

topics.question: Web-to-Case: how HTML forms submit customer inquiries directly as cases, the daily case creation limit (5,000 per day), and how assignment rules interact with Web-to-Case submissions
topics.answer:
Web-to-Case generates an HTML form that customers submit on a website. Salesforce converts submissions into Case records automatically.

- Daily limit: 5,000 cases per day via Web-to-Case. Submissions beyond the limit are sent to the Default Case Owner.

- Assignment rules: Standard Case Assignment Rules fire on Web-to-Case submissions, just as they do on manually created cases. Configure an active assignment rule to route web cases to the appropriate queue or user.

- The default Case Status and Case Origin (Web) are set automatically.

topics.question: Email-to-Case vs. On-Demand Email-to-Case: the difference in how emails are routed (on-demand uses Salesforce-generated email address; standard requires firewall routing), and the email-to-case attachment size limits
topics.answer:
| | Email-to-Case | On-Demand Email-to-Case |

|---|---|---|

| Routing | Emails sent to your email server, forwarded to Salesforce via a local agent behind your firewall | Emails sent directly to a Salesforce-generated address (no firewall agent needed) |

| Setup | Requires installing a local agent on a server | Simpler — just configure the Salesforce email address |

| Attachment limit | 25 MB per email | 25 MB per email |

On-Demand is easier to set up. Standard Email-to-Case is used when emails must pass through your own mail server for compliance or filtering.

topics.question: Omni-Channel routing models: queue-based routing (pushes work from queue to available agents by priority/capacity) vs. skill-based routing (routes to agent with matching skills) vs. external routing
topics.answer:
- Queue-Based Routing: Work items (cases, chats, leads) are pushed from a queue to the most available agent based on the queue's priority and the agent's capacity. Agents must be members of the queue.

- Skill-Based Routing: Routes work to agents who have the specific skills required by the work item (e.g., "Spanish Language," "Billing Expert"). Skills are assigned to agents and required on routing configurations.

- External Routing: Work is routed by a third-party system (e.g., a custom telephony platform) via the Omni-Channel APIs. Salesforce provides the presence framework; routing logic lives externally.

topics.question: Omni-Channel presence statuses: how presence configurations control which channels an agent can work on simultaneously and what capacity limits apply
topics.answer:
Presence Statuses (e.g., "Available - Phone," "Available - Chat," "Busy") are created by admins and assigned to Service Channels via a Presence Configuration. The Presence Configuration defines:

- Which statuses are available to agents.

- The agent's capacity — the maximum number of work items they can handle simultaneously (measured in capacity units, where each channel's routing config assigns a capacity cost per work item).

Agents select their status in the Omni-Channel widget. Choosing "Available - Chat" makes them eligible only for chat work items. Capacity limits prevent agents from being overloaded.

topics.question: Omni-Channel service channels: how service channels map work items (Cases, Chats, Social Posts, Leads) to Omni-Channel routing, and what happens when a work item reaches a queue that has no available agents
topics.answer:
Service Channels map Salesforce objects to Omni-Channel routing. You create a service channel for Cases, one for Chats, one for Leads, etc., and assign a capacity cost per work item. When a new work item (e.g., a new Case) is created and meets routing criteria (via a Flow or Omni-Channel routing configuration), it is placed into the configured queue.

If no agents are available in that queue (all at capacity or offline), the work item stays in the queue until an agent becomes available. Work is not lost — it simply waits. Admins can configure queue prioritization to ensure high-priority items are routed first when capacity opens up.

topics.question: Experience Cloud community access levels: Guest User vs. Authenticated Customer/Partner User, and which license type (Customer Community, Customer Community Plus, Partner Community) grants which Salesforce object access
topics.answer:
| License | Object Access |

|---|---|

| Guest User (no login) | Public-facing pages only. Very limited, read-only access to objects explicitly shared. No standard object editing. |

| Customer Community | Accounts, Contacts, Cases, and Knowledge. Cannot access standard reporting or share records with other community members (limited visibility). |

| Customer Community Plus | Same as Customer Community plus: full sharing rules support, reports, dashboards, and more object access. |

| Partner Community | Full CRM object access relevant to partners: Leads, Opportunities, Campaigns, Contacts, Accounts, Cases, plus Salesforce Reports and Dashboards. Most powerful of the three. |

admin2.title: Given a scenario, understand the standard Salesforce suite of products that enable extending the core platform.

objectives.title: Given a scenario, understand the standard Salesforce suite of products that enable extending the core platform.

topics.question: AppExchange managed vs. unmanaged packages: what differentiates them in terms of upgradeability, code visibility, and namespace locking
topics.answer:
| | Managed Package | Unmanaged Package |

|---|---|---|

| Upgradeability | Publisher can push upgrades to subscribers | No upgrade path; each install is a snapshot |

| Code visibility | Apex classes/triggers are protected (cannot be viewed) | All metadata is fully visible and editable |

| Namespace | Has a locked namespace prefix (e.g., `mypkg__Field__c`) | No namespace; components go into the default org namespace |

| Deletion by subscriber | Cannot delete managed components | Can delete any installed component |

Managed packages are for ISV products. Unmanaged packages are for open templates or internal distribution.

topics.question: Salesforce Connect and External Objects: how external objects use OData adapters to surface data from external systems without storing it in Salesforce, and the query limitations compared to standard objects
topics.answer:
Salesforce Connect uses an OData 2.0 or 4.0 adapter (or custom adapter) to create External Objects that map to data in an external database or API. Data is not stored in Salesforce — queries are passed through to the external system in real time. This is useful for surfacing large datasets (ERP data, legacy systems) without ETL.

Limitations vs. standard objects:

- Cannot be used in standard Salesforce reports.

- Cannot have roll-up summary fields from external objects to standard objects.

- SOQL on external objects is passed through to the external source; all governor limits still apply.

- No triggers, flows, or workflow rules on external objects.

- Query performance depends on the external system's response time.

admin2.title: Explain the tools and best practices for assessing, improving, and enriching data quality (...)

objectives.title: Explain the tools and best practices for assessing, improving, and enriching data quality (...)

topics.question: Custom field data types: the difference between Text, Text Area, Long Text Area, and Rich Text Area in terms of character limits
topics.answer:
| Type | Character Limit | Notes |

|---|---|---|

| Text | Up to 255 | Single line. Searchable, filterable. |

| Text Area | Up to 255 | Multi-line (but limited). Searchable. |

| Long Text Area | Up to 131,072 | Multi-line. Not indexed/searchable via standard search. |

| Rich Text Area | Up to 131,072 | Multi-line with HTML formatting. Not indexed. |

For search and filtering, use Text or Text Area. For large freeform content, use Long Text Area. For formatted content (bold, bullets, images), use Rich Text Area.

topics.question: Custom field data types: which field types can be used in reports, SOQL WHERE clauses, or duplicate matching rules
topics.answer:
- Reports: Most field types are available as report columns and filters, including Text, Number, Date, Picklist, Checkbox, Currency, Email, Phone, URL. Long Text Area and Rich Text Area are not filterable in reports.

- SOQL WHERE clauses: Text, Number, Date, Picklist, Checkbox, Currency, Email, Phone can all be filtered. Long Text Area and Rich Text Area cannot be used in WHERE clauses.

- Duplicate Matching Rules: Support Text, Email, Phone, Name fields. Long Text Area, Rich Text Area, and most complex types are not supported in matching rules.

topics.question: Validation rules: order of evaluation relative to required field checks and other automation, and what happens when a before-save Flow and a validation rule both fire on the same record save
topics.answer: Order of execution on save (simplified):

topics.question: System checks (required fields at the platform level).
**Before-save Flows** run (can modify field values).
**Validation rules** evaluate — they see the field values as modified by the before-save flow.
If validation passes: record is committed (DML).
After-save Flows and other automation run.
topics.answer: If a before-save flow changes a field value, the validation rule evaluates the new value (post-flow). This means a before-save flow can be used to set values that help a record pass validation — or inadvertently cause a record to fail validation if the flow sets a bad value.

topics.question: Duplicate Management: how Matching Rules and Duplicate Rules work together, the difference between Alert and Block actions, and when a bypass permission overrides a Block
topics.answer:
- Matching Rules: Define the algorithm for detecting duplicates (which fields to compare, how to compare them — exact, fuzzy, etc.). Salesforce provides standard matching rules for Contacts, Leads, and Accounts.

- Duplicate Rules: Reference a matching rule and define the action to take when a duplicate is detected: Alert (warn but allow save) or Block (prevent save).

Alert: User sees a warning and can still save if they choose. Best for scenarios where some duplicates are acceptable.

Block: User cannot save the record until the potential duplicate issue is resolved.

Bypass permission: Users with the "Bypass Duplicate Prevention" permission can save a record even when a Block action fires. Typically granted only to data stewards or admins.

topics.question: Duplicate rules scope: how an org-wide duplicate rule can be configured to match across different objects (e.g., Leads against Contacts) using a cross-object matching rule, and what happens when a matching record is found on a different object
topics.answer: When creating a Duplicate Rule, you can reference a cross-object matching rule that compares a Lead being saved, for example, against existing Contacts. If a matching Contact is found, the Duplicate Rule fires its Alert or Block action. The user sees the matching Contact records as potential duplicates, even though they are a different object type. This prevents creating Leads for people who are already Contacts in the system. The action (alert/block) and the matching object are all configured on the Duplicate Rule.

admin2.title: Given a scenario, determine the appropriate analytic tools to meet complex reporting requirements (...)

objectives.title: Given a scenario, determine the appropriate analytic tools to meet complex reporting requirements (...)

topics.question: Report formats (Tabular, Summary, Matrix, Joined): which format supports grouping, subtotals, cross-object comparison, and which is required for reporting snapshots or dashboard components
topics.answer:
| Format | Grouping | Subtotals | Cross-Object | Dashboard | Snapshot |

|---|---|---|---|---|---|

| Tabular | No | No | No | No (list only) | No |

| Summary | Yes (rows) | Yes | No | Yes | Yes |

| Matrix | Yes (rows + cols) | Yes | No | Yes | Yes |

| Joined | Yes (per block) | Yes | Yes (multiple blocks) | No | No |

Tabular reports are flat lists. Summary and Matrix are required for dashboards and snapshots. Joined reports allow comparing data from different report types side by side.

topics.question: Joined reports: maximum number of blocks (5), ability to use different primary objects per block, requirement that all blocks share at least one common field, and what chart type is available for joined reports
topics.answer:
- Maximum blocks: 5 per joined report.

- Different primary objects: Each block can have a different primary object (e.g., Block 1 = Accounts, Block 2 = Opportunities).

- Common field requirement: All blocks must share at least one common field (typically a standard field like Account Name or Report Date) to allow cross-block analysis.

- Available chart types: Joined reports support only the vertical bar chart (grouped bar chart). They do not support all chart types available to summary/matrix reports.
