Best practices recommend monitoring escalation rate daily for the first two weeks and investigating any increase greater than 20% above baseline by pulling trace files from escalated sessions to identify the common instruction gap or missing subagent coverage.

topics.question: What is the risk of interpreting raw deflection rate as genuine resolution?
topics.answer: Raw deflection rate counts all sessions that ended without escalation as deflected, including sessions where the agent responded with a graceful failure message like 'I cannot find your order, please contact support.' Sessions ending without escalation are classified as deflected even when the agent failed to resolve the user's need. This creates an inflated metric giving false confidence. Best practices recommend building a quality-corrected deflection measure by identifying sessions where error steps occurred and cross-referencing against non-escalated sessions. A more robust approach uses a custom 'resolved' variable that the agent sets only when genuine resolution is achieved, then filters the deflection metric to count only sessions where that variable is true.

objectives.title: Understand the Data Cloud STDM table model for building custom analytics.

topics.question: What are the core STDM tables and what does each contain?
topics.answer: Core tables: ssot__AiAgentSession__dlm holds session-level data (start time, end time, session ID). ssot__AiAgentInteraction__dlm holds interaction metadata (intent, subagent, resolution status, TelemetryTraceId for joining to Platform Tracing). ssot__AiAgentInteractionMessage__dlm holds user and agent message content for conversation analysis. ssot__AiAgentInteractionStep__dlm holds action steps with error tracking. ssot__AiAgentSessionParticipant__dlm records agent participation. AiAgentGenerativeAiUsage_std__dlm records token usage per session. ssot__TelemetryTraceSpan__dlm holds back-end execution spans from Platform Tracing. Custom dashboards on these tables surface insights unavailable in any out-of-the-box panel.

topics.question: What are the Einstein Trust Layer Audit Trail DMO tables?
topics.answer: The Trust Layer generates audit trail DMOs: GenAIGatewayRequest__dlm captures the compiled prompt sent to the LLM gateway (not the user's raw utterance — that comes from ssot__AiAgentInteractionMessage__dlm where role equals 'user'). GenAIGatewayResponse__dlm captures the raw LLM response. GenAIGeneration__dlm holds generation metadata per LLM call. GenAIFeedback__dlm records user feedback signals (thumbs up/down ratings). An important distinction: GenAIGatewayRequest__dlm captures the compiled Agent Script prompt, not the user's original utterance. These tables only populate when their corresponding data streams are explicitly enabled in Einstein Trust Layer settings.

topics.question: What are the six categories of proactive monitoring alerts?
topics.answer: Six categories: Agent Rate Limit Errors fire when the org-level LLM rate limit is reached, indicating delays at peak load. Voice Agent Response Failures fire on TTS/STT pipeline error spikes, signaling a voice channel SLA breach. Planner Session Start Failures fire when the agent cannot initialize sessions, indicating complete channel outage. LLM Model Latency alerts fire when response time exceeds a threshold — critical for voice agents where sub-2-second is the target. Agent Escalation Rate alerts fire at more than 10 fallbacks per 5-minute window, indicating systemic routing failure. Error Volume alerts fire at more than 25 errors per 5-minute window, indicating platform-level issues. All thresholds are configurable and should be calibrated relative to expected traffic volume before go-live.

objectives.title: Apply a systematic diagnostic approach to the most common Agentforce agent failure modes.

topics.question: How do you diagnose Pattern A: Wrong subagent routing?
topics.answer: This pattern presents when a user asks about one topic but the agent routes to an incorrect subagent. Start at the LLMStep for the routing turn, checking tools_sent to confirm all transition actions are listed. If a transition action is absent from tools_sent, its 'available when' condition is blocking it. If all transition actions are visible but the wrong one was selected, the subagent descriptions are ambiguous or overlap. Add disambiguation language that explicitly excludes the topic handled by the other subagent — exclusive phrasing on each description is more reliable than relying on the model to infer the boundary from inclusive descriptions alone.

topics.question: How do you diagnose Pattern B: Action not firing despite being expected?
topics.answer: First check the EnabledToolsStep — if the expected action is absent, the action's 'available when' guard isn't being met. Cross-reference the guard condition against the NodeEntryStateStep to see which variable values were present and identify which condition failed. If the action is listed in enabled tools but wasn't called, the action's description doesn't match the user's phrasing closely enough for model recognition. Fix: relax or restructure the guard condition (first case), or strengthen the action description with trigger keywords from actual utterances (second case).

topics.question: How do you diagnose Pattern C: Behavioral loop repeating the same question?
topics.answer: Examine repeated LLMStep entries across consecutive turns and check messages_sent for the instruction triggering the repeated question. The typical root cause is an instruction evaluating a variable condition rather than checking conversation history. When the variable hasn't been explicitly set by a prior action, the condition always evaluates as true and the question fires again regardless of what the user said. Restructure instructions to treat conversation history as the authoritative source, and use slot-filling patterns with the '...' input syntax rather than requiring explicit variable assignment.

topics.question: How do you diagnose Pattern D: Terminal 'unexpected error' response?
topics.answer: The 'I apologize, but I encountered an unexpected error' message fires only when grounding fails twice consecutively. Find the consecutive pair of ReasoningStep entries both showing UNGROUNDED status and examine the preceding FunctionStep. Two root causes: (1) the action executed successfully but the model embellished or paraphrased beyond what the data supports — fix with verbatim-usage instructions; (2) the action returned an error or empty data, leaving nothing to ground against — fix the backing code to return valid data rather than throwing exceptions on edge-case inputs.

topics.question: How do you diagnose Pattern E: Action returns data but response is generic?
topics.answer: A FunctionStep shows successful execution with data, but the agent's reply is generic. Examine the LLMStep following the FunctionStep — if the model invoked a different tool or generated a response without referencing the action output, the instructions don't explicitly direct the model to use specific output fields. Update reasoning instructions to name specific fields by reference using {{!@actions.ActionName.fieldName}} syntax, creating an explicit connection between action output and expected response content. Generic responses ignoring action data are almost always an instruction authoring gap, not a data retrieval failure.

topics.question: How do you diagnose Pattern F: Latency complaint with no visible errors?
topics.answer: The agent responds successfully, actions complete with OK status, no alerts fired — but users report slowness. This requires Agent Platform Tracing. Query ssot__TelemetryTraceSpan__dlm with the performance-by-operation-type query to identify which operation type has elevated average duration. Drill into span attributes, specifically db.rows_affected and db.operation.name. A high db.rows_affected value (e.g., several thousand rows on what should be a targeted lookup) indicates the backing query is unfiltered or missing a LIMIT clause. The model then processes a large dataset, creating downstream LLM latency that traces record as success while Platform Tracing reveals the data volume problem.

objectives.title: Use a structured fix reference to match symptoms to remediation strategies.

topics.question: What is the fix strategy matrix for mapping symptoms to configuration targets?
topics.answer: The fix mapping: Subagent not matched → update the subagent's description field with trigger keywords from the failing utterance. Action not invoked → make the action's description in reasoning.actions more trigger-specific. Action blocked by guard → relax or restructure the 'available when' condition to match the variable state present when the action should be invocable. Two actions overlap → update both description fields with mutual exclusion language. Grounding failure (UNGROUNDED) → add explicit output references in reasoning: instructions: -> block. Low safety score → add explicit safety guidelines and scope boundary definitions in system: instructions block.

objectives.title: Understand the differences in tracing approach between sandbox and production environments.

topics.question: What are the key differences between sandbox and production observability configuration?
topics.answer: Observability configuration is not automatically inherited from sandbox to production. In sandbox, the primary tracing tool is the CLI preview generating local trace files that are ephemeral and practical for manual review at low volume. In production, primary surfaces are Data Cloud STDM tables and Platform Tracing DMOs requiring queries — the only scalable approach at high session volume. Platform Tracing must be enabled separately in each org. Alert thresholds are not typically configured in sandbox but must be configured before production go-live. Credit consumption occurs in both environments for live action execution — simulated mode is the only way to avoid costs during iterative development.

topics.question: How can Platform Tracing be deployed via metadata instead of manual Setup steps?
topics.answer: Agent Platform Tracing can be enabled as a metadata deployment via the AgentforcePlatformTracingSettings custom metadata type with an isEnabled field. Deploying this metadata in the same pipeline stage as agent metadata ensures Platform Tracing is always enabled in target environments without depending on a manual step that may be missed. This is consistent with best practices for configuration that affects observability: if a setting affects production behavior, it should be version-controlled and deployed as metadata rather than configured ad-hoc.

topics.question: What is the recommended sequence for transitioning from sandbox to production monitoring?
topics.answer: Best practices recommend: (1) Verify Platform Tracing is enabled in production by confirming the metadata deployment or Setup toggle. (2) Confirm Data Cloud DMO accessibility by running the DataKnowledgeSpace verification query and checking permission set assignments. (3) Seed baseline metrics during the first 48 hours of production traffic — dashboards need real data before alerts can be meaningfully calibrated. (4) Configure all alert thresholds relative to expected traffic volume before launch. (5) Transition the team from individual local trace file review to query-based STDM queries as the primary diagnostic workflow. The sandbox habit of opening individual trace files does not scale at production volumes of hundreds or thousands of sessions per day.

objectives.title: Translate technical observability metrics into business KPIs and executive-facing outcomes.

topics.question: How do you map technical metrics to business KPIs for executive reporting?
topics.answer: Key mappings: Deflection rate from ssot__AiAgentSession__dlm maps to cost-per-interaction reduction. Escalation rate maps to agent quality and user trust for CX leadership. Action span duration from ssot__TelemetryTraceSpan__dlm maps to time-to-resolution and UX quality. Error volume by operation type maps to IT operations efficiency and MTTR. Token usage per session from AiAgentGenerativeAiUsage_std__dlm maps to AI cost-per-transaction for finance. Safety score distribution from PlannerResponseStep.safetyScore maps to brand risk and compliance posture. User feedback from GenAIFeedback__dlm maps to NPS and user satisfaction for CX leadership.

topics.question: How do you build a quantitative ROI case using observability data?
topics.answer: Five steps: (1) Establish the human cost baseline by querying historical case volume and average handle time. (2) Measure genuine deflection rate using a quality-corrected query — counting only sessions where an action executed successfully and no escalation occurred. (3) Calculate cost avoidance by multiplying genuine deflections by the difference between human cost per interaction and AI credit cost per session. (4) Use Platform Tracing latency data to surface efficiency gains from action optimization, expressed as reductions in time-to-resolution. (5) Track error span trends over time to demonstrate reliability improvements. These five data points constitute a defensible ROI narrative built entirely from observability data.

topics.question: How does latency connect to cost-per-interaction as a business metric?
topics.answer: Action span duration is both a performance metric and a cost driver. In voice agent deployments where sub-2-second response is the threshold for natural conversation, sessions exceeding this have measurably higher probability of escalation or abandonment. An abandoned interaction escalating to a human costs significantly more than a genuinely deflected one. Quantify this by pulling the distribution of span durations, identifying sessions above the 2,000-millisecond threshold, and cross-referencing against escalation status. If strong correlation exists between above-threshold latency and escalation, each 100-millisecond reduction translates to measurable decrease in escalation rate and corresponding cost reduction.

objectives.title: Understand credit consumption patterns and apply cost-aware debugging practices.

topics.question: What are the credit consumption rules by operation type?
topics.answer: Framework operations are free: @utils.transition, @utils.setVariables, @utils.escalate, if/else control flow, before_reasoning/after_reasoning hooks — all execute deterministically without LLM involvement. The LLM reasoning turn itself is also free; credits apply to actions invoked as a result of reasoning. Flow actions cost 20 credits per execution. Apex actions cost 20 credits per execution. Any other action type also costs 20 credits. Prompt Template actions cost 2-16 credits depending on complexity. A session with five action executions costs 100 credits in live mode. Simulated preview avoids these costs because no real actions execute.

topics.question: What are cost-aware debugging practices to minimize credit expenditure?
topics.answer: Use simulated mode for all instruction authoring and routing iteration since it generates fake outputs at no credit cost. Reserve live preview for grounding validation, variable-driven branching verification, and final behavioral testing before go-live. An escalation spike alert at >10 fallbacks per 5 minutes represents both a UX problem and unplanned credit consumption if the fallback path involves action retries — each failed action call still costs 20 credits. Actions exceeding Apex governor limits appear as FunctionStep errors and represent 20 credits consumed per failed call. Optimizing actions to stay within governor limits has both performance and cost benefits.

objectives.title: Distinguish between currently available features and roadmap items, and communicate limitations accurately.

topics.question: What observability features are currently available in production?
topics.answer: Currently available: out-of-the-box Tableau Next dashboards for consumption and agent analytics; session-level trace files via the CLI preview; Agent Platform Tracing via ssot__TelemetryTraceSpan__dlm requiring manual enablement; Data Cloud STDM tables for custom query-based dashboards; Einstein Trust Layer audit trail DMOs when data streams are explicitly enabled; safety scoring on every agent response via PlannerResponseStep.safetyScore; and Slackbot integration for natural language trace queries requiring manual canvas configuration. Practitioners should verify features referenced in stakeholder conversations are confirmed available in the current release.

topics.question: What capabilities are on the roadmap and what are the current workarounds?
topics.answer: Roadmap items with current workarounds: Error Rate Metric Splitting (approximated by manually querying and categorizing errors from ssot__AiAgentInteractionStep__dlm). Latency Split Tracking (approximated by extracting ssot__DurationNumber__c from individual spans). Custom Evaluations using LLM-as-a-Judge for semantic conflict detection (requires custom queries with manual pattern detection). Spend and consumption reporting within agent analytics (approximated by cross-referencing AiAgentGenerativeAiUsage_std__dlm with session data). Sentiment analysis and RAG quality metrics are not available without custom external pipelines.

topics.question: How should roadmap limitations be framed in stakeholder conversations?
topics.answer: Effective framing: (1) Acknowledge what is available today with specificity — real-time escalation rate monitoring, session-level execution traces, and back-end performance profiling down to individual Apex and Flow invocations. (2) Acknowledge what is coming without committing to a delivery timeline — granular error categorization and latency split reporting by subagent are on the roadmap. (3) Bridge the gap — custom queries against the STDM tables can approximate both capabilities today while native implementation arrives. This approach maintains credibility with technical stakeholders while setting realistic expectations for what requires custom development versus what will eventually be configuration.
